courses.title: First Steps with Mia
courses.promise: You can tune and hold the guitar comfortably, read tab and chord boxes, change cleanly between 14 open chords plus F and Bm while strumming steady patterns in 4/4, 3/4 and 6/8, play melodies, riffs, power chords and a 12-bar blues shuffle, improvise a solo with A minor pentatonic, play along with other people, and keep a daily practice habit.

units.title: Hello, guitar
units.goal: Hold the guitar comfortably, tune it, make clear sounds with thumb and pick, and play your first tune.

lessons.title: Meet your guitar
lessons.goal: Name the parts of the guitar you will use and find any string by its number, from 1 (thinnest) to 6 (thickest).
lessons.explain: The strings run from the tuning pegs on the headstock, over the nut, along the neck and its metal frets, to the bridge on the body; you play them over the soundhole or the pickups. They are numbered from the thinnest, string 1, to the thickest, string 6, which is the one nearest your face when you hold the guitar. A string played with no finger on it is an open string, and today open strings are all you need.
lessons.show: Fretboard figure, frets 0 to 3, with the six open strings dotted and labelled by number and name: the open string 6 (E), the open string 5 (A), the open string 4 (D), the open string 3 (G), the open string 2 (B), the open string 1 (E); audio plays them from string 6 (E2) up to string 1 (E4). A labelled drawing of the whole guitar (headstock, pegs, nut, frets, neck, body, soundhole or pickups, bridge) belongs here; see gaps.
practice: Lesson: match-pairs of guitar parts and their jobs (pegs tune the strings, frets change the note, the bridge holds the strings), then true-false: string 1 is the thickest string (false).

Mic (play-note): with the guitar on your lap, pluck each open string with your thumb as Mia names it by number (6, 3, 1, 5, 2, 4); the microphone checks you chose the right one (E2 A2 D3 G3 B3 E4). Without a microphone: fretboard-find, tap that string on the neck.

Player: play along with bars 1 to 4 of the Open-String Duet (a bar is a group of four beats, the steady pulse you could tap your foot to): only the open string 6 (E), one thumb stroke per beat, while the app plays the tune above you. That is your first music.

lessons.title: Sitting and holding
lessons.goal: Sit with the guitar balanced and relaxed, both hands in place, and play the whole Open-String Duet with your thumb.
lessons.explain: Rest the guitar's waist on your right thigh (left thigh if you play left-handed), with the neck pointing slightly up, your back upright and your shoulders down. Your fretting thumb rests behind the neck, roughly opposite your middle finger, and your picking forearm lies over the top edge of the body so the hand falls naturally over the strings. Every few minutes, freeze and check your jaw, shoulders and thumb for tension: sore fingertips in the first weeks are normal, but aching joints, numbness or sharp pain are not, so stop and rest.
lessons.show: Posture checklist card (thigh, neck angle, back, shoulders, fretting thumb, picking forearm) with a side-view posture drawing (see gaps); then the tab of the Open-String Duet: the open string 6 for bars 1 to 4, the open string 5 for bars 5 to 8, the open string 4 for bars 9 to 12, then E A D E, with audio of the teacher part.
practice: Lesson: go through the posture checklist one item at a time and tap each one when it is true; then hold the position, relaxed, for one minute while a timer runs.
Metronome: at 60 bpm (60 beats per minute, one click a second), play the open string 6 (E) with your thumb on every click for 8 clicks, then the open string 5 (A), then the open string 4 (D).

Player: the whole Open-String Duet at 60 bpm with the app playing the chords and melody; the microphone listens for each of your notes. Without a microphone the Player still plays along; count the beats aloud.

lessons.title: Tuning up
lessons.goal: Tune all six strings to E A D G B E with the Tuner, finishing each one by tightening up to the note.
lessons.explain: Strings drift out of tune every day, so tuning is the first thing you do whenever you pick up the guitar. Pluck one string and read the Tuner: flat means too low (tighten the peg a little), sharp means too high (loosen it). Finish by tightening up to the note: if you go past it, drop below and come back up, because a string brought up to pitch tends to stay there.
lessons.show: The Tuner in standard tuning, string by string: string 6 E2, string 5 A2, string 4 D3, string 3 G3, string 2 B3, string 1 E4; a fretboard figure of the six open strings; audio of each reference tone.
practice: Tuner: tune string 6 to E, then strings 5 to 1, until each one shows in tune. Without a microphone, play the Tuner's reference tone for each string and turn the peg until your string and the tone stop wobbling against each other.
Tuner: loosen string 3 a little on purpose, then bring it back up to G; do the same on string 1, so you learn which way each peg turns.
Mic (play-note): play the six open strings once more; the lesson moves on when all six are in tune. Without a microphone, choose in tune or out of tune for six recorded strings (listen-choice).
Player: play the Open-String Duet again, in tune, and hear how much better your notes blend with the app.

lessons.title: Holding the pick
lessons.goal: Hold a pick and play even downstrokes, then down-up strokes, on each open string in time with the metronome.
lessons.explain: Hold the pick between the pad of your thumb and the side of your index finger near its tip, with just 2 to 3 mm showing. The motion is a small one from the wrist, like flicking a drop of water off your hand, not a swing from the elbow. Strike one string and stop just past it; then try down-up: down on the click, up halfway between clicks, with the pick passing back through the same string.
lessons.show: Tab snippet: one bar of the open string 6 in quarter notes marked with downstroke signs, then one bar of the open string 1 in eighth notes marked down, up, down, up; audio at 60 bpm.
practice: Metronome: at 60 bpm, four downstrokes per bar on the open string 6 for 4 bars, then 4 bars on each string from 5 to 1; aim for the same loudness every time.
Mic (play-phrase): 8 downstrokes on the open string 3 (G) with the click; the microphone checks they are on the beat. Without a microphone: tap-rhythm, tap the 8 beats on screen.
Technique: Alternate Picking on Open Strings at 60 bpm: down-up eighths on string 1, then strings 2 to 6; go up 4 bpm only after two clean passes in a row.
Player: the Open-String Duet again, this time with the pick.

lessons.title: Your first tune: Hot Cross Buns
lessons.goal: Press clean notes on string 3 and play Hot Cross Buns from tab, first in wait mode and then in time.
lessons.explain: Press with the very tip of the finger just behind the fret wire, on the side nearer the body: not on top of the wire and not in the middle of the space. Use just enough pressure for a clear note; if it buzzes, move closer to the wire or press a little harder, and if it sounds muffled, curve the finger so it stands up on its tip. Hot Cross Buns uses three notes on string 3, B at fret 4, A at fret 2 and the open G; in tab each string has a line, the numbers on it are the frets to press, and 0 means open.
lessons.show: Tab of Hot Cross Buns (version A), all on string 3: 4 2 0 | 4 2 0 | 0 0 2 2 | 4 2 0, using string 3 fret 4 (B) for finger 3, string 3 fret 2 (A) for finger 1 and the open string 3 (G); a fretboard figure of the hand in second position (finger 1 over fret 2, finger 3 over fret 4). Audio at 72 bpm.
practice: Mic (play-note): play each note alone until it rings clearly: string 3 fret 4 (B3) with finger 3, string 3 fret 2 (A3) with finger 1, the open string 3 (G3). Without a microphone: fretboard-find, tap where each note is.
Player, wait mode: the tab waits until you play each right note, so take all the time you need. Then Player loop: the 4 bars at 60 bpm with the teacher part, then at 72.
Player: version B, where bar 3 becomes eight eighth notes (G G G G A A A A); count 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & aloud and play it at 60 bpm.
Player: bars 1 to 4 of First Notes on String 3, the open G and A at string 3 fret 2 (A), in wait mode; its second half crosses to strings 2 and 1, so it waits until you know them.

lessons.title: Your first-week show
lessons.goal: Play Hot Cross Buns and the Open-String Duet start to finish with the app's band, keeping going through any mistake.
lessons.explain: Musicians have one rule when the band is playing: keep going. If a note goes wrong, let it go and come back in on the next beat; nobody remembers a wrong note, but everybody notices a stop. Today you play two whole pieces from start to finish, and from now on every session starts with tuning and a five-minute warm-up.
lessons.show: Both tabs side by side (Hot Cross Buns on string 3, the Open-String Duet on strings 6, 5 and 4) and a four-click count-in.
practice: Tuner: tune all six strings.
Technique: the Five-Minute Warm-Up (open-string picking, a slow finger exercise, an easy change); from now on it starts every session.
Player: Hot Cross Buns at 72 bpm with the teacher part, start to finish in normal mode (not wait mode); the microphone listens, and about 8 notes in 10 right and on time is a pass.
Player: the Open-String Duet with the pick at 72 bpm, start to finish.
Practice Plan: set a daily goal you can keep (10 minutes is plenty to begin) and choose the time of day you will play.

units.title: Your first chords
units.goal: Read a chord box, play Em, E, Am, A, E7 and a one-finger G, and strum your first songs with them.

lessons.title: Chord boxes and your first chord, Em
lessons.goal: Read a chord box and play a ringing Em chord with four steady downstrums per bar.
lessons.explain: A chord is several notes played together, and a chord box is a picture of where your fingers go: the vertical lines are the strings with string 6 on the left, the horizontal lines are frets, the thick top line is the nut, the numbers in the dots are fingers (1 index, 2 middle, 3 ring, 4 little), o means play the string open and x means leave it out. Em is the friendliest first chord: two fingers at fret 2 and all six strings ring. Arch your fingers so each one touches only its own string.
lessons.show: Chord box of Em (022000) with finger 2 on string 5 fret 2 (B) and finger 3 on string 4 fret 2 (E), beside the same two dots on a horizontal fretboard figure so the two views connect; audio of Em strummed, then picked string by string.
practice: Lesson: chord-build, place the two fingers of Em on an empty chord box; then choice: which strings does Em play? (all six).
Mic (play-chord): play Em one string at a time from 6 to 1 so every note rings, then strum it; the microphone checks the chord. Without a microphone: chord-build again, from memory.
Metronome: 60 bpm, four downstrums per bar on Em for 4 bars, which are bars 1 to 4 of Strumming: Steady Quarters. Keep the strumming hand going even if the chord is not perfect yet.

lessons.title: E and Am: one shape, two chords
lessons.goal: Turn Em into E by adding one finger, slide that shape one string over to make Am, and change between the three in time.
lessons.explain: E is Em plus one finger: keep fingers 2 and 3 where they are and add finger 1 on string 3 fret 1 (G#), and the dark Em turns bright. Now move the whole E shape one string toward string 1 without changing it: finger 2 on string 4 fret 2 (E), finger 3 on string 3 fret 2 (A) and finger 1 on string 2 fret 1 (C) make Am, strummed from string 5 with string 6 left out. One shape that moves to make a new chord is the first secret of how the guitar works.
lessons.show: Chord boxes of Em (022000), E (022100) and Am (x02210) in a row, with the added finger circled in E and the whole shape drawn sliding one string over for Am; audio of Em then E, so you hear one note (G to G#) brighten the chord, then Am.
practice: Mic (play-chord): E (022100), then Am (x02210), first string by string and then strummed; for Am, start the strum on string 5. Without a microphone: chord-build for each.
Chords: change trainer, Em to E and then E to Am, one change every 4 beats at 60 bpm for one minute each; the microphone counts your clean changes.
Player: Change: Am-E and E-B7, the Am-E half only, at 60 bpm (one strum per bar, then two, then four, then a change every 2 beats); B7 comes later.

Player: the first 8 bars of the Open-String Duet with the parts swapped: you strum Em for bars 1 to 4 and Am for bars 5 to 8, four downstrums per bar, while the app plays the open strings and the tune.

lessons.title: One finger, one song: Frere Jacques
lessons.goal: Strum a one-finger G on strings 4 to 1 and accompany Frere Jacques all the way through without stopping.
lessons.explain: This G uses one finger: finger 3 on string 1 fret 3 (G), with strings 4, 3 and 2 open, and you strum only strings 4 to 1 (the x over strings 6 and 5 means miss them). Aim the pick at string 4 and let the strum stop after string 1. A whole round can be played on this one chord, so all your attention can go into a steady beat.
lessons.show: Chord box of the one-finger G (xx0003) with x over strings 6 and 5; a rhythm line of four quarter-note downstrums per bar; audio of Frere Jacques sung by the app over the strummed G.
practice: Mic (play-chord): strum G (xx0003) four times; the microphone checks you play strings 4 to 1 and not the low strings. Without a microphone: choice, which strings does this G use? (4 to 1).
Player: Frere Jacques at 76 bpm: four downstrums per bar for all 8 bars while the app sings the tune; then at 88 bpm.
Player: a second pass as a round: keep strumming while two app voices sing it in canon, the second entering after 2 bars.

lessons.title: The A chord and your first change
lessons.goal: Play an A chord with three fingers side by side and switch between Em and A while strumming in time.
lessons.explain: A puts three fingers in a row at fret 2: finger 1 on string 4, finger 2 on string 3 and finger 3 on string 2, squeezed in so each one sits just behind the fret; strum from string 5 and miss string 6. Changing chords is a skill of its own: look at the next chord before you need it, move all the fingers together, and it is fine to strum open strings for the last beat while your hand travels. The beat matters more than the chord.
lessons.show: Chord box of A (x02220) with fingers 1-2-3 on strings 4-3-2; a second box with the 2-1-3 fingering for wide fingertips; the strum chart of Strumming: Steady Quarters (Em 4 bars, A 4 bars, twice).
practice: Mic (play-chord): play A (x02220) string by string, then strum it; the microphone checks all five strings ring. Without a microphone: chord-build.
Chords: change trainer, Em to A and back, one change every 4 beats at 60 bpm for one minute; the microphone counts your clean changes.
Player: Strumming: Steady Quarters, all 16 bars (Em, A, Em, A) at 60 bpm with an accent (a slightly louder strum) on beat 1; then at 64.

lessons.title: E7 and the change that lands on the beat
lessons.goal: Play E7 and change cleanly between A and E7 on the beat.
lessons.explain: E7 needs just two fingers: finger 2 on string 5 fret 2 (B) and finger 1 on string 3 fret 1 (G#), with every string ringing. No finger can stay down between A and E7, so practise the shapes in the air: lift all the fingers together and land them together. The rule from now on: the change lands on the beat, even if the strum just before it has to be on open strings.
lessons.show: Chord boxes of A (x02220) and E7 (020100) side by side with the finger moves drawn as arrows; the rhythm plan of Change: A and E7 (one strum per bar, then two, then four, then a change every 2 beats).
practice: Mic (play-chord): E7 (020100) string by string, then strummed. Without a microphone: chord-build.
Away from the guitar: form the E7 shape in the air above the neck 5 times, then the A shape, then switch between them with your eyes closed.
Player: Change: A and E7 at 60 bpm, the 8-bar plan twice (a change every 2 bars, every bar, then every 2 beats).
Chords: one-minute changes, A to E7, one strum per beat; the trainer keeps your score, which is your first personal best.

lessons.title: Skip to My Lou
lessons.goal: Strum and sing (or hum) Skip to My Lou with A and E7, changing on time.
lessons.explain: Skip to My Lou has two beats in a bar (2/4) and only two chords, A and E7, changing every two bars. Strum one downstroke per beat and sing the words; if singing and strumming together feels impossible, that is normal: hum first, then speak the words in rhythm, then sing. Slow the tempo (the speed of the beat) until every change lands on time, then speed up.
lessons.show: Chord chart in 2/4: A for line 1, E7 for line 2, A for line 3, E7 then A for the last line, with the two chord boxes above it; audio of the song at 80 bpm.
practice: Player: the song at 80 bpm with the chord chart while the app sings; you strum one downstroke per beat.
Player: again at 80 bpm with only the backing while you hum the tune; then speak the words in rhythm; then sing.
Player: raise the tempo by 4 bpm per pass toward 100 bpm; stop raising it when a change is late and stay there for two clean passes.

lessons.title: Your first songbook
lessons.goal: Play Em, E, Am, A, E7 and the one-finger G from memory and play your two chord songs at full speed.
lessons.explain: Chords stick when you recall them, not when you look them up, so today Mia asks for each shape from memory. Then you play your first songbook: Frere Jacques and Skip to My Lou. One song you can really play is worth three you almost can.
lessons.show: Six empty chord boxes to fill in (Em, E, Am, A, E7, G), then the two songs' chord charts.
practice: Lesson: chord-build from memory for Em (022000), E (022100), Am (x02210), A (x02220), E7 (020100) and the one-finger G (xx0003); then choice, name each shape from its picture.
Mic (play-chord): Mia names a chord and you play it, four in a row. Without a microphone: chord-build for each one.
Chords: one-minute changes, A to E7, Em to A and E to Am; try to beat last time's score.
Player: Frere Jacques at 88 bpm and Skip to My Lou at 100 bpm, start to finish.

units.title: Melodies from tab
units.goal: Read tab together with its rhythm and play well-known melodies on the top three strings.

lessons.title: Tab and its rhythm
lessons.goal: Read tab and its rhythm: which string, which fret, and how long each note lasts.
lessons.explain: In tab the top line is string 1, the thinnest, and the bottom line is string 6, so it looks upside down until you hold the guitar and look down at the strings. A number is a fret and 0 is an open string. Plain tab does not show how long notes last, so the app's tab adds stems like sheet music, and the best habit is to listen first: hear the tune, then read it.
lessons.show: Tab of the first 4 bars of Au Clair de la Lune on strings 3 and 2 (G G G A | B as a half note, A as a half note | G B A A | G as a whole note), using the open string 3 (G), string 3 fret 2 (A) and the open string 2 (B), with rhythm stems and the counts under it; audio at 80 bpm.
practice: Lesson: choice, Mia shows a number on a tab line and you choose the string and fret it stands for; then tap-rhythm, tap bar 2 (two half notes).
Player, wait mode: Au Clair de la Lune, the first 4 bars.
Player: the same 4 bars at 80 bpm with the teacher part, counting quarter notes aloud.

lessons.title: Notes on strings 1 and 2
lessons.goal: Play E, F and G on string 1 and B, C and D on string 2 with one finger per fret.
lessons.explain: One finger per fret: finger 1 plays fret 1 and finger 3 plays fret 3, so the hand stays still and the fingers do the work. On string 1 the open string is E, string 1 fret 1 (F) and string 1 fret 3 (G); on string 2 the open string is B, string 2 fret 1 (C) and string 2 fret 3 (D). E to F and B to C are only one fret apart: they are the two places in the musical alphabet with no note in between.
lessons.show: Fretboard figure, frets 0 to 3: the open string 1 (E), string 1 fret 1 (F) for finger 1, string 1 fret 3 (G) for finger 3; the open string 2 (B), string 2 fret 1 (C) for finger 1, string 2 fret 3 (D) for finger 3; the tabs of the two First Notes studies.
practice: Mic (play-note): Mia names a note among E F G B C D and you play it, 8 in a row. Without a microphone: fretboard-find.
Player, wait mode, then at 72 bpm: First Notes on String 1 with the teacher's chords.
Player: First Notes on String 2, where bars 5 to 8 cross between strings 2 and 1.
Player: First Notes on String 3 again, all 8 bars: bars 5 to 8 cross strings 3, 2 and 1 with the notes you have just learned.
Technique: Chromatic Spider (1-2-3-4) at 50 bpm, on one string only, to wake up all four fingers.

lessons.title: Mary Had a Little Lamb
lessons.goal: Play Mary Had a Little Lamb on strings 3 and 2, crossing between the strings without a gap.
lessons.explain: This tune lives on two strings: the open string 3 (G), string 3 fret 2 (A) with finger 2, the open string 2 (B) and string 2 fret 3 (D) with finger 3. The tricky moment is crossing from string 3 to string 2: keep the pick movement small and close to the strings so it has less distance to travel. Play steady quarter notes, like walking.
lessons.show: Tab of all 8 bars (B A G A | B B B | A A A | B D D | B A G A | B B B B | A A B A | G) on strings 3 and 2, with a fretboard figure of the four notes and their fingers; audio at 96 bpm.
practice: Player, wait mode: the whole tune.
Player loop: bars 3 and 4 (A A A, then B D D), the string crossing, at 72 bpm until it is smooth.
Player: the whole tune at 80 bpm with the teacher part (G, with D7 in bars 3 and 7), then at 96.
Player: a second tune on the same two strings, Lightly Row, which adds C at string 2 fret 1 (C) for finger 1: wait mode, then at 72 and 88 bpm.

lessons.title: Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star
lessons.goal: Play Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star on three strings, including the jump from G up to D.
lessons.explain: Twinkle uses six notes across strings 3, 2 and 1: open G, A at fret 2, open B, C at fret 1, D at fret 3 and open E. Its first move is a jump of a fifth, from the open G to D on string 2 (a fifth because G to D spans five letter names, G A B C D), so practise just that jump until your pick lands on string 2 without looking. The tune has an A B A shape: the first line comes back at the end.
lessons.show: Tab of the 12 bars in G (G G D D | E E D | C C B B | A A G | D D C C | B B A, that line twice, then the first 4 bars again), using the open string 3 (G), string 3 fret 2 (A), the open string 2 (B), string 2 fret 1 (C), string 2 fret 3 (D) and the open string 1 (E); audio at 92 bpm.
practice: Mic (play-phrase): just the jump, G G D D, five times; the microphone checks you land on D. Without a microphone: the Player in wait mode on bar 1.
Player, wait mode, then at 72 bpm with the teacher's chords (G, C, D7).
Player: at 92 bpm, start to finish.
Player: London Bridge, two beats in a bar, with its short dotted rhythm on the word London: wait mode, then at 80 and 92 bpm.

lessons.title: Ode to Joy
lessons.goal: Play the Ode to Joy theme with its dotted rhythm, including the low open D.
lessons.explain: Beethoven's theme moves almost entirely by step, one note to the next, on strings 3 and 2 through G, A, B, C and D. Its famous rhythm comes at the end of the first line: B held for a beat and a half (a dotted quarter), A short, then A held. Count 1 2 & 3 4: B on 1, the short A on the and of 2, the long A on 3.
lessons.show: Tab of the 16-bar theme in A A B A form on strings 3 and 2 with the open string 4 (D) for the low D, using string 3 fret 2 (A), string 2 fret 1 (C) and string 2 fret 3 (D); a rhythm line of the dotted quarter, eighth and half note; audio at 96 bpm.
practice: Rhythm: tap the rhythm of bar 4 (dotted quarter, eighth, half) along with the click until it feels natural.
Player, wait mode for the whole theme, then Player loop: phrase B (with the B-C eighth notes and the low D) at 72 bpm.
Player: the whole theme at 80, then 96 bpm, with the teacher part (G and D).

lessons.title: Melody recital
lessons.goal: Play three melodies in a row with the band, then add the Jingle Bells chorus as an encore.
lessons.explain: A recital is playing songs one after another without restarting, and that is a different skill from practising one song. Tune, take a breath, count in, and treat each mistake as a speed bump, not a stop sign. Jingle Bells is your encore: it sits on strings 3 and 2 with lots of repeated notes, so it is quick to learn and fun to play.
lessons.show: Set list card: Mary Had a Little Lamb, Twinkle Twinkle, Ode to Joy; then the tab of the Jingle Bells chorus on strings 3 and 2, using the open string 3 (G), string 3 fret 2 (A), the open string 2 (B), string 2 fret 1 (C) and string 2 fret 3 (D).
practice: Tuner: tune up.
Player: the three melodies back to back at their target tempos (96, 92 and 96 bpm) with the band; the microphone listens to each one, and about 8 notes in 10 right and on time is a pass.
Player, wait mode, then at 84 and 100 bpm: the Jingle Bells chorus with the teacher's chords.

units.title: D, A7 and the steady beat
units.goal: Count and keep a steady beat, add D and A7, strum down-up eighth notes and feel waltz time.

lessons.title: Counting the beat
lessons.goal: Count 1 2 3 4 out loud while strumming quarter notes with the metronome, and keep going when you slip.
lessons.explain: The beat is the steady pulse you tap your foot to, and the tempo is how fast it goes, in beats per minute (bpm). Music in 4/4 groups the beats in fours, so you count 1 2 3 4, 1 2 3 4, with a little more weight on 1. Counting out loud feels silly for a week, and then it becomes the thing that holds every song together.
lessons.show: Rhythm line of a 4/4 bar of quarter notes counted 1 2 3 4, then a bar of two half notes (1 2, 3 4) and a bar with one whole note; metronome at 70 bpm with the first beat of each bar accented.
practice: Rhythm: tap quarter notes with the click for 30 seconds; the click then drops out for 4 beats and comes back: are you still with it?
Lesson: tap-rhythm, a bar of half notes, then a bar mixing quarter notes and a half note.
Metronome: 70 bpm, accent on 1: Strumming: Steady Quarters (Em and A) while counting aloud; raise to 80 when it is steady.

lessons.title: The D chord
lessons.goal: Play a D chord on strings 4 to 1 and change between Em and D on the beat.
lessons.explain: D is a little triangle: finger 1 on string 3 fret 2 (A), finger 3 on string 2 fret 3 (D) and finger 2 on string 1 fret 2 (F#). Strum only strings 4 to 1: start the strum on the open string 4 and miss strings 6 and 5. Em to D is a big move, so look at the D triangle before the change and put finger 3 down first; the others fall in around it.
lessons.show: Chord box of D (xx0232) with x over strings 6 and 5; chord boxes of Em (022000) and D side by side for the change; audio of D strummed on strings 4 to 1 and then on all six (the muddy version), so you hear why the x matters.
practice: Mic (play-chord): D string by string, then strummed on strings 4 to 1. Without a microphone: chord-build.
Technique: Strum Only the Right Strings, the D and A bars only (D on strings 4 to 1, A on strings 5 to 1), aiming the first strum at the right string; the E bars come in a later lesson.
Player: Change: Em-D and Em-G, the Em-D half only, at 60 bpm (one strum per bar, then two, then four, then a change every 2 beats).
Chords: one-minute changes, Em to D; note your score.

lessons.title: Down-up eighth notes
lessons.goal: Strum steady down-up eighth notes, down on the beat and up on the and, on Em and D.
lessons.explain: Eighth notes split each beat in two: 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 &. Your strumming hand swings like a pendulum, down on every number and up on every &, and it never stops, not even while you change chord. Upstrums catch just the top three or four strings, and that lighter sound is right.
lessons.show: Rhythm line of eighth notes with arrows, down on 1 2 3 4 and up on each &; the strum chart of Strumming: Down-Up Eighths (Em 2 bars, D 2 bars); audio at 70 bpm.
practice: Technique: Constant Strumming Motion on Em at 60 bpm, touching the strings on every down and every up for now.
Rhythm: strum or tap along with eighth notes and say 1 & 2 & aloud; the trainer scores your timing.
Player: Strumming: Down-Up Eighths at 60, then 70 bpm; in the last 8 bars, accent beats 2 and 4.

lessons.title: Drunken Sailor
lessons.goal: Strum Drunken Sailor with Em and D, first with an accent on beat 1, then in down-up eighths.
lessons.explain: This old sea shanty has two beats in a bar and a dark, minor sound, and it lives on Em and D: Em for line 1, D for line 2, Em for line 3, and D then Em for the last line, with the chorus the same. Start with two downstrums per bar and a strong accent on beat 1, like sailors hauling on a rope together. Then switch to down-up eighths.
lessons.show: Chord chart by line (Em, D, Em, then D and Em; the chorus the same) with Em (022000) and D (xx0232) boxes; audio of the song at 80 bpm.
practice: Player: the song at 80 bpm, two downstrums per bar, accent on beat 1.
Player: the same with down-up eighths, at 80 then 96 bpm.
Ear: listen-choice, is this chord Em or D? Eight rounds.

lessons.title: A7 and waltz time
lessons.goal: Play A7 and strum a waltz pattern in 3/4: a bass note on 1, strums on 2 and 3.
lessons.explain: A7 is A with a gap: finger 2 on string 4 fret 2 (E) and finger 3 on string 2 fret 2 (C#), with string 3 left open. Waltz time, 3/4, has three beats in a bar: count 1 2 3, play a single bass note on 1 and strum the higher strings on 2 and 3. Under D the bass note is the open string 4 (D); under A7 it is the open string 5 (A).
lessons.show: Chord boxes of D (xx0232) and A7 (x02020); a rhythm line of one 3/4 bar (bass on 1, downstrums on strings 3 to 1 on 2 and 3); audio of Strumming: Waltz (Bass-Strum-Strum) at 80 bpm.
practice: Mic (play-chord): A7 (x02020), then the D to A7 change four times. Without a microphone: chord-build.
Player: Strumming: Waltz (Bass-Strum-Strum) at 72 bpm, counting 1 2 3 aloud; then at 84.
Player: Change: D-A7 and A-D, both halves, at 60 bpm.
Chords: one-minute changes, D to A7.

lessons.title: Two waltzes
lessons.goal: Play two waltzes, Down in the Valley (A and E7) and Clementine (D and A7), with the bass-strum-strum pattern.
lessons.explain: Both songs are in 3/4, so the bass-strum-strum pattern from the last lesson carries them all the way. Down in the Valley uses A and E7, and the bass note under E7 is the open string 6 (E). Clementine uses D and A7 and starts with a pickup: the singer begins on beat 3, before the first full bar, so you wait and come in with your bass note on the next 1.
lessons.show: Two chord charts in 3/4 (Down in the Valley: A and E7; Clementine: D and A7, with the pickup marked); a rhythm line of the pickup bar; audio of both at 96 bpm.
practice: Player: Down in the Valley at 96, then 108 bpm.
Lesson: tap-rhythm, tap where the singing starts in Clementine (beat 3, before bar 1), then where your first bass note goes (beat 1 of bar 1).
Player: Clementine at 96, then 108 bpm, the chorus and one verse.

units.title: G, C and three-chord songs
units.goal: Add G, C and D7 and play the three main chords of a key in real songs.

lessons.title: The G chord
lessons.goal: Play a full six-string G and change from Em to G keeping one finger down.
lessons.explain: This G stretches across the neck: finger 2 on string 6 fret 3 (G), finger 1 on string 5 fret 2 (B) and finger 3 on string 1 fret 3 (G), with strings 4, 3 and 2 open. From Em, play Em with fingers 1 and 2 instead of 2 and 3: finger 1 then never leaves string 5. It is the anchor, and the other fingers swing around it.
lessons.show: Chord box of G (320003) with fingers 2-1-3; chord boxes of Em (022000) fingered 1 and 2 and of G side by side, with the anchor finger highlighted; audio of the change.
practice: Mic (play-chord): G string by string, listening closely to the open strings 4, 3 and 2, which fingers 1 and 2 must not touch. Without a microphone: chord-build.
Player: Change: Em-D and Em-G, the Em-G half, at 60 bpm.
Chords: one-minute changes, Em to G.

lessons.title: Michael, Row the Boat Ashore
lessons.goal: Strum Michael, Row the Boat Ashore with D, G and A, first in four downstrums per bar, then in down-up eighths.
lessons.explain: This spiritual was sung by enslaved people on the Sea Islands and printed in 1867: one voice sings a line and everyone answers Hallelujah. It uses three chords, D, G and A, the chords built on the 1st, 4th and 5th notes of the D major scale (D E F# G A B C#, the notes of the key in order), which is why they sound like a family. Remember which strings each one uses: D strings 4 to 1, A strings 5 to 1, G all six.
lessons.show: Chord chart with D (xx0232), G (320003) and A (x02220) boxes and the call and response marked; audio at 92 bpm.
practice: Player: the song at 80 bpm, four downstrums per bar; then at 92.
Player: down-up eighths at 92 bpm; sing or hum the Hallelujah response.
Chords: one-minute changes, D to G and G to A.

lessons.title: The C chord
lessons.goal: Play a clean C chord and change between G and C.
lessons.explain: C climbs the neck in steps: finger 3 on string 5 fret 3 (C), finger 2 on string 4 fret 2 (E) and finger 1 on string 2 fret 1 (C), with strings 3 and 1 open and string 6 left out. The usual problem is finger 1 or 2 leaning on the open string 3 or 1, so arch the fingers like a bridge. For G to C, many players switch G to fingers 3, 2 and 4 (3 on string 6, 2 on string 5, 4 on string 1), because then the 3-2 pair keeps its shape and simply moves one string toward string 1.
lessons.show: Chord box of C (x32010); chord boxes of G (320003) fingered 3-2-4 and C, with the 3-2 pair moving across one string; audio of a muffled string 1 next to a clean one.
practice: Mic (play-chord): C string by string from string 5, listening for strings 3 and 1. Without a microphone: chord-build.
Player: Change: G-C and C-G7, the G-C half, at 60 bpm.
Chords: one-minute changes, G to C. This is the hardest change so far; whatever your score is today, it is the number to beat.

lessons.title: D7 and the pull toward home
lessons.goal: Play D7 and change between G and D7 and between D and G.
lessons.explain: D7 is a small slanted triangle: finger 2 on string 3 fret 2 (A), finger 1 on string 2 fret 1 (C) and finger 3 on string 1 fret 2 (F#), strummed on strings 4 to 1. The 7 adds one note, C, that makes the chord lean forward, wanting to move home to G. For D to G, try the four-finger G (320033): finger 3 on string 2 fret 3 (D) stays put through the change.
lessons.show: Chord boxes of D7 (xx0212), G (320003) and the four-finger G (320033); audio comparing D and D7 before G, so you hear the pull of the 7.
practice: Mic (play-chord): D7. Without a microphone: chord-build.
Ear: listen-choice, does the chord sound finished (G) or leaning (D7)? Six rounds.
Player: Change: G-D7 and D-G at 60 bpm, both halves.
Chords: one-minute changes, G to D7 and D to G.

lessons.title: She'll Be Coming 'Round the Mountain
lessons.goal: Play She'll Be Coming 'Round the Mountain with G, C and D7 in down-up eighths with accents on 2 and 4.
lessons.explain: Three chords, G, C and D7, are the I, IV and V7 of G major (roman numerals for the chords built on its 1st, 4th and 5th notes), and together they carry thousands of folk songs. This one goes G for line 1, D7 for line 2, G moving to C for line 3, and G, D7, G for the last line. Accent beats 2 and 4 to give it bounce, and add a verse each time through, the way the song is meant to be sung.
lessons.show: Chord chart by line with G (320003), C (x32010) and D7 (xx0212) boxes; a rhythm line of down-up eighths with accents on 2 and 4; audio at 96 bpm.
practice: Lesson: order, put the chords of each line in order from the chart.
Rhythm: down-up eighths with accents on 2 and 4 along with the trainer.
Player: the song at 84, then 96, then 108 bpm.

lessons.title: Amazing Grace, from memory
lessons.goal: Play Amazing Grace in 3/4 with G, C and D7 from memory: bass on 1, down-up on 2 and 3.
lessons.explain: Amazing Grace is a waltz-time hymn whose melody uses only five notes, and it is the first song you will play without looking at a chart. The pattern is a bass note on 1, then down-up on 2 and down-up on 3. The tune starts with a pickup on beat 3, so count 1 2 and let the singer start on 3; you come in on the next 1.
lessons.show: Chord chart with G (320003), C (x32010), D7 (xx0212) and the optional Em (022000); a rhythm line of bass, down-up, down-up in 3/4; audio at 84 bpm.
practice: Player: with the chart at 72, then 84 bpm.
Player: the chart hidden, from memory; if you get lost, listen for the bass line and come back in on the next bar.
Ear: hum the first note of the melody before you start, and find it on the guitar: it is D, so try the open string 4 (D), a pickup that rises to G.

Player: an encore in the same three chords and the same 3/4: Brahms' Lullaby. First strum G, D7 and C under the app's melody, then swap and play the melody, which runs from the open string 3 (G) up to string 1 fret 3 (G).

units.title: Minor chords, minor songs
units.goal: Add Dm and B7 to Am and E, and use them in minor-key songs.

lessons.title: C to Am: the finger that moves
lessons.goal: Change between C and Am by moving just one finger, and hear major turn to minor.
lessons.explain: You know Am from your first week; today it meets C. Put them side by side: fingers 1 and 2 stay in exactly the same place, string 2 fret 1 (C) and string 4 fret 2 (E), and only finger 3 moves, from string 5 fret 3 (C) to string 3 fret 2 (A). The two chords share two of their three notes, C and E, which is why the change sounds so smooth, and looking for fingers that stay is the secret of every smooth change.
lessons.show: Chord boxes of C (x32010) and Am (x02210) with the two shared fingers highlighted and finger 3's move drawn as an arrow; audio of C and Am, major and minor.
practice: Mic (play-chord): C, then Am, then C again, four times each way, keeping fingers 1 and 2 pressed the whole time. Without a microphone: chord-build for each.
Player: Change: C-Am and Am-Dm, the C-Am half, at 60, then 72 bpm.
Ear: listen-choice, C or Am, major or minor? Eight rounds.

lessons.title: Dm, and E again
lessons.goal: Play Dm, and change from Am to Dm and from Am to E.
lessons.explain: Dm: finger 2 on string 3 fret 2 (A), finger 3 on string 2 fret 3 (D), finger 1 on string 1 fret 1 (F), strummed on strings 4 to 1. From Am to Dm the note on string 3 fret 2 (A) stays, but the finger changes from 3 to 2. E you met in your first week as the Am shape moved one string toward string 6 (finger 2 on string 5 fret 2 (B), finger 3 on string 4 fret 2 (E), finger 1 on string 3 fret 1 (G#)); in songs built around Am, it is the chord that leads back home to Am.
lessons.show: Chord boxes of Am (x02210), Dm (xx0231) and E (022100), with the Am-to-E move shown as the whole shape sliding one string over; audio of E and Em, so you hear one note (G# or G) change the chord from major to minor.
practice: Mic (play-chord): Dm, string by string from string 4 and then strummed. Without a microphone: chord-build.
Player: Change: C-Am and Am-Dm, the Am-Dm half, at 60 bpm; then Change: Am-E and E-B7, the Am-E half.
Chords: one-minute changes, Am to Dm and Am to E.

lessons.title: Go Down, Moses
lessons.goal: Play Go Down, Moses in A minor with Am, Dm and E7, slow and heavy, one strum per beat.
lessons.explain: Go Down, Moses is a spiritual first printed in 1862 as Oh! Let My People Go. It is in A minor, and it uses E7 rather than Em: E7 contains G#, string 3 fret 1 (G#), the note that pulls back up to A and makes the return to Am feel like coming home. Play it slowly, one heavy downstrum per beat.
lessons.show: Chord chart with Am (x02210), Dm (xx0231) and E7 (020100), the G# on string 3 fret 1 highlighted in the E7 box; audio at 72 bpm.
practice: Ear: listen-choice, Mia plays E7 then Am, and Em then Am; which return sounds more like home? (E7, because of its G#).
Player: the song at 60, then 72 bpm, one downstrum per beat.
Chords: one-minute changes, Am to E7 and Dm to E7.
Player: Korobeiniki, a Russian folk melody in A minor on the same three chords: you strum Am, E7 and Dm while the app plays the tune; the melody itself can wait for another day.

lessons.title: B7, your first four-finger chord
lessons.goal: Play B7 and change from Em and from E to B7 with finger 2 as an anchor.
lessons.explain: B7 uses all four fingers: finger 2 on string 5 fret 2 (B), finger 1 on string 4 fret 1 (D#), finger 3 on string 3 fret 2 (A) and finger 4 on string 1 fret 2 (F#), with string 2 open and string 6 left out. From Em or from E, finger 2 stays on string 5 fret 2 (B): put it down first and build the rest of the chord around it. B7 leads home to Em just as E7 leads home to Am.
lessons.show: Chord box of B7 (x21202); chord boxes of Em (022000) fingered 2 and 3, and of E (022100), with the anchor finger 2 highlighted; audio of B7 moving to Em.
practice: Mic (play-chord): B7, checking that the open string 2 rings. Without a microphone: chord-build.
Player: Change: Am-E and E-B7, the E-B7 half; then Change: Em-Am and Em-B7, both halves, at 60 bpm.
Chords: one-minute changes, Em to B7.

lessons.title: Wade in the Water
lessons.goal: Play Wade in the Water in E minor with Em, Am and B7, slow and heavy, with every change to B7 on time.
lessons.explain: This spiritual, printed in 1901, moves between Em, Am and B7, the three main chords of E minor. Strum it slow and heavy with the down-up eighths you already know, leaning on beats 2 and 4, so all your attention can go to the new B7 changes. The song has its own swaying strum too: you will learn it, and come back to this song, in the strumming unit.
lessons.show: Chord chart with Em (022000), Am (x02210) and B7 (x21202); a rhythm line of down-up eighths with accents on 2 and 4; audio at 84 bpm.
practice: Rhythm: down-up eighths with accents on 2 and 4 along with the trainer at 72 bpm, until the accents feel natural.
Player: the song at 72, then 84 bpm.
Chords: one-minute changes, Em to Am and Am to B7.

lessons.title: Major or minor?
lessons.goal: Hear and play the difference between major and minor chords, and play God Rest Ye Merry, Gentlemen, which moves between E minor and G major.
lessons.explain: E and Em, A and Am, D and Dm each differ by one note, the third, and lowering that note by one fret makes the chord minor. You can now play twelve chords. God Rest Ye Merry, Gentlemen uses six of them, and its refrain leans from E minor toward G major, its relative major (the major key that uses the same notes), before coming home.
lessons.show: Three pairs of chord boxes, E (022100) and Em (022000), A (x02220) and Am (x02210), D (xx0232) and Dm (xx0231), with the third circled in each; then the chord chart of God Rest Ye Merry, Gentlemen with Em, B7, C, D, G and Am.
practice: Ear: the chord-quality drill, major or minor, 10 rounds; aim for 8.
Mic (play-chord): Mia names a chord from your twelve and you play it, ten in a row. Without a microphone: chord-build for each.
Player: God Rest Ye Merry, Gentlemen at 84, then 100 bpm.
Player: We Three Kings in 3/4: a minor verse (Em, B7, Am, D) and a major refrain (G, C, D); hear the mood change.

units.title: Strumming patterns
units.goal: Play the folk pattern, accents and muted strums, 6/8 and boom-chick, and keep any of them going through a whole song.

lessons.title: The folk pattern
lessons.goal: Strum the all-purpose folk pattern (down, down-up, miss, up, down-up) on G, C and D.
lessons.explain: This is the pattern you hear in countless folk and pop songs. Count 1 2 & 3 & 4 &: down on 1, down on 2, up on the and of 2, miss on 3 (the hand moves down but skips the strings), up on the and of 3, down on 4, up on the and of 4. The secret is the miss: the hand never stops moving.
lessons.show: Rhythm line of the pattern with arrows and the missed beat drawn as a ghost arrow; the strum chart of Strumming: The Folk Pattern (G, C, D, G, 4 bars each); audio at 72 bpm.
practice: Technique: Constant Strumming Motion on Em, the full pattern with the miss, 8 bars at 60 bpm, then on G.
Rhythm: tap the pattern with the trainer until it is in your body.
Player: Strumming: The Folk Pattern at 60, then 76 bpm.
Player: Wade in the Water again, now with the folk pattern: it is that song's own swaying groove, down on 1, down-up on 2, up on the and of 3, down-up on 4.

lessons.title: Down by the Riverside
lessons.goal: Keep the folk pattern going through Down by the Riverside and Go Tell It on the Mountain.
lessons.explain: Down by the Riverside sits on one chord for long stretches (G, then D7, then C), which is perfect for keeping a pattern going while you sing. Go Tell It on the Mountain uses the same three chords with a livelier refrain. If a change is not ready, keep strumming the old chord: the beat matters more than the chord.
lessons.show: Chord charts of both songs with G (320003), D7 (xx0212) and C (x32010) boxes and the folk pattern drawn above; audio at 96 bpm.
practice: Player: Down by the Riverside at 84, then 108 bpm, with the folk pattern.
Player: Go Tell It on the Mountain at 84, then 100 bpm.
Chords: one-minute changes, G to D7 and D7 to C.

lessons.title: Accents and chucks
lessons.goal: Accent beats 2 and 4 and play a muted chuck strum by relaxing the fretting hand.
lessons.explain: An accent is a strum played a little louder than the others. A muted strum, or chuck, is percussive: relax the fretting fingers so they still touch the strings but no longer press them (with an open chord, lay the fingers lightly across all the strings), and strum; you hear a click instead of a chord. Put the chuck on beats 2 and 4 and any song gets a drummer's backbeat.
lessons.show: Rhythm line of down-up eighths with accents on 2 and 4, then the same with an X (a chuck) on 2 and 4; audio of each version on G at 80 bpm.
practice: Metronome: 80 bpm, down-up eighths on G with accents on beats 2 and 4.
Rhythm: the strumming-pattern drill with chucks on 2 and 4.
Technique: Strum Only the Right Strings, all three chords (D, A and E), now that you know E.
Player: She'll Be Coming 'Round the Mountain at 108 bpm with chucks on 2 and 4.

lessons.title: Feeling 6/8
lessons.goal: Feel 6/8 as two big beats, each split in three, and strum it on Em, C and D.
lessons.explain: 6/8 has six quick counts in a bar grouped in two threes: 1 2 3 4 5 6, with weight on 1 and 4. It rocks like a boat rather than marching. The strum: down on 1, down on 2, up on 3, down on 4, down on 5, up on 6, with accents on 1 and 4.
lessons.show: Rhythm line of a 6/8 bar with the two groups of three bracketed and accents on 1 and 4; the strum chart of Strumming: 6/8 (Em, C, D, Em, 4 bars each); audio at 50 big beats (dotted quarters) per minute.
practice: Rhythm: tap the six counts with a stronger tap on 1 and 4, then tap only 1 and 4 while saying all six.
Player: Strumming: 6/8 at 44, then 56 bpm, counting one beat per group of three.

Player: a melody that rocks in 6/8, Row, Row, Row Your Boat, in first position (one finger per fret from fret 1): wait mode, then at 48 and 56 bpm; then play it as a round with the app, the second voice entering after 2 bars.
Player: Greensleeves in 6/8 with Am, G, E and C, mostly one chord per bar (the cadence bars go Am to E), strumming on 1 and 4 while the app plays the tune.
Ear: listen-choice, is this 3/4 or 6/8? Four short examples.

lessons.title: Silent Night, strummed and picked
lessons.goal: Accompany Silent Night in 6/8 with G, D7 and C, first strummed and then with your first fingerpicking pattern.
lessons.explain: Silent Night was composed in 1818 by Franz Xaver Gruber, and it is in 6/8: two slow beats in each bar, each made of three counts. First strum softly on counts 1 and 4 only. Then try your first fingerpicking: the thumb (p) plays a bass note on counts 1 and 4, and the index (i), middle (m) and ring (a) fingers pluck strings 3, 2 and 1 in between.
lessons.show: Chord chart in 6/8 with G (320003), D7 (xx0212) and C (x32010); tab of one bar of the picking pattern on G: count 1, the thumb on string 6 fret 3 (G); 2, i on the open string 3 (G); 3, m on the open string 2 (B); 4, the thumb again; 5, a on string 1 fret 3 (G); 6, m on the open string 2 (B). Audio at 50 big beats per minute.
practice: Player: Silent Night at 44, then 50 bpm, strumming softly on counts 1 and 4.
Technique: Free-Stroke Arpeggios (p i m a), chords played one string at a time, the first pattern only, at 60 bpm, to meet your picking fingers.
Player: the picking pattern on G, then on D7 (thumb on the open string 4 (D)) and on C (thumb on string 5 fret 3 (C)), then through the whole song at 44 bpm.

lessons.title: Boom-chick
lessons.goal: Play boom-chick, a bass note then a strum, with alternating bass notes, and use it in Oh! Susanna.
lessons.explain: Boom-chick is country and folk accompaniment: pick one bass note (boom), then strum the higher strings (chick); in 4/4 the bass goes on beats 1 and 3 and the strum on 2 and 4. Alternate two bass notes in each chord: under G, string 6 fret 3 (G) then the open string 4 (D); under C, string 5 fret 3 (C) then string 6 fret 3 (G), with finger 3 hopping across; under D7, the open string 4 (D) then the open string 5 (A). Keep the strum short and light so the bass notes stand out.
lessons.show: Tab of one bar of each chord in boom-chick with the bass notes marked; audio of Strumming: Boom-Chick at 80 bpm.
practice: Player, wait mode: the bass notes alone, string 6 fret 3 (G) then the open string 4 (D), string 5 fret 3 (C) then string 6 fret 3 (G), the open string 4 (D) then the open string 5 (A), so your pick learns the jumps before the strums come in.
Player: Strumming: Boom-Chick at 72, then 88 bpm.

Player: Oh! Susanna with boom-chick at 80, then 92 bpm: in its 2/4 time the bass goes on beat 1 and the strum on beat 2. Mia says in one sentence where it comes from: it was written for minstrel shows, which mocked Black Americans, and we sing only the verse and chorus that do not.

lessons.title: Three songs, three strums
lessons.goal: Play three songs with three different strums back to back: boom-chick, the folk pattern and the waltz.
lessons.explain: Choosing a strum is part of playing a song, because the pattern sets its mood. Today's set: Oh! Susanna in boom-chick, Down by the Riverside with the folk pattern, and Amazing Grace as a waltz. Play the set without stopping between songs, like a short concert.
lessons.show: Set list card with each song's pattern drawn as a rhythm line, and its chords.
practice: Tuner: tune up; then Technique: the Five-Minute Warm-Up.
Player: the three songs back to back at 92, 108 and 84 bpm; the microphone listens to your chords, and about 8 bars in 10 clean and on time is a pass.
Practice Plan: log the set and pick the song that felt weakest for tomorrow's practice.

units.title: Riffs and melodies on all six strings
units.goal: Play notes on all six strings, add hammer-ons and pull-offs, and play melodies and a fiddle tune in first position.

lessons.title: Notes on the low strings
lessons.goal: Play the first notes on strings 4, 5 and 6 and name them.
lessons.explain: The low strings carry bass lines and riffs (short patterns repeated through a song). On string 4: the open D, string 4 fret 2 (E) and string 4 fret 3 (F). On string 5: the open A, string 5 fret 2 (B) and string 5 fret 3 (C). On string 6: the open E, string 6 fret 1 (F) and string 6 fret 3 (G). Again E to F and B to C are one fret apart: the two natural half steps.
lessons.show: Fretboard figure, frets 0 to 3 on strings 6, 5 and 4, with the open strings marked and string 4 fret 2 (E), string 4 fret 3 (F), string 5 fret 2 (B), string 5 fret 3 (C), string 6 fret 1 (F) and string 6 fret 3 (G); the tabs of the three First Notes studies.
practice: Mic (play-note): Mia names a note on strings 4 to 6 and you play it, 10 in a row. Without a microphone: fretboard-find.
Player: First Notes on String 4, String 5 and String 6, each in wait mode and then at 72 bpm with the teacher part.
Fretboard: the string 6 game, frets 0 to 3, for one minute.

Player: Sakura, Sakura, a Japanese melody that uses string 4 fret 2 (E), string 4 fret 3 (F) and string 5 fret 2 (B) among its notes: slowly, in wait mode, letting each long note ring for its full length.

lessons.title: Hammer-ons and pull-offs
lessons.goal: Sound a second note with a hammer-on and with a pull-off, picking only the first note.
lessons.explain: A hammer-on sounds a note by bringing a finger down hard and fast onto the string just behind the fret wire, without picking again. A pull-off is the reverse: the fretting finger plucks the string slightly sideways as it leaves, so the lower note sounds. They make lines smooth and are the first step into lead guitar; today you use them in two licks, short phrases you learn once and reuse.
lessons.show: Tab of Lick: Hammer-Ons in open position: the open string 4 hammered to string 4 fret 2 (E), the open string 3 to string 3 fret 2 (A), the open string 2 to string 2 fret 3 (D), the open string 1 to string 1 fret 3 (G), with the h sign; then Lick: Pull-Offs, from string 1 fret 3 (G), string 2 fret 3 (D) and string 3 fret 2 (A) to the open strings, with the p sign.
practice: Mic (play-phrase): one hammer-on, the open string 3 to string 3 fret 2 (A), five times; the microphone checks you get two notes from one pick stroke. Without a microphone: the Player in wait mode.
Player: Lick: Hammer-Ons at 60 bpm, then Lick: Pull-Offs.
Technique: Hammer and Pull Chains, slowly, one string at a time.

lessons.title: Deck the Halls and your first F#
lessons.goal: Play Deck the Halls in first position, stepping down the G major scale and meeting your first F#.
lessons.explain: Each line of Deck the Halls starts high on string 2 fret 3 (D) and steps down the scale, one note to the next. At the end of the fa-la-la line comes a new note, F#, at string 4 fret 4 (F#) with finger 4, rising to the open G. A sharp (#) raises a note by one fret.
lessons.show: Tab of the tune in G, first position, with string 4 fret 4 (F#) highlighted on a fretboard figure next to string 4 fret 3 (F) to show the one-fret difference; audio at 108 bpm.
practice: Mic (play-note): F# on string 4 fret 4, then G on the open string 3, five times. Without a microphone: fretboard-find.
Player, wait mode, then at 84 and 108 bpm with the teacher's chords (G, C, D7).
Player loop: the fa-la-la line until the F# feels easy.

lessons.title: Joy to the World: a scale in a song
lessons.goal: Play the first phrase of Joy to the World, the D major scale stepping down, with its dotted rhythm.
lessons.explain: Joy to the World begins with a whole major scale walking down from D to D: string 2 fret 3 (D), string 2 fret 2 (C#), the open string 2 (B), string 3 fret 2 (A), the open string 3 (G), string 4 fret 4 (F#), string 4 fret 2 (E), the open string 4 (D). That is the sound of the major scale: eight steps, home to home. The rhythm starts long, then quick: D, then C# with a dot, then a short B.
lessons.show: Tab of the first phrase with its rhythm (D quarter, C# dotted eighth, B sixteenth | A dotted quarter, G eighth | F# E | D); a fretboard figure of the eight notes; audio at 72 bpm.
practice: Mic (play-phrase): the eight notes as even quarter notes, top to bottom. Without a microphone: the Player in wait mode.
Rhythm: tap the phrase's rhythm with the trainer.
Player: the phrase in rhythm at 60, then 72 bpm, then the rest of the carol with the teacher's chords (D, G, A7).

Player: for contrast, the opening of Mozart's Eine kleine Nachtmusik, which leaps through the notes of the G chord instead of stepping: the open string 3 (G), the open string 4 (D), the open string 2 (B) and string 2 fret 3 (D); wait mode, then at 72 bpm, observing every rest.

lessons.title: A first fiddle tune: The Rakes of Mallow
lessons.goal: Flatpick The Rakes of Mallow, an Irish polka, in AABB form, with downstrokes on the beat and upstrokes in between.
lessons.explain: Fiddle tunes are melodies for dancing, and guitarists flatpick them. The Rakes of Mallow is an Irish polka with two 8-bar parts, A and B, each played twice (AABB), and it moves mostly by step and repeats its notes, which makes it the perfect first one. The picking rule makes it flow: a downstroke on every beat and an upstroke on every and, so the pick moves just like your strumming hand.
lessons.show: Tab of the A part in first position with down and up stroke signs; a form chart A A B B; audio at 80 bpm.
practice: Player, wait mode: the A part, then the B part.
Player loop: each part at 60 bpm, then 72, picking down on the beat and up on the and.
Player: the whole tune, AABB, at 80 bpm, while the app plays backup chords (G, D, C).

lessons.title: Your first showpiece: Fur Elise
lessons.goal: Play the opening theme of Beethoven's Fur Elise as your first showpiece.
lessons.explain: Fur Elise starts with a rocking figure, E D# E D# E B D C A, using the open string 1 (E), string 2 fret 4 (D#), string 2 fret 3 (D), string 2 fret 1 (C), the open string 2 (B) and string 3 fret 2 (A). It is in 3/8: three quick counts in each bar. The answering bass outlines the chords Am and E; keep G#, not G, in the E chord, or the magic goes.
lessons.show: Tab of the A section with the rocking figure highlighted; a fretboard figure of the six melody notes; audio slowly, then at the target tempo.
practice: Mic (play-phrase): E D# E D# E B D C A, slowly. Without a microphone: the Player in wait mode.
Player loop: the opening 4 bars until they are even, then the whole A section in wait mode.
Player: the A section in time with the app's left-hand part at 80, then 120 bpm (eighth-note counts); then play it for someone.

units.title: Power chords and the blues
units.goal: Play power chords open and movable, palm-mute, play a 12-bar blues shuffle and write a rock riff of your own.

lessons.title: Power chords
lessons.goal: Play the two-finger power chords E5, A5 and D5 and keep the other strings quiet.
lessons.explain: A power chord has only a root, the note it is named after, and the fifth above it, often with the root again on top (the same note an octave higher), so it is neither major nor minor; with distortion it sounds huge, which is why rock is built on it. E5 is the open string 6 with string 5 fret 2 (B) and string 4 fret 2 (E); A5 is the same shape one string over, and D5 two strings over, except that its top note moves up one fret, to string 2 fret 3 (D), because string 2 is tuned differently from the others. Play only those strings, and let the underside of your fretting fingers lightly touch the thinner strings so they stay silent.
lessons.show: Chord boxes of E5 (022xxx), A5 (x022xx) and D5 (xx023x); tab of the first 4 bars of Power Chords: Open Riff; audio clean and with a little drive.
practice: Mic (play-chord): E5, A5 and D5. Without a microphone: chord-build.
Technique: Fretting-Hand Muting, first part: hold E5 and strum all six strings; only strings 6, 5 and 4 should sound.

Player: Power Chords: Open Riff, bars 1 to 4, eighth-note downstrokes at 80 bpm: you play E5, D5 and A5, and the Player plays C5 and G5 (they come next lesson) while you rest and come back in on time.

lessons.title: One shape, any chord
lessons.goal: Slide one power-chord shape along strings 6 and 5 and name the chord from its root.
lessons.explain: Fret the root with finger 1 and put finger 3 (and 4) two frets higher on the next two strings: G5 (355xxx) has its root at fret 3 on string 6, and C5 (x355xx) at fret 3 on string 5. The shape never changes, so the root note names the chord: on string 6, fret 3 is G, fret 5 is A, fret 7 is B and fret 8 is C. This is your first movable shape, and your first step toward knowing the whole neck.
lessons.show: Chord boxes of G5 (355xxx) and C5 (x355xx); a fretboard figure of the natural notes on string 6: string 6 fret 1 (F), string 6 fret 3 (G), string 6 fret 5 (A), string 6 fret 7 (B), string 6 fret 8 (C), string 6 fret 10 (D), string 6 fret 12 (E); and on string 5: string 5 fret 3 (C), string 5 fret 5 (D), string 5 fret 7 (E).
practice: Fretboard: the natural notes on string 6, frets 0 to 12, for two minutes.
Mic (play-chord): Mia names G5, A5, C5 or D5 and you play it with the root on string 6 or 5. Without a microphone: fretboard-find, tap the root.
Player: Power Chords: Open Riff, all 8 bars, moving between E5, A5, D5, G5 and C5 at 80, then 96 bpm.

lessons.title: Palm muting
lessons.goal: Palm-mute a chugging eighth-note rhythm on E5 and switch between muted and open in time.
lessons.explain: Rest the edge of your picking hand lightly on the strings right where they leave the bridge saddle, and the notes turn short and thick: the classic chug. Too far toward the neck and the note dies; too far back and it rings, so move the hand a centimetre at a time until it sounds right. Rock rhythm lives on the contrast between muted chugs and open, ringing chords.
lessons.show: Tab of E5 eighth notes with P.M. over 2 bars, then 2 bars open; audio of both; a close-up drawing of the picking hand resting at the bridge (see gaps).
practice: Technique: Palm Muting at 80 bpm: 2 bars muted, 2 bars open, on E5 (022xxx).
Player: Power Chords: Open Riff with the E5 bars palm-muted, at 96 bpm.
Technique: climb the Palm Muting ladder by 8 bpm per clean pass toward 120 bpm.

lessons.title: The 12-bar blues shuffle
lessons.goal: Play the 12-bar blues shuffle in A with a swung two-string riff, twice through.
lessons.explain: The 12-bar blues is a 12-bar chord pattern that thousands of songs share: A A A A | D D A A | E D A E, built on the 1st, 4th and 5th notes of the key. The shuffle figure uses two strings: on A, the open string 5 (A) with string 4 fret 2 (E), alternating with string 4 fret 4 (F#). Swing the eighths, long-short, long-short, like a heartbeat.
lessons.show: Tab of one bar of the shuffle on each chord (A on strings 5 and 4; D on strings 4 and 3, the open string 4 (D) with string 3 fret 2 (A) and string 3 fret 4 (B); E on strings 6 and 5, the open string 6 (E) with string 5 fret 2 (B) and string 5 fret 4 (C#)); the 12-bar form as a grid; audio straight, then swung, at 80 bpm.
practice: Rhythm: tap straight eighths, then swung eighths (long-short), with the trainer, and hear the difference.
Player loop: one bar of each chord at 60 bpm, swung.
Lesson: order, put the 12 bars of the form in order (A A A A, D D A A, E D A E).
Player: 12-Bar Blues Shuffle in A, twice through, at 72, then 88 bpm.

lessons.title: John Henry: a blues ballad
lessons.goal: Strum John Henry, a blues ballad, with E7, A7 and B7 and a driving strum accented on 2 and 4.
lessons.explain: John Henry is an early African American ballad about a steel-driving man who raced a steam drill. Its seventh chords, E7, A7 and B7, give it the blues colour: the 7 adds a slightly sour note that the blues loves. Drive the strum with down-up eighths and lean on beats 2 and 4.
lessons.show: Chord chart with E7 (020100), A7 (x02020) and B7 (x21202); a rhythm line of down-up eighths with accents on 2 and 4; audio at 92 bpm.
practice: Chords: one-minute changes, E7 to A7 and E7 to B7.
Ear: listen-choice, plain E or E7? Six rounds.
Player: John Henry at 80, then 92 bpm.

lessons.title: Write your own riff
lessons.goal: Write a 2-bar riff from power chords and play it with the backing band.
lessons.explain: A riff is a short, catchy pattern repeated through a song, and you already have everything you need to write one: power chords, palm muting, rests and accents. Rule one: keep it short, two bars. Rule two: leave a gap, because the silence is part of the riff. Rule three: play it the same way every time, so the band can lock onto it.
lessons.show: A riff builder: a 2-bar grid of eighth notes where each slot is a power chord (E5, G5 or A5), a palm-muted E or a rest; an original example riff by Mia as tab, with audio.
practice: Create: build your riff on the grid and hear it played back; change one slot at a time until you like it.
Player: loop your riff at 80 bpm until you can play it 8 times in a row without a slip.
Jam: jam track rock-i-biii-iv in E (E5, G5, A5) at 100 bpm: your riff for 4 bars, then strum the chords for 4 bars, and repeat.

units.title: Your first barre chord
units.goal: Play Fmaj7, the small F, the full F barre and Bm, and use them in songs.

lessons.title: Fmaj7 and the small F
lessons.goal: Play Fmaj7 and the small F on strings 4 to 1, and change from Am to Fmaj7 and from C to F.
lessons.explain: F is the famous hurdle, so we climb toward it in steps. Fmaj7 first: finger 3 on string 4 fret 3 (F), finger 2 on string 3 fret 2 (A), finger 1 on string 2 fret 1 (C), with string 1 open; from Am, finger 1 does not move at all. Then the small F: finger 1 lies flat across strings 2 and 1 at fret 1, a two-string barre, so string 1 now sounds F. Strum strings 4 to 1 for both.
lessons.show: Chord boxes of Am (x02210), Fmaj7 (xx3210), C (x32010) and the small F (xx3211), with the two-string barre drawn as a bar; audio of each.
practice: Mic (play-chord): Fmaj7, then the small F; for F, pick strings 2 and 1 one at a time until both ring under the flat finger. Without a microphone: chord-build.
Player: Change: Am-Fmaj7 and C-F at 60 bpm.
Chords: one-minute changes, Am to Fmaj7 and C to the small F.

lessons.title: La Cucaracha, and G7
lessons.goal: Add G7 and play La Cucaracha with C, G7 and the small F, bright and bouncy.
lessons.explain: La Cucaracha is a Spanish and Mexican folk song known in the 19th century, and it bounces on C, G7 and F. G7 (320001) is the one new chord, and an easy one: from C, the 3-2 finger pair moves back one string toward string 6 and finger 1 moves to string 1 fret 1 (F), and just as D7 leans toward G, G7 leans toward home, C. The F is the small F from the last lesson; keep the strum light, down-up eighths with an accent on 2 and 4.
lessons.show: Chord chart with C (x32010), G7 (320001) and F (xx3211), with the C to G7 move drawn as arrows; audio at 100 bpm.
practice: Mic (play-chord): G7 (320001), then the C to G7 change four times. Without a microphone: chord-build.
Chords: one-minute changes, C to G7 and C to the small F.
Player: La Cucaracha at 88, then 104 bpm.
Player: again at 104 bpm with chucks on 2 and 4 for extra bounce; then try the target tempo, 120.

lessons.title: The full F barre
lessons.goal: Play the full F barre chord with every string ringing, and change from C to F and from Am to F.
lessons.explain: The barre: finger 1 lies flat across all six strings at fret 1, rolled slightly onto its bony side and right behind the fret wire, while fingers 3, 4 and 2 make an E shape in front of it: finger 3 on string 5 fret 3 (C), finger 4 on string 4 fret 3 (F), finger 2 on string 3 fret 2 (A). Squeeze with the hand and let the weight of the arm pull back slightly, rather than crushing with the thumb. If a string is dead, play string by string and adjust; if it hurts, stop, because strength comes in weeks, not minutes.
lessons.show: Chord box of F (133211) with the barre drawn across all six strings; a fretboard figure showing that it is the E (022100) shape moved up one fret, with finger 1 as a new nut; audio string by string.
practice: Technique: Barre Strength Without Strain: the barre alone at fret 5, string by string, then press for 2 beats and release for 2 beats, 8 times; then at fret 3 and fret 1.
Mic (play-chord): F (133211); if it does not pass, pick it string by string to find the dead string and adjust that finger. Without a microphone: pick string by string and listen, then chord-build.
Player: First Barre: F at 60 bpm, C to F and back, then Am to F, in half-note strums. On a bad day, Fmaj7 (xx3210) is a fine stand-in.

lessons.title: The barre F at work: the key of C
lessons.goal: Use the full F barre in the key of C, changing between C, Am, F and G with the backing band.
lessons.explain: C, F and G are the I, IV and V of C major and Am is its vi, so the barre F you have just learned opens up a whole new key. Keep the barre light between chords and squeeze only as you land, on the beat; if a change is not ready, play the small F (xx3211) and try the barre again next time round. Listen to how the progression, the chords in their order, sounds with the full six-string F: deeper and stronger.
lessons.show: Chord boxes of C (x32010), Am (x02210), F (133211) and G (320003); two charts: C | Am | F | G and C | F | C | G.
practice: Chords: one-minute changes, C to F and Am to F, with the barre.
Jam: jam track fifties-i-vi-iv-v in C at 66 bpm (C, Am, F, G) with down-up eighths.
Jam: jam track folk-i-iv-i-v in C at 92 bpm (C, F, C, G) with the folk pattern.

lessons.title: Bm, a barre from string 5
lessons.goal: Play Bm with a barre at fret 2 and change between Bm and D, G and A.
lessons.explain: Bm is the Am shape moved up two frets, with finger 1 barring strings 5 to 1 at fret 2: finger 3 on string 4 fret 4 (F#), finger 4 on string 3 fret 4 (B) and finger 2 on string 2 fret 3 (D). Strum from string 5. It shows up all over songs in D major, as the chord built on the 6th note of the scale.
lessons.show: Chord box of Bm (x24432); a fretboard figure comparing Am (x02210) and Bm, the same shape two frets up behind the barre; audio.
practice: Mic (play-chord): Bm, string by string from string 5. Without a microphone: chord-build.
Technique: Barre Strength Without Strain at fret 2, strings 5 to 1 only.
Chords: one-minute changes, D to Bm and Bm to G.

lessons.title: Auld Lang Syne
lessons.goal: Play Auld Lang Syne with D, A, G and Bm, including the barre, from start to finish.
lessons.explain: Auld Lang Syne sets Robert Burns's 1788 words to a Scottish tune, and it is sung at New Year all over the world. Each line starts with a pickup, so count yourself in and come in on the first full bar. This is your barre-chord milestone: the Bm change must land on time, even if it is not perfect yet.
lessons.show: Chord chart with D (xx0232), A (x02220), G (320003) and Bm (x24432); audio at 80 bpm.
practice: Chords: one-minute changes, A to Bm.
Player: Auld Lang Syne at 66, then 80 bpm, with the folk pattern or down-up eighths.
Record: one take, start to finish; listen back and choose one thing to improve.

units.title: Your first scale and your first solo
units.goal: Learn A minor pentatonic box 1, play licks in it and improvise over a groove and a 12-bar blues.

lessons.title: A minor pentatonic, box 1
lessons.goal: Play A minor pentatonic box 1 at fret 5, up and down, with alternate picking and the right fingers.
lessons.explain: A scale is a set of notes that sound good together, and A minor pentatonic has five: A C D E G. On the neck they make a box at fret 5 with two notes on every string: finger 1 always plays fret 5, finger 3 plays fret 7 on strings 5, 4 and 3, and finger 4 plays fret 8 on strings 6, 2 and 1. The lowest note, string 6 fret 5 (A), is the root, the home note.
lessons.show: Fretboard figure, frets 5 to 8, of the 12 notes of box 1 with their fingers: string 6 fret 5 (A), string 6 fret 8 (C), string 5 fret 5 (D), string 5 fret 7 (E), string 4 fret 5 (G), string 4 fret 7 (A), string 3 fret 5 (C), string 3 fret 7 (D), string 2 fret 5 (E), string 2 fret 8 (G), string 1 fret 5 (A), string 1 fret 8 (C), with the three A roots highlighted.
practice: Mic (play-phrase): the box up from string 6 fret 5 to string 1 fret 8 and back, one note per click at 60 bpm. Without a microphone: the Player in wait mode.
Scales: A minor pentatonic, box 1, with the note names shown; find the three A roots.
Arcade: the box 1 note-chase game for two minutes.

lessons.title: Phrases that ask and answer
lessons.goal: Play the call-and-response phrases of the Pentatonic Box 1 Lick study, ending each answer on a chord tone.
lessons.explain: A scale becomes music when you play phrases: short ideas with a beginning and an end, like sentences. In call and response, the first phrase asks a question and the second answers it, and an answer sounds most finished when it lands on A, C, E or G, the notes of the Am7 chord underneath. The study also has a hammer-on inside the box, such as string 3 fret 5 (C) to string 3 fret 7 (D).
lessons.show: Tab of the 8-bar study (four 2-bar phrases: ask, answer, ask, answer) over an Am7 groove; a fretboard figure of box 1 with the chord tones A C E G marked.
practice: Player, wait mode: phrases 1 and 2, then 3 and 4.
Player loop: the whole study at 70, then 84 bpm with the groove.
Ear: listen-choice, does this phrase end on a chord tone (finished) or not (open)? Six rounds.

lessons.title: Your first improvisation
lessons.goal: Improvise over a one-chord A minor groove using three notes, then all five, leaving space between phrases.
lessons.explain: Improvising is making up phrases on the spot, and one fact makes it easy: over this groove there are no wrong notes in this box. Start with only three notes, string 3 fret 5 (C), string 3 fret 7 (D) and string 2 fret 5 (E), and play short phrases with rests between them. Then use the whole box, and end your last phrase on an A.
lessons.show: Fretboard figure of box 1 with the three starting notes highlighted; a rhythm line of a 2-bar phrase followed by 2 bars of rest; audio of an original example by Mia.
practice: Jam: jam track funk-one-chord-minor in A at 90 bpm: 4 bars with three notes, 4 bars of rest, repeated for 2 minutes.
Jam: jam track funk-one-chord-minor in A again, now with all five notes: play a phrase, copy it, then change one note of it.
Record: one minute of your improvisation; listen back and keep your favourite phrase.

lessons.title: Box 1 over the blues
lessons.goal: Play box 1 over a 12-bar blues in A and finish your phrases on A at the end of the form.
lessons.explain: A minor pentatonic over a blues in A is one of the great sounds in music: the minor notes rub against the major chords in a way the ear loves. Follow the form you know from the shuffle: A for 4 bars, D for 2, A for 2, then E, D, A, E. Play a phrase every two bars, and in bar 11 aim for the A at string 4 fret 7 (A).
lessons.show: Fretboard figure of box 1; the 12-bar grid with a marker showing where you are; audio of a blues chorus with an original example solo.
practice: Jam: jam track blues-12-bar in A at 80 bpm: in the first chorus play the shuffle from your lessons; in the second, box 1 phrases.
Jam: jam track blues-12-bar in A, three choruses of soloing; land on A in bar 11 every time.
Ear: listen-choice, where in the 12 bars are we? (the change to D in bar 5, back to A in bar 7, E in bar 9).

lessons.title: E minor pentatonic in open position
lessons.goal: Play E minor pentatonic in open position and improvise with it over Em, C and D.
lessons.explain: The same five-note box exists in open position for E minor (E G A B D), with the open strings doing finger 1's job: on every string you play the open note and one fretted note, string 6 fret 3 (G), string 5 fret 2 (B), string 4 fret 2 (E), string 3 fret 2 (A), string 2 fret 3 (D) and string 1 fret 3 (G). You already know these notes from your hammer-ons. Move the shape up to fret 12 and it is E minor pentatonic again, an octave higher.
lessons.show: Fretboard figure, frets 0 to 3, of E minor pentatonic in open position with the E roots marked (the open string 6 (E), string 4 fret 2 (E) and the open string 1 (E)); the same shape at frets 12 to 15.
practice: Mic (play-phrase): the open-position box up and down. Without a microphone: the Player in wait mode.
Jam: jam track minor-i-bvi-bvii in E (Em, C, D) at 92 bpm: improvise with the open-position box, using hammer-ons and pull-offs.
Arcade: the E minor pentatonic note-chase game.

lessons.title: Rhythm, then a solo
lessons.goal: Play a 12-bar blues in A twice through: one chorus of shuffle rhythm and one chorus of your own solo.
lessons.explain: This is what guitarists do in a band: play rhythm, take a solo, then hand back. Plan a little: start your solo low and simple, climb in the middle, and end on A in bar 11 so the band knows you are done. Keep the beat no matter what.
lessons.show: The 12-bar form as a two-chorus map (chorus 1: shuffle, chorus 2: solo in box 1) with a three-part solo plan: low and simple, climb, land on A.
practice: Technique: the Five-Minute Warm-Up.
Jam: jam track blues-12-bar in A at 84 bpm: chorus 1 shuffle, chorus 2 solo; then the other way round.
Record: the two-chorus take, then Mia's checklist: did the shuffle stay swung, did the solo leave space, did you end on A?

units.title: Playing with others, and a habit for life
units.goal: Tune by ear, hold your part with other players, use a capo, follow a chart with a band, build your own routine and give a short concert.

lessons.title: Tuning by ear
lessons.goal: Tune the strings to each other with the fifth-fret rule and check them by ear.
lessons.explain: Each string pressed at fret 5 sounds the same note as the next open string: string 6 fret 5 (A) matches the open string 5, string 5 fret 5 (D) the open string 4, string 4 fret 5 (G) the open string 3, and string 2 fret 5 (E) the open string 1. The one exception is string 3, where fret 4 matches: string 3 fret 4 (B) and the open string 2. When two notes are nearly the same you hear a slow wobble, called beating; turn the peg until it stops.
lessons.show: Fretboard figure with the five matching pairs joined by lines (fret 5 on strings 6, 5, 4 and 2, fret 4 on string 3); audio of two strings slightly out of tune (beating), then in tune.
practice: Tuner: tune string 6 only, tune the rest by the fifth-fret rule, then check each string with the Tuner to see how close you were.
Ear: higher or lower, is the second note higher or lower than the first? Ten pairs, getting closer each time.
Lesson: match-pairs, each fretted note with the open string it matches.
Player: Amazing Grace, to hear your tuning in a song.

lessons.title: Rounds and duets
lessons.goal: Hold your own part while another part enters: play Frere Jacques as a round and an original duet round.
lessons.explain: Playing with others means hearing two things at once, your part and theirs. In a round, everyone plays the same tune but starts at different times, so for a moment your ears want to follow the other voice. Count, keep your eyes on your own part, and let the other voice wash over you.
lessons.show: Tab of the Frere Jacques round melody in first position on strings 4 to 1, with the point where the second voice enters (bar 3) marked; the tab of Duet: An Original Round.
practice: Player: Frere Jacques (round), your voice alone at 80 bpm, then with the app's second voice entering after 2 bars, then at 96.
Player: Duet: An Original Round the same way; then swap and play the second voice.
With others: play either round with a friend or a family member.

lessons.title: The capo
lessons.goal: Use a capo to play the shapes you know in a higher key, to suit a singer or another player.
lessons.explain: A capo is a clamp that presses all the strings at one fret, acting like a new nut. With the capo at fret 2 the G, C and D shapes sound as A, D and E: every chord moves up two frets, which is two half steps. Tab and chord charts for capo songs count frets from the capo, so a shape stays a shape.
lessons.show: Fretboard figure with a capo at fret 2 and the G (320003) shape behind it, labelled shape G, sounds A; a table: capo 2 turns G C D into A D E, capo 3 into Bb Eb F, capo 5 into C F G.
