practice: Lesson: choice, the capo is at fret 2 and you play a C shape: what sounds? (D). Five rounds with the capo at frets 1 to 5.
Tuner: check the tuning after putting the capo on, because a capo can pull the strings slightly sharp.
Jam: jam track folk-i-iv-i-v in A at 100 bpm: capo at fret 2, play the shapes G, C, G, D; the band plays A, D, A, E and you match it.
Player: O Come, All Ye Faithful, once in G and once with the capo at fret 2; sing along with the one that fits your voice.

lessons.title: Following a chart with the band
lessons.goal: Follow a 4-chord chart with the backing band, change on every bar, and get back in after a mistake without stopping.
lessons.explain: In a band the beat never waits for you, so the most important skill is getting back in: if you lose your place, stop strumming, listen for the next chord change and come back in on the next beat 1. Two progressions cover a huge number of songs: I-vi-IV-V (G Em C D) and I-V-vi-IV (G D Em C). Learn to hear which one is playing.
lessons.show: Two chord charts in G, G | Em | C | D and G | D | Em | C, with a bar counter and the roman numerals under the chords; audio.
practice: Jam: jam track fifties-i-vi-iv-v in G at 72 bpm with the folk pattern, 3 minutes without stopping.
Jam: jam track pop-axis in G at 88 bpm with down-up eighths; on purpose, stop for 2 bars and come back in on beat 1.
Ear: listen-choice, which of the two progressions is playing? Six rounds.

lessons.title: Your own practice routine
lessons.goal: Build a daily practice routine that fits your time and keeps you improving.
lessons.explain: Short and regular beats long and rare: 15 focused minutes a day usually does more than two hours on a Sunday. A good session has a shape: tune and warm up, a technique exercise, one hard thing (a change or a passage) played slowly, a song you love, something new, and a cool-down. End on something that went well, and write down one thing to work on tomorrow.
lessons.show: A sample 20-minute routine in the Practice Plan: 2 minutes tuning and warm-up, 4 minutes one-minute changes, 5 minutes the hard passage at a slow tempo, 6 minutes songs, 2 minutes something new, 1 minute cool-down.
practice: Practice Plan: build your own routine from the blocks and set its length and your daily goal.
Practice Plan: run the routine once now, with the timer.

lessons.title: Graduation concert
lessons.goal: Give a four-song concert, record it, and check that you are ready for Dev's course.
lessons.explain: Look how far you have come: from one open string to barre chords, riffs and your own solo. Your concert has four songs: a melody, a strummed song with a barre chord, the blues with a solo, and one song you choose. Afterwards Dev takes over; he will show you the whole neck, and everything he teaches stands on what you can now do.

courses.title: The Whole Neck with Dev
courses.promise: You can play any major, minor or seventh chord in several places on the neck, solo with the five pentatonic boxes and the major scale in every position using slides, bends and vibrato, play rhythm guitar in rock, blues, funk, reggae, country and folk styles, fingerpick with a steady thumb, read simple notation in first position, work out songs by ear, and hold your own in a band.

units.title: Barre chords that move
units.goal: Play major and minor barre chords with the root on string 6 or 5 anywhere on the neck, and change between them in songs.

lessons.title: Welcome to the band
lessons.goal: Show Dev what you already play and set your targets for this course.
lessons.explain: Dev assumes you can change between the open chords, play an F barre, strum in 4/4, 3/4 and 6/8 and solo a little in A minor pentatonic box 1. Today you show him with four quick checks, and the scores become your baseline. Anything shaky gets a link back to the lesson that fixes it; everything else, we build on, starting tonight.
lessons.show: A checklist card with the four checks and their targets: one-minute changes G to C and Am to F (30 clean changes or more), the F (133211) barre ringing on all six strings, the folk pattern on G, C and D at 90 bpm, and box 1 up and down in eighth notes at 80 bpm.
practice: Chords: one-minute changes, G to C, then Am to F; the trainer stores your scores.
Mic (play-chord): F (133211). Without a microphone, play it string by string and rate it yourself.
Metronome: A minor pentatonic box 1 up and down in eighth notes at 80 bpm.
Metronome: the folk pattern at 90 bpm, two bars each of G, C and D, round and round without stopping.
Practice Plan: Dev's suggested 30-minute routine for this course: warm-up, technique, the lesson's new skill, songs, a jam.

lessons.title: E-shape barres, root on string 6
lessons.goal: Play E-shape major and minor barre chords with the root on string 6, and find any of them by its root.
lessons.explain: Your F chord is an E shape with finger 1 acting as a moving nut. Slide it up two frets and it is G (355433), two more and it is A (577655); lift finger 2 and you get the minor versions, Fm (133111), Gm (355333) and Am (577555). The chord is named by the note under finger 1 on string 6, so from now on the notes on string 6 are your map.
lessons.show: Chord boxes of G (355433) and Gm (355333) with the root on string 6 marked; a fretboard figure of the natural notes on string 6: string 6 fret 1 (F), string 6 fret 3 (G), string 6 fret 5 (A), string 6 fret 7 (B), string 6 fret 8 (C), string 6 fret 10 (D), string 6 fret 12 (E).
practice: Fretboard: name notes on string 6 for one minute; aim for 20 right.
Mic (play-chord): Dev names a chord (G, Am, C, Bm, D) and you play it as an E-shape barre. Without a microphone: fretboard-find, tap the root on string 6.
Player: Barre Shapes: E, Em, A and Am Shapes, the E and Em bars (F, G, A, Fm, Gm, Am), saying each root aloud.

lessons.title: A-shape barres, root on string 5
lessons.goal: Play A-shape major and minor barre chords with the root on string 5.
lessons.explain: The A shape works the same way from string 5: finger 1 barres at the root fret and the other fingers (or one flattened finger) cover strings 4, 3 and 2 two frets higher: Bb (x13331), B (x24442), C (x35553). The minor version is the Am shape, Bm (x24432) and Cm (x35543). Between the E shape on string 6 and the A shape on string 5, every major and minor chord is within reach in two places.
lessons.show: Chord boxes of C (x35553) and Cm (x35543) with the root on string 5 marked; a fretboard figure of the natural notes on string 5: string 5 fret 2 (B), string 5 fret 3 (C), string 5 fret 5 (D), string 5 fret 7 (E), string 5 fret 8 (F), string 5 fret 10 (G), string 5 fret 12 (A).
practice: Fretboard: name notes on string 5 for one minute.
Player: Barre Shapes, the A and Am bars (Bb, B, C, Bm, Cm).
Lesson: fretboard-find, find D major in two places: D (x57775), the A shape at fret 5, and D (10-12-12-11-10-10), the E shape at fret 10.

lessons.title: Barre chords in real progressions
lessons.goal: Play the I-vi-IV-V progression with barre chords in A and in C, and the chords of the Canon in D.
lessons.explain: Barre chords let you play any progression in any key with the same hand movements. In A, the I-vi-IV-V is A, F#m (244222), D, E; in C, with barres only, it is C (x35553), Am (577555), F (133211) and G (355433). Mixing E shapes and A shapes keeps your hand in one area of the neck instead of jumping around.
lessons.show: Chord grids of both progressions with each chord's shape (E or A) and root string labelled; then the Canon in D chords, D A Bm F#m G D G A, with the ground bass line.
practice: Player: Barre Progression: I-vi-IV-V at 72 bpm with the folk strum, in A, then in C.

Player: Canon in D (duet): first the ground bass, one note per beat (the open string 4 (D), the open string 5 (A), string 5 fret 2 (B), string 6 fret 2 (F#), string 6 fret 3 (G), the open string 4 (D), string 6 fret 3 (G), the open string 5 (A)), then the chords, while the app plays the canon above.
Chords: one-minute changes, A to F#m and F to G.

lessons.title: Faster barre changes
lessons.goal: Change between barre chords quickly by keeping finger 1 in light contact as it slides.
lessons.explain: The barre does not need full pressure between chords: release it, glide on the surface of the strings, and squeeze again only when you land. Lead with the finger that has farthest to go and keep the shape of the hand as you move. Little by little the squeeze gets lighter; most players press far harder than they need.
lessons.show: Chord boxes of F (133211), Bb (x13331), C (x35553) and Dm (x-5-7-7-6-5); a fretboard animation of finger 1 gliding between frets 1, 3 and 5.
practice: Technique: Barre Change Speed: F, Bb, C, Dm, changing every 2 beats at 50 bpm, then every beat; raise 5 bpm per clean pass.
Technique: Barre Strength Without Strain: find the least pressure that still rings.
Chords: one-minute changes, F to Bb.

lessons.title: Songs with barre chords
lessons.goal: Play Waltzing Matilda and Loch Lomond, using barre chords where they help.
lessons.explain: Both songs are in D major and both need Bm, the vi chord. Waltzing Matilda also has E7, which is not in the key of D: it is the chord that pulls toward A, a little detour that gives the tune its lift. Use open chords where they ring and barres where you need them: that is how real players choose.
lessons.show: Chord charts: Waltzing Matilda with D, A, G, Bm (x24432), Em and E7; Loch Lomond with D, G, A, Bm and Em; Dev marks where the barre Bm sounds best and where the open shapes do.
practice: Player: Loch Lomond at 72, then 84 bpm, keeping the dotted rhythm.
Player: Waltzing Matilda at 84, then 96 bpm.
Lesson: match-pairs of the Australian words and their meanings (a swagman is a wandering worker, a billabong a water hole, a jumbuck a sheep).

units.title: CAGED: one chord, five places
units.goal: See the five open shapes as movable shapes, play any major chord in five places, and use triads high on the neck.

lessons.title: Five shapes, one neck
lessons.goal: See the five open shapes C, A, G, E and D as movable shapes and find the root in each.
lessons.explain: There are only five open major-chord shapes, C, A, G, E and D, and the full major-chord grips up the neck are these same five shapes moved up, with a barre or your fingers acting as the nut. Up the neck they link in the order C-A-G-E-D and then start again, each shape sharing notes with the next. Learn where the roots sit in each shape and you can find any chord anywhere.
lessons.show: Five chord boxes in a row, C (x32010), A (x02220), G (320003), E (022100) and D (xx0232), with every root highlighted; a fretboard figure of C major showing the five shapes overlapping up the neck.
practice: Lesson: choice, Dev shows a shape with its roots marked and you name it (C, A, G, E or D).
Lesson: order, put the shapes in the order they climb the neck from C (C A G E D).
Mic (play-chord): the five open shapes in CAGED order. Without a microphone: chord-build.

lessons.title: C everywhere
lessons.goal: Play C major in all five CAGED shapes, climbing the neck in order.
lessons.explain: From the open C shape, the next C up the neck is the A shape at fret 3, then the G shape with its root on string 6 fret 8 (C), then the E shape at fret 8, then the D shape at fret 10, and then the C shape again, an octave up. Some shapes are comfortable full grips and some work better as partial chords; what matters is seeing the roots.
lessons.show: Six chord boxes: C (x32010), C (x35553), C (875558), C (8-10-10-9-8-8), C (x-x-10-12-13-12) and C (x-15-14-12-13-12); a fretboard figure with every C on the neck.
practice: Player: CAGED: One Chord, Five Shapes, the C bars, one shape per bar at 60 bpm, up and back down.
Fretboard: find every C on the neck in one minute.
Mic (play-chord): Dev names a shape (the G shape, the D shape and so on) and you play that C. Without a microphone: fretboard-find, tap its roots.

lessons.title: G everywhere
lessons.goal: Play G major in five shapes, starting from the open G and climbing.
lessons.explain: The order is the same from any chord; it just starts somewhere else. G begins with the G shape in open position, then the E shape at fret 3, the D shape at fret 5, the C shape at fret 7 and the A shape at fret 10. Moving one system to a new chord is far easier than learning a new system, and that is the whole point of CAGED.
lessons.show: Chord boxes of G (320003), G (355433), G (x-x-5-7-8-7), G (x-10-9-7-8-7) and G (x-10-12-12-12-10); a fretboard figure of all the Gs.
practice: Player: CAGED: One Chord, Five Shapes, the G bars, up and down.
Lesson: choice, you play a D shape with its root on string 4 fret 5 (G): which chord is it? (G). Five rounds with other roots.
Jam: jam track pop-i-iv in G at 90 bpm: play G in a different shape each time it comes round, and find C in the nearest shape.

lessons.title: Triads on the top strings
lessons.goal: Play major triads on strings 3, 2 and 1 in all three inversions, and move G, C and D through one area of the neck.
lessons.explain: A triad is a chord's three notes, root, third and fifth, and on the top three strings each triad has three shapes, named by its lowest note: root position, first inversion (third in the bass) and second inversion (fifth in the bass). These little shapes are the pieces CAGED chords are made of, and they cut through a band where full chords get muddy. Between frets 3 and 8 you can play G/B (x-x-x-4-3-3), C (x-x-x-5-5-3), D (x-x-x-7-7-5) and G/D (x-x-x-7-8-7): listen to the top note climb G, G, A, B.
lessons.show: Fretboard figure of the three C triads on strings 3 to 1: C (x-x-x-5-5-3), C/E (x-x-x-9-8-8) and C/G (x-x-x-12-13-12); then the G, C, D, G set with the top line marked.
practice: Mic (play-chord): the three C triads, low to high. Without a microphone: chord-build.
Player: the G, C, D, G triad set at 72 bpm, one bar each, picked as three single notes, then strummed.
Technique: Triad Inversions on the Top Strings: C, F and G in three shapes each, naming the top note, then C, F, G, C joined by the nearest shapes.
Jam: jam track folk-i-iv-i-v in G at 96 bpm: the triads as a second guitar part while the band strums.

lessons.title: A whole key on three strings
lessons.goal: Play minor triads on strings 3, 2 and 1 and all the main chords of G major in one area of the neck.
lessons.explain: Lower the third of a major triad by one fret and it becomes minor: C (x-x-x-5-5-3) becomes Cm (x-x-x-5-4-3). With major and minor triads you can play every main chord of a key in one small area: in G, between frets 2 and 7, G, Am, Bm, C, D and Em are all within reach. Use them to play songs high on the neck, behind a singer or another guitar.
lessons.show: Fretboard figures of the G major key on strings 3 to 1 between frets 2 and 7: G/B (x-x-x-4-3-3), Am/C (x-x-x-5-5-5), Bm (x-x-x-4-3-2), C (x-x-x-5-5-3), D (x-x-x-7-7-5) and Em/B (x-x-x-4-5-3).
practice: Lesson: chord-build, turn a major triad minor by moving its third.
Mic (play-chord): Dev names a chord of G major and you play its triad between frets 2 and 7. Without a microphone: chord-build.
Jam: jam track fifties-i-vi-iv-v in G at 72 bpm (G, Em, C, D), triads only.
Player: Simple Gifts in G, accompanying the app's melody with triads on strings 3 to 1 instead of open chords.

lessons.title: CAGED check and a second guitar part
lessons.goal: Play any major chord in at least three shapes on request, and accompany a song high on the neck.
lessons.explain: A CAGED test is quick: Dev calls a chord and a shape, and you find it without peeking. Then you play The First Noel as a second guitar, using shapes between frets 5 and 10 while the app plays the open-chord version. Two guitars in different registers sound bigger than two in the same place.
lessons.show: Shape quiz cards; the chord chart of The First Noel (D, G, A) with Dev's high voicings: D (x57775), G (x-10-9-7-8-7) and A (577655).
practice: Lesson: fretboard-find, 10 quick calls (for example, A in the C shape, E in the D shape); tap the roots.
Mic (play-chord): five of the calls, played on the guitar. Without a microphone: fretboard-find.
Player: The First Noel, the second-guitar part with the high shapes, at 80, then 92 bpm.

units.title: Lead guitar: the expressive techniques
units.goal: Play hammer-ons, pull-offs, slides, bends and vibrato in tune and in time, and combine them into phrases that sing.

lessons.title: Legato: hammer, pull, trill
lessons.goal: Play even hammer-ons, pull-offs and trills inside box 1.
lessons.explain: Legato means smooth: notes joined without a new pick stroke. Hammer from just above the string, landing right behind the fret; pull off with a small sideways flick so the string is plucked, not just released. The test of good legato is that every note is as loud as the picked one.
lessons.show: Tab of Hammer and Pull Chains (frets 5-7-8 up across the strings with fingers 1, 3 and 4, then 8-7-5 back down) and a trill on string 3 between string 3 fret 5 (C) and string 3 fret 7 (D); audio.
practice: Technique: Hammer and Pull Chains at 60 bpm, then up the ladder in 4 bpm steps.
Technique: Trills, each finger pair for 10 seconds, four notes per beat at 60 bpm.
Technique: Finger Permutations, starting with 1 this week, then 2, then 3 and 4, and Anchored Fingers: the warm-ups that make every finger independent.
Mic (play-phrase): string 3 fret 5 (C) hammered to string 3 fret 7 (D) and pulled back, eight times; the microphone checks every note sounds. Without a microphone: Record it and listen.

lessons.title: Slides
lessons.goal: Slide to a target note in time, with steady pressure, over short and long distances.
lessons.explain: A slide moves the fretting finger along the string while it stays pressed, so the pitch glides to the new fret. Keep the pressure steady (too light and the note dies, too hard and it drags) and arrive exactly on the beat. Short slides connect notes inside a box; long slides carry you to a new box.
lessons.show: Tab of Lick: Slides: string 3 fret 7 (D) to string 3 fret 9 (E), string 2 fret 8 (G) to string 2 fret 10 (A), and the long slide from string 4 fret 5 (G) to string 4 fret 10 (C); audio.
practice: Technique: Slides to a Target at 60 bpm: land each slide on the click.
Mic (play-phrase): slide from string 3 fret 7 to string 3 fret 9 and check you land on E. Without a microphone: play the target fret first, then compare by ear.
Player: Lick: Slides at 72, then 92 bpm.

lessons.title: Bends in tune
lessons.goal: Bend a whole step and a half step exactly in tune, checked by the microphone.
lessons.explain: A bend pushes the string across the fretboard to raise its pitch. Bend with three fingers together (the ring finger, with the middle and index behind it helping) and turn the wrist as if turning a door handle, rather than pushing with one finger. Always know your target: play the note two frets up first, then bend until you match it.
lessons.show: Tab of the whole-step bends, string 3 fret 7 (D) to the pitch of string 3 fret 9 (E) and string 2 fret 8 (G) to the pitch of string 2 fret 10 (A), and the half-step bend from string 2 fret 8 (G) to the pitch of string 2 fret 9 (G#); a pitch line showing each target.
practice: Technique: Whole-Step Bend in Tune: the target first, string 3 fret 9 (E), then the bend from string 3 fret 7 (D); the microphone checks the held pitch is within 10 cents. Without a microphone: alternate the target and the bend and listen for a match.
Technique: Half-Step Bend in Tune, string 2 fret 8 (G) up to G#.
Player: Lick: Bends in Tune at 60, then 80 bpm.
Technique: Picking-Hand Muting of the Low Strings, so the strings you are not playing stay silent while you bend.

lessons.title: Vibrato
lessons.goal: Add an even vibrato in time to held notes, rising above the pitch and back, never below it.
lessons.explain: Vibrato is a small bend and release, repeated, and it makes a held note sing. This bending vibrato, the usual kind on electric and steel-string guitar, goes up from the note and back, never below it, and it should be even and in time: two waves per beat, then three, then four. Start it a moment after the note and keep it going until the note ends.
lessons.show: Tab of Lick: Vibrato with long notes on string 1 fret 5 (A), string 2 fret 8 (G) and string 3 fret 7 (D) and the vibrato sign; a pitch line of an even vibrato next to a wobbly one.
practice: Technique: Bending Vibrato in Time on string 2 fret 8 (G): 2 waves per beat at 60 bpm, then 3, then 4.
Mic (play-note): hold string 1 fret 5 (A) with vibrato for 4 beats; the microphone shows the pitch line and checks it never dips below A. Without a microphone: Record and compare with Dev's example.
Player: Lick: Vibrato over the slow A minor blues.

lessons.title: Unison bends and pre-bends
lessons.goal: Play a unison bend and a pre-bend and release, in tune and in time.
lessons.explain: A unison bend plays two strings at once: string 2 fret 5 (E) held still and string 3 fret 7 (D) bent up until it matches; when they meet, the beating stops and the sound blooms. A pre-bend is bent silently before you pick it, then released slowly back down, like a sigh. Both need the bending accuracy you built last lesson.
lessons.show: Tab of the unison bend and of the pre-bend and release on string 3 fret 7 (D), silently bent to E, picked and released over one beat; a pitch line of each.
practice: Technique: Unison Bend: bend until the beating stops; the microphone checks the two notes agree. Without a microphone: listen for the wobble to stop.
Technique: Pre-Bend and Release: the microphone checks the start (E) and the end (D). Without a microphone: compare the start with string 3 fret 9 (E) by ear.
Jam: jam track blues-minor in A at 80 bpm: one unison bend and one pre-bend in each chorus.

lessons.title: Phrase like a singer
lessons.goal: Combine slides, hammer-ons, bends and vibrato into short phrases that sound like a voice.
lessons.explain: Listen to a good singer: they rarely sing note, note, note; they slide into notes, bend them, hold them with vibrato and leave space to breathe. Play a phrase you could sing, using one technique per phrase at first. A few notes played with meaning beat many notes played fast.
lessons.show: Three original 2-bar phrases by Dev in box 1, one with a slide in, one with a hammer-on and pull-off, one with a bend and vibrato, as tab with audio.
practice: Player: Dev's three phrases at 70 bpm.
Away from the guitar: sing a short phrase over the backing, then find it in box 1.
Jam: jam track minor-i-bvi-bvii in A at 92 bpm (Am, F, G, Am): call and response with yourself, one technique per phrase.
Record: two minutes; mark your best phrase and learn it properly.

units.title: The pentatonic, all five boxes
units.goal: Learn the other four A minor pentatonic boxes through music, connect them, and use the same shapes as major pentatonic.

lessons.title: Box 2
lessons.goal: Play A minor pentatonic box 2 (frets 7 to 10) and join it to box 1 by their shared notes.
lessons.explain: Box 1 is home, but the same five notes, A C D E G, fill the whole neck in five boxes that overlap like tiles. Box 2 starts where box 1's upper notes are: the notes at fret 8 on strings 6, 2 and 1 and at fret 7 on strings 5, 4 and 3 belong to both. Learn each new box through music, not just up and down.
lessons.show: Fretboard figure, frets 5 to 10, with box 1 and box 2 in two colours and the shared notes outlined; the box 2 notes: string 6 fret 8 (C), string 6 fret 10 (D), string 5 fret 7 (E), string 5 fret 10 (G), string 4 fret 7 (A), string 4 fret 10 (C), string 3 fret 7 (D), string 3 fret 9 (E), string 2 fret 8 (G), string 2 fret 10 (A), string 1 fret 8 (C), string 1 fret 10 (D).
practice: Mic (play-phrase): box 2 up and down at 60 bpm. Without a microphone: the Player in wait mode.
Player: Pentatonic Box 2 Lick at 70, then 90 bpm, with its slide.
Arcade: note-chase in boxes 1 and 2 together.
Jam: jam track funk-one-chord-minor in A at 90 bpm: improvise in boxes 1 and 2 only, crossing between them at the shared notes, and end each phrase on a chord tone.

lessons.title: Box 3
lessons.goal: Play box 3 (frets 9 to 13), the widest of the five, and its lick with a pull-off.
lessons.explain: Box 3 is the widest box, reaching from fret 9 to fret 13, so on some strings you either stretch or shift the hand by a fret; the fingering on screen marks where. Its roots sit at string 5 fret 12 (A) and string 2 fret 10 (A), a handy pair to aim phrases at.
lessons.show: Fretboard figure of box 3: string 6 fret 10 (D), string 6 fret 12 (E), string 5 fret 10 (G), string 5 fret 12 (A), string 4 fret 10 (C), string 4 fret 12 (D), string 3 fret 9 (E), string 3 fret 12 (G), string 2 fret 10 (A), string 2 fret 13 (C), string 1 fret 10 (D), string 1 fret 12 (E), with the A roots marked.
practice: Mic (play-phrase): box 3 up and down slowly. Without a microphone: the Player in wait mode.
Player: Pentatonic Box 3 Lick at 70, then 90 bpm.
Jam: jam track minor-i-bvi-bvii in A at 92 bpm: phrases in box 3 aimed at its two A roots, then slide down into box 2 and back up.
Technique: Gentle Stretch, Walking Down, for the reach box 3 needs; stop as soon as it feels like strain rather than effort.

lessons.title: Boxes 4 and 5
lessons.goal: Play boxes 4 and 5, high on the neck and in their lower octave, with their licks.
lessons.explain: Box 4 lies at frets 12 to 15 and, an octave lower, in open position, where it mixes open strings with notes at frets 1 to 3. Box 5 lies at frets 2 to 5 (or 14 to 17) and leads straight back into box 1 at fret 5, so the circle is closed. The bend in the box 4 lick and the vibrato in the box 5 lick come from your earlier lessons.
lessons.show: Fretboard figures of box 4 at frets 12 to 15 (string 6 fret 12 (E), string 6 fret 15 (G), string 5 fret 12 (A), string 5 fret 15 (C), string 4 fret 12 (D), string 4 fret 14 (E), string 3 fret 12 (G), string 3 fret 14 (A), string 2 fret 13 (C), string 2 fret 15 (D), string 1 fret 12 (E), string 1 fret 15 (G)) and of box 5 at frets 2 to 5 (string 6 fret 3 (G), string 6 fret 5 (A), string 5 fret 3 (C), string 5 fret 5 (D), string 4 fret 2 (E), string 4 fret 5 (G), string 3 fret 2 (A), string 3 fret 5 (C), string 2 fret 3 (D), string 2 fret 5 (E), string 1 fret 3 (G), string 1 fret 5 (A)).
practice: Player: Pentatonic Box 4 Lick, both versions (frets 12 to 15 and open position), with its bend.
Player: Pentatonic Box 5 Lick, ending with vibrato on the last note.
Arcade: note-chase across boxes 4, 5 and 1.
Jam: jam track blues-minor in A at 80 bpm: one chorus in box 4 at fret 12 and one in box 5 at fret 2, ending every phrase on an A.

lessons.title: One map of the neck
lessons.goal: Play one melody that climbs from box 5 through boxes 1, 2, 3 and 4 and back down, moving between boxes by slides.
lessons.explain: Boxes are training wheels; the goal is one map of the neck. The trick is to move between boxes on purpose: slide up one string into the next box, play a phrase there, then slide again. In the Pentatonic Across the Neck study the same climb is played over Am7 and then over C, where the very same notes sound like C major pentatonic.
lessons.show: Fretboard figure, frets 2 to 17, with all five boxes outlined and the study's slide points marked; the study's tab.
practice: Player: Pentatonic Across the Neck, bars 1 to 8 (the climb), in wait mode, then in time at 60 bpm.
Player: all 16 bars at 80 bpm, then the second time through over the C groove.
Arcade: the whole-neck A minor pentatonic chase.

lessons.title: Major pentatonic in the same shapes
lessons.goal: Use the same five shapes as major pentatonic, and play a major-pentatonic melody, Mo Li Hua.
lessons.explain: A minor pentatonic and C major pentatonic contain exactly the same notes, so every box is also a major-pentatonic box: only the home note changes. The practical trick: to play A major pentatonic (A B C# E F#), take the box 1 shape you know and slide it down three frets, to fret 2, because those are the notes of F# minor pentatonic, the relative minor of A. Major pentatonic sounds sweet and open, the sound of country, folk and many melodies.
lessons.show: Fretboard figure of the F# minor box 1 shape at frets 2 to 5, labelled A major pentatonic, with the A roots at string 6 fret 5 (A), string 3 fret 2 (A) and string 1 fret 5 (A) highlighted; then G major pentatonic (G A B D E) for Mo Li Hua.
practice: Mic (play-phrase): the shape at fret 2 from A to A (string 6 fret 5 up to string 3 fret 2), then the whole shape. Without a microphone: the Player in wait mode.
Jam: jam track pop-i-v in A at 96 bpm (A and E): improvise with A major pentatonic, ending on A.
Player: Mo Li Hua (Jasmine Flower) at 56, then 66 bpm, with light slides into the long notes.
Player: two more major-pentatonic melodies: the opening of Morning Mood (E major pentatonic, E F# G# B C#) and the Largo theme from the New World Symphony (D major pentatonic, D E F# A B).

lessons.title: Same notes, two moods
lessons.goal: Improvise across all five boxes over a minor progression, then over a major one using the same notes.
lessons.explain: Same notes, two moods: over Am, G, F and G the boxes sound minor and A is home; over C, G, Am and F the same notes sound major and C is home. Move up the neck during the solo instead of staying in one box, and end each solo on the home note of the progression.
lessons.show: A fretboard map of all five boxes with the A roots and the C roots in two colours; the two chord charts.
practice: Jam: jam track minor-i-bvii-bvi-bvii in A at 96 bpm: two minutes, at least three boxes, end on A.
Jam: jam track pop-axis in C at 92 bpm: the same notes, end on C.
Record: one take of each; listen for where the solo got stuck in one box.

units.title: The blues
units.goal: Play the 12-bar blues in E and A with shuffles, sevenths and turnarounds, solo over it with the blues scale and target notes, and play the minor blues.

lessons.title: The 12-bar in E, quick change
lessons.goal: Play the 12-bar shuffle in E with the quick change, using the open-string shuffle and B7.
lessons.explain: This 12-bar in E adds the quick change: bar 2 jumps to A and back, so the form is E A E E | A A E E | B7 A E B7. The shuffle on E uses the open string 6 with string 5 fret 2 (B) and string 5 fret 4 (C#); on A, the open string 5 with string 4 fret 2 (E) and string 4 fret 4 (F#). The last B7 turns the form around, back to the top.
lessons.show: The 12-bar grid with the quick change marked; tab of one bar of the E and the A shuffle; chord box of B7 (x21202).
practice: Lesson: order, the 12 bars of the quick-change form.
Player: 12-Bar Blues Shuffle in E (quick change), twice through, at 80 bpm.
Jam: jam track blues-quick-change in E at 96 bpm: the shuffle for three choruses.

lessons.title: Seventh chords up the neck
lessons.goal: Play movable dominant-seventh shapes and a whole 12-bar blues in A with A7, D7 and E7 around the 5th fret.
lessons.explain: A blues usually turns all three chords into dominant sevenths, and they all have the same restless job: they want to move. Movable shapes keep the whole blues near the 5th fret: A7 (575655), the E shape, and D7 (x57575) and E7 (x79797), the A shape. The flat seventh in each one (G in A7, C in D7, D in E7) is the blues' signature.
lessons.show: Chord boxes of A7 (575655), D7 (x57575) and E7 (x79797) with the seventh highlighted; the 12-bar in A with these shapes.
practice: Mic (play-chord): the three shapes. Without a microphone: chord-build.
Jam: jam track blues-12-bar in A at 88 bpm: a shuffle strum with these shapes, with short chops on 2 and 4.
Player: 12-Bar Blues Shuffle in A twice through: the two-string shuffle in the first chorus, the three seventh shapes around the 5th fret in the second.
Ear: the seventh-chord drill, major or dominant seventh?

lessons.title: Turnarounds
lessons.goal: Play two turnarounds, in E and in A, that lead back to the top of the form.
lessons.explain: A turnaround fills bars 11 and 12 and says here we go again. In E, over the open string 6, a line falls by half steps on string 3, string 3 fret 7 (D), string 3 fret 6 (C#), string 3 fret 5 (C), string 3 fret 4 (B), each with the open string 1, then B7. In A, the same idea on string 4, from string 4 fret 5 (G) through string 4 fret 4 (F#) and string 4 fret 3 (F) to string 4 fret 2 (E), then E7. Both lines run b7, 6, b6, 5 of the key.
lessons.show: Tab of both turnarounds from Blues Turnarounds in E and A; audio, swung, at 80 bpm.
practice: Player loop: the E turnaround at 60 bpm, then the A turnaround.
Player: Blues Turnarounds in E and A, the full 12-bar choruses, at 80 bpm.
Jam: jam track blues-quick-change in E at 90 bpm: shuffle, and play your turnaround every time bars 11 and 12 come round.

lessons.title: The blues scale
lessons.goal: Solo over a 12-bar in A with the A blues scale, using the blue note as a passing note.
lessons.explain: Add one note to A minor pentatonic and you have the A blues scale: A C D Eb E G. The new note, Eb, is the flat fifth, one of the blue notes (the flat third and flat seventh, C and G, are blue notes too); in box 1 it sits at string 5 fret 6 (Eb) and string 3 fret 8 (Eb). Treat it as a passing note: slide or step through it to D or E rather than stopping on it.
lessons.show: Fretboard figure of box 1 with the two Eb notes added in another colour; tab of an original Dev lick that passes through the blue note.
practice: Mic (play-phrase): string 3 fret 7 (D), string 3 fret 8 (Eb), string 2 fret 5 (E), the blue-note passage, five times. Without a microphone: the Player in wait mode.
Scales: A minor blues, box 1, with the degrees shown.
Jam: jam track blues-12-bar in A at 84 bpm: three choruses, the blue note in every chorus but never as the last note of a phrase.

lessons.title: Major and minor, mixed
lessons.goal: Mix A major and A minor pentatonic over a blues and aim for each chord's notes at the changes.
lessons.explain: Over a blues in A, minor pentatonic sounds tough and bluesy and major pentatonic (the F# minor shape at fret 2) sounds sweet; great blues players mix the two. The ear-opener is to target the chord: over A7 land on its third, string 3 fret 6 (C#); over D7 land on its seventh, string 3 fret 5 (C); over E7 land on its third, string 4 fret 6 (G#).
lessons.show: Fretboard figure, frets 2 to 8, with A minor pentatonic box 1 and A major pentatonic (frets 2 to 5) in two colours and the three target notes highlighted.
practice: Mic (play-note): Dev names a chord (A7, D7 or E7) and you play its target note. Without a microphone: fretboard-find.
Jam: jam track blues-12-bar in A at 80 bpm: chorus 1 minor pentatonic, chorus 2 major pentatonic, chorus 3 both, landing on the targets.
Record: one chorus; listen for whether the targets land at the changes.

lessons.title: The minor blues
lessons.goal: Play the minor blues in A, rhythm and melody, with Am7, Dm7 and E7.
lessons.explain: The minor blues keeps the 12-bar form but makes the I and IV chords minor, Am7 (x02010) and Dm7 (xx0211), while E7 (020100) stays dominant, because its G# pulls home to A. A minor pentatonic fits the whole form, and over the E7 bars the G# is a lovely target.
lessons.show: Chord chart of Minor Blues in A (Am7 4 bars, Dm7 2, Am7 2, E7, Dm7, Am7, E7) with the three boxes; tab of the study's melody in box 1.
practice: Player: Minor Blues in A, the rhythm part, at 72 bpm.
Player: the melody part at 72, then 88 bpm.
Jam: jam track blues-minor in A at 80 bpm: alternate a chorus of the melody with a chorus of your own solo.

units.title: Rhythm guitar in every style
units.goal: Play convincing rhythm in rock, funk, reggae, country, swing and folk.

lessons.title: Rock: the palm-muted gallop
lessons.goal: Play a palm-muted gallop rhythm with accented power chords, picking down, down-up.
lessons.explain: The gallop is an eighth note and two sixteenths, picked down, down-up, over and over: da, da-da. Palm-mute the open string 6 for the gallop and lift the palm for the accented chords, A5 (577xxx), G5 (355xxx), C5 (x355xx) and D5 (x577xx). Rock rhythm is all about tightness: every chug exactly with the drums.
lessons.show: Tab of Power Chords: Palm-Muted Gallop with P.M. and the down, down-up picking marked; a rhythm line of the gallop.
practice: Rhythm: tap the gallop (an eighth and two sixteenths) with the trainer.
Technique: Palm Muting at 100 bpm, then the gallop on the open string 6.
Player: Power Chords: Palm-Muted Gallop at 80, then 100 bpm.
Jam: jam track metal-aeolian in E at 100 bpm (E5, C5, D5, E5): the gallop on E5, accented chords on the changes.

lessons.title: Funk: sixteenths and scratches
lessons.goal: Keep a constant sixteenth-note strumming hand and place E9 chords and muted scratches on chosen sixteenths.
lessons.explain: Funk guitar is a drum part with notes: the strumming hand moves in sixteenths the whole time (down, up, down, up, four strokes per beat), and you decide which strokes hit the chord and which hit muted strings, the scratch. E9 (x-7-6-7-7-7) is the classic funk chord. Release the fretting pressure between hits so everything else stays percussive.
lessons.show: Rhythm grids of two original 2-bar sixteenth patterns with chord hits and scratches marked; chord box of E9 (x-7-6-7-7-7).
practice: Metronome: 70 bpm, sixteenths on muted strings for one minute without stopping.
Player: Strumming: Sixteenth-Note Funk, pattern 1 at 70, then 90 bpm, then pattern 2.
Jam: jam track funk-one-chord-dominant in E at 96 bpm: invent your own pattern of chord hits and keep the hand moving.

lessons.title: Reggae: the offbeat chop
lessons.goal: Play short offbeat chops in a reggae groove, muting each one at once.
lessons.explain: In reggae the guitar plays short, crisp chords off the beat, on the and of each beat (count the same music twice as fast and those chops fall on beats 2 and 4), on strings 4, 3 and 2, and the beats themselves belong to the bass and drums. The chop is short because you release the fretting pressure right after the strum. In the Offbeat Chops study the chords sit high on the neck, starting with Am (x-x-7-5-5-x); for a major groove, G (x-x-5-4-3-x) and C/G (x-x-5-5-5-x) sit right next to each other.
lessons.show: Rhythm line with chops on each and; chord boxes of Am (x-x-7-5-5-x), G (x-x-5-4-3-x) and C/G (x-x-5-5-5-x); audio.
practice: Rhythm: tap only the ands while the trainer plays the beat.
Player: Strumming: Offbeat Chops at 70, then 84 bpm.
Jam: jam track reggae-i-iv in G at 72 bpm: chops on G (x-x-5-4-3-x) and C/G (x-x-5-5-5-x).

lessons.title: Country and bluegrass rhythm
lessons.goal: Play bluegrass-style bass-strum rhythm with alternating bass notes and the G-run ending.
lessons.explain: Country and bluegrass rhythm is boom-chick with more motion: the bass notes alternate, and phrases end with a quick run. The G-run style ending: the open string 3 (G), string 4 fret 2 (E), the open string 4 (D), then a hammer-on from the open string 5 to string 5 fret 2 (B), landing on string 6 fret 3 (G) on beat 1. Pick it with alternate strokes and keep it strictly in time.
lessons.show: Tab of the G-run ending and of one bar of bass-strum on G, C and D; audio of Bluegrass Rhythm and the G Run.
practice: Player loop: the G-run ending at 60, then 90 bpm.
Player: Bluegrass Rhythm and the G Run at 90, then 110 bpm.
Jam: jam track country-ii7 in G at 110 bpm (G, A7, D7, G): bass-strum, ending every 8 bars with the run; under A7 alternate the open string 5 (A) and the open string 6 (E).

lessons.title: Swing, and the click on 2 and 4
lessons.goal: Feel swing and play a shuffle against a metronome that clicks only on beats 2 and 4.
lessons.explain: Swing turns pairs of eighth notes into long-short, like a triplet with the middle note left out, and jazz, blues and rockabilly all live on it. Set the click on beats 2 and 4 only, where the snare drum plays: you feel 1 and 3 yourself, and your time gets much stronger.
lessons.show: Rhythm line comparing straight eighths, triplets and swung eighths; the metronome set to click on 2 and 4.
practice: Rhythm: straight versus swung eighths; tap them and hear the difference.
Technique: Metronome on 2 and 4 at 60 bpm: swung eighths on A7, then up the ladder toward 100.
Jam: jam track blues-slow-12-8 in A at 56 bpm: feel the slow 12/8 groove, chords on the beat.

lessons.title: Folk colour: sus chords
lessons.goal: Decorate open chords with sus2 and sus4 hammer-ons and pull-offs, folk style, and use them in Shenandoah.
lessons.explain: Folk players keep a chord ringing and move one finger to add colour: from D, lift finger 2 for Dsus2 (xx0230) or add finger 4 for Dsus4 (xx0233), then come back. On A, Asus2 (x02200) and Asus4 (x02230) work the same way. The suspended note wants to resolve back to the chord's third, which gives a gentle push and release.
lessons.show: Chord boxes of D (xx0232), Dsus2 (xx0230), Dsus4 (xx0233), A (x02220), Asus2 (x02200) and Asus4 (x02230); a rhythm line of a strum with a hammer-on on the and of 2.
practice: Mic (play-chord): D, Dsus4, D, Dsus2, D. Without a microphone: chord-build.

Player: Sus Chords and Chord Embellishments, the folk pattern with the decorated chord on beat 3: D with Dsus4 and Dsus2, A with Asus4 and Asus2, then C with Cadd9 (x32030), which keeps its third and adds the ninth.
Jam: jam track folk-sus in D at 90 bpm (D, Dsus4, D, Dsus2).
Player: Shenandoah at 52, then 60 bpm, with your own sus decorations on the long D and A chords.

units.title: Fingerstyle: thumb and fingers
units.goal: Play arpeggio patterns, Travis picking, thumb-lead and fingerstyle blues, and a complete fingerstyle solo.

lessons.title: Thumb and fingers: p i m a
lessons.goal: Give the thumb the bass and i, m and a strings 3, 2 and 1, and play three arpeggio patterns.
lessons.explain: Fingerstyle gives each finger a job: the thumb (p) plays the bass strings, the index (i) string 3, the middle (m) string 2 and the ring finger (a) string 1. Pluck from the knuckle, not by pulling the whole hand, and keep the hand still above the strings. Start with p-i-m-a, then p-a-m-i, then p-i-m-a-m-i.
lessons.show: Tab of Fingerstyle: p i m a over C (x32010), Am (x02210), Dm (xx0231) and G7 (320001) with the finger letters above the notes; a hand diagram with p, i, m and a labelled.
practice: Technique: Free-Stroke Arpeggios (p i m a) on C, one bar per pattern at 60 bpm.
Player: Fingerstyle: p i m a, bars 1 to 8, at 60, then 80 bpm.
Player: bars 9 to 16 (p-a-m-i, then p-i-m-a-m-i with the pinch on beat 1).
Player: All Through the Night, a slow p-i-m-a accompaniment on G, C, D and Em under the app's melody.

lessons.title: A flowing arpeggio in 3/4
lessons.goal: Play the p-i-m-a-m-i arpeggio across a 3/4 bar and accompany The Ash Grove with it.
lessons.explain: Six eighth notes fill a 3/4 bar exactly: p-i-m-a-m-i, the thumb on the root, then up and back down. It flows like water, which is why it suits waltzes and slow songs. Later in the study a melody note goes on top on beat 1, played by a together with the thumb: your first pinch.
lessons.show: Tab of Fingerstyle: p i m a m i in 3/4 over Am (x02210), Dm (xx0231), E (022100) and Am, with the thumb on strings 5, 4, 6 and 5; audio.
practice: Player: the study, bars 1 to 8 at 60 bpm, then bars 9 to 16 with the melody notes.
Player: The Ash Grove at 72, then 96 bpm: the app plays the melody and you play the p-i-m-a-m-i accompaniment on G, C, D and Em.
Record: one verse; check that the thumb notes are a little louder than the fingers.

lessons.title: Travis picking
lessons.goal: Play a Travis pattern: an alternating thumb that never stops, with the fingers picking in between.
lessons.explain: Travis picking is the engine of folk and country fingerstyle: the thumb alternates between two bass strings on every beat, steady as a clock, while i and m pick the treble strings between the thumb notes. On C (x32010) the thumb plays string 5 fret 3 (C), string 4, string 6 fret 3 (G), string 4, so finger 3 hops between strings 5 and 6. Get the thumb on autopilot first, then add the fingers.
lessons.show: Tab of Travis Thumb, Muted on C, then of Travis Picking over C, G7 and Am, with the thumb notes stems down and the finger notes stems up; audio.
practice: Technique: Travis Thumb, Muted: the thumb only, palm lightly muting, 2 minutes at 60 bpm.
Player: Travis Picking at 60, then 80 bpm.
Away from the guitar: tap the thumb part on your knee and the finger part on a table, together.

lessons.title: A melody over the Travis thumb
lessons.goal: Carry a melody on top of the Travis thumb and play Down by the Riverside fingerstyle.
lessons.explain: Now the fingers stop playing a pattern and play a tune: the thumb keeps its job, and each melody note falls either with a thumb note (a pinch) or between thumb notes (syncopated). If the thumb stumbles, slow down, because the thumb is your metronome. Down by the Riverside in C uses C, G7 and F (xx3211), and under F the thumb alternates string 4 fret 3 (F) and string 3.
lessons.show: Tabs of Travis Picking with a Melody and of Down by the Riverside (Travis style), with the melody notes highlighted; audio.
practice: Player: Travis Picking with a Melody at 60, then 76 bpm.
Player, wait mode: Down by the Riverside (Travis style), the first 8 bars.
Player: the whole arrangement at 64, then 80 bpm.

lessons.title: Thumb-lead and fingerstyle blues
lessons.goal: Play a melody with the thumb on the bass strings, and a fingerstyle blues over a steady thumb.
lessons.explain: Two more fingerstyle engines. In thumb-lead style the thumb plays the melody on strings 6 to 4 while the index brushes the top strings on the offbeats. In fingerstyle blues the thumb thumps steady quarter notes on the open low strings while the fingers play a blues melody in open E, including the flat fifth, a blue note, at string 3 fret 3 (Bb).
lessons.show: Tabs of Thumb-Lead Melody with Brush Strums (C, F, G7) and of Fingerstyle Blues in E (steady thumb); audio.
practice: Technique: Thumb Independence at 50 bpm: a steady thumb on the open string 6 and string 4 fret 2 (E) under E, with i playing off the beat on string 3.
Player: Thumb-Lead Melody with Brush Strums at 70 bpm.
Player: Fingerstyle Blues in E at 60, then 76 bpm.

lessons.title: A complete fingerstyle solo: Greensleeves
lessons.goal: Play a complete fingerstyle solo, Greensleeves, with melody and bass together in 6/8.
lessons.explain: Greensleeves was registered in 1580 and is still one of the best fingerstyle tunes there is. The setting puts a bass note on each dotted-quarter beat, the melody on top and arpeggios in between, over the harmony Am, G, Am, E and so on. Both F and F# are traditional for the melody's sixth note: choose one and keep it.
lessons.show: Tab of Greensleeves (fingerstyle) with the melody notes highlighted and the chord names above; chord boxes of Am (x02210), G (320003), E (022100) and C (x32010).
practice: Player, wait mode: the A section.
Player loop: two bars at a time at 40 bpm (dotted-quarter beat), then join them.
Player: the whole piece at 46, then 54 bpm.
Record: a complete performance. If you want a second solo, Si Bheag, Si Mhor is next.

units.title: Seventh chords
units.goal: Hear, play and use the four main seventh chords, in open and movable shapes, in a key and in songs.

lessons.title: Four seventh-chord colours
lessons.goal: Hear the four main seventh chords, maj7, 7, m7 and m7b5, and play the major and minor sevenths in open position.
lessons.explain: Add a fourth note, the seventh, to a triad and the chord gets a whole new colour. Major seventh (1 3 5 7) is dreamy, dominant seventh (1 3 5 b7) wants to move, minor seventh (1 b3 5 b7) is smooth, half-diminished (1 b3 b5 b7) is dark and restless. Open shapes to start: Cmaj7 (x32000), Fmaj7 (xx3210), Amaj7 (x02120), Dmaj7 (xx0222), Am7 (x02010), Em7 (022030) and Dm7 (xx0211).
lessons.show: Chord boxes of the seven open shapes grouped by type; a keyboard figure of Cmaj7 = C E G B, C7 = C E G Bb, Cm7 = C Eb G Bb and Cm7b5 = C Eb Gb Bb; audio of each.
practice: Ear: the seventh-chord quality drill (maj7, 7, m7, m7b5), 10 rounds.
Mic (play-chord): the seven open shapes in turn. Without a microphone: chord-build.
Jam: jam track soul-imaj7-ivmaj7 in C at 70 bpm: Cmaj7 and Fmaj7, slow strums.
Player: Gymnopedie No. 1, the opening accompaniment only: Gmaj7 (3x443x) and Dmaj7 (xx0222), bass on beat 1 and the chord on beats 2 and 3, very slow.

lessons.title: Movable seventh chords
lessons.goal: Play movable seventh chords with the root on string 6 and on string 5.
lessons.explain: With the root on string 6: A7 (575655), Am7 (575555) and Amaj7 (5x665x). With the root on string 5: D7 (x57575), Dm7 (x57565), Dmaj7 (x5767x) and the half-diminished Bm7b5 (x2323x). The rule is the same as for barre chords: the root on string 6 or 5 names the chord, so you can now play any seventh chord in any key.
lessons.show: Chord boxes in two rows (root on string 6, root on string 5) with the root and the seventh of each marked.
practice: Mic (play-chord): Dev names a seventh chord (for example Gm7, Cmaj7, F7, Em7b5) and you find it. Without a microphone: fretboard-find for the root, then chord-build.
Lesson: match-pairs, chord type and formula.
Jam: jam track funk-ii-v-vamp in C at 96 bpm (Dm7, G7): Dm7 (x57565) to G7 (353433).

lessons.title: The seventh chords of a key
lessons.goal: Play the seven seventh chords of C major and hear how each one behaves.
lessons.explain: Stack every note of C major in thirds and you get its seven sevenths: Cmaj7 Dm7 Em7 Fmaj7 G7 Am7 Bm7b5. The pattern is the same in every major key: maj7 on I and IV, m7 on ii, iii and vi, a dominant 7 only on V, and m7b5 on vii. Only one chord in the key is a dominant seventh, which is why it is so good at leading home.
lessons.show: A table of the seven chords with their numerals (Imaj7, ii7, iii7, IVmaj7, V7, vi7, vii m7b5) and a movable shape for each between frets 3 and 10; audio.
practice: Lesson: fill-blanks, the qualities of the seven chords of C.
Mic (play-chord): the seven chords up the neck in order. Without a microphone: chord-build.
Jam: jam track rnb-descending in C at 70 bpm (Fmaj7, Em7, Dm7, Cmaj7).

lessons.title: Dominants that point elsewhere
lessons.goal: Play songs whose dominant chords lead somewhere other than home: Home on the Range and Danny Boy.
lessons.explain: Sometimes a dominant seventh points at a chord other than I. In Home on the Range, A7 leads to D7, which leads home to G: A7 is the dominant of D. In Danny Boy, in C, D7 leads to G and E7 to Am. When you meet a dominant seventh that is not the V of the key, look where it goes next: it is a signpost.
lessons.show: Chord charts of Home on the Range (G, C, D7, A7) and Danny Boy (C, C7, F, G7, Am, Dm, D7, E7), with an arrow from each signpost chord to its target.
practice: Player: Home on the Range at 84, then 96 bpm, waltz strum.
Player: Danny Boy at 56, then 66 bpm, melody with chords: the app plays the melody first, then you do.
Ear: listen-choice, after A7, which chord comes next, D7 or C? Six rounds with different signposts.

lessons.title: The ragtime cycle
lessons.goal: Strum and fingerpick the ragtime cycle of dominant sevenths, C A7 D7 G7, with a swing feel.
lessons.explain: Chain those signposts and you get the ragtime progression: C, A7, D7, G7, each one the dominant of the next, until G7 leads home to C. It is the sound of ragtime, early jazz and a lot of country swing. Strum it with swing first; then try the Ragtime Blues study, where the thumb alternates bass strings under a syncopated melody.
lessons.show: Chord boxes of C (x32010), A7 (x02020), D7 (xx0212) and G7 (320001); a circle diagram showing each chord falling a fifth to the next.
practice: Lesson: order, put the cycle in order so each chord is the dominant of the next (A7, D7, G7, C).
Jam: jam track secondary-ragtime in C at 110 bpm, swung strumming.
Player: Ragtime Blues in C, the first 8 bars, in wait mode, then at 60 bpm.

lessons.title: Seventh-chord songbook
lessons.goal: Use seventh chords in three songs and pass a seventh-chord quiz by ear and by shape.
lessons.explain: Seventh chords are now part of your vocabulary, so use them where they belong: Nobody Knows the Trouble I've Seen with C7 as a bluesy IV7, La Paloma's habanera rhythm over G, D7 and C, and John Henry's E7, A7 and B7. Then the quiz: quality by ear, shape by name.
lessons.show: Three chord charts; a rhythm line of the habanera (dotted eighth, sixteenth, eighth, eighth).
practice: Player: Nobody Knows the Trouble I've Seen at 66 bpm with C7 (x32310) under the IV.
Player: La Paloma at 66 bpm with the habanera rhythm.
Ear: the seventh-chord quality drill, 10 rounds; aim for 8.
Mic (play-chord): five named seventh chords from anywhere on the neck. Without a microphone: chord-build.

units.title: The major scale, everywhere
units.goal: Play the major scale in first position and in the five CAGED positions, make music with it, and flatpick fiddle tunes and jigs.

lessons.title: G major in first position
lessons.goal: Play G major over two octaves in first position with strict alternate picking.
lessons.explain: The major scale is the ruler behind everything you have played: its seven notes give you keys, chords and melodies. G major in first position runs from string 6 fret 3 (G) up two octaves to string 1 fret 3 (G), with F# at string 4 fret 4 (F#) and string 1 fret 2 (F#). Pick strictly down-up, starting down, even when you cross strings.
lessons.show: Fretboard figure of G major, frets 0 to 4, with the degrees 1 to 7 coloured and the three Gs marked; tab of Alternate Picking: G Major, Two Octaves.
practice: Technique: Alternate Picking: G Major, Two Octaves at 60 bpm in eighths, up the ladder in 4 bpm steps.
Mic (play-phrase): the scale up and down at 60 bpm. Without a microphone: the Player in wait mode.
Lesson: degree-in-key drill, for example which degree is B in G major? (3).

lessons.title: C major in five positions
lessons.goal: Play C major in the five CAGED positions and join them up the neck.
lessons.explain: Each CAGED chord shape has a scale position around it: C major in the C shape (frets 0 to 3), the A shape (frets 2 to 6), the G shape (frets 4 to 8), the E shape (frets 7 to 10) and the D shape (frets 9 to 13). Play each position from its lowest C to its highest C and back, then find where neighbouring positions overlap. The chord shape inside each position shows you where the roots are.
lessons.show: Fretboard figures of the five positions with the C roots and the chord shape inside each outlined; tab of CAGED: The Major Scale in Five Positions.
practice: Player: CAGED: The Major Scale in Five Positions, one position per session, root to root at 60 bpm.
Scales: C major in the CAGED system, each position with the degrees shown.
Arcade: the C major position game, one position at a time.

lessons.title: One melody, five places
lessons.goal: Play the same 8-bar melody in all five positions, with the matching chord shape as accompaniment.
lessons.explain: Knowing a position means you can play music in it, not just a scale. The study takes one original 8-bar melody and moves it through all five positions: the same notes in different places with different fingerings. This is how you stop being stuck in one area of the neck.
lessons.show: Tab of the melody in the C shape and in the E shape side by side, with the matching chord shapes from CAGED: One Chord, Five Shapes.
practice: Player: CAGED: One Melody Everywhere, position 1 (the C shape) in wait mode, then in time at 72 bpm.
Player: the next position each session until all five are done.
Fretboard: name each melody note in the position you are learning.

lessons.title: Scale sequences
lessons.goal: Play the major scale in thirds and in groups of three and four within one position.
lessons.explain: Running a scale straight up and down is like reciting the alphabet; sequences turn it into music and train the hand to skip. In thirds you play 1-3, 2-4, 3-5; in groups of three, 1-2-3, 2-3-4, 3-4-5; in groups of four, 1-2-3-4, 2-3-4-5. The Scales screen lays any sequence out in any position.
lessons.show: Tab of C major in the E-shape position (frets 7 to 10) in thirds and in groups of three; a degree line showing each pattern.
practice: Scales: C major, E-shape position, the thirds sequence at 60 bpm.
Scales: groups of three, then groups of four.
Technique: Double Stops: Thirds and Sixths, the thirds of G major on strings 3 and 2, both notes together, moving up the neck.
Jam: jam track pop-axis in C at 92 bpm: improvise with sequences only for a minute, then break out of them.

lessons.title: Fiddle tunes
lessons.goal: Flatpick two fiddle tunes, Soldier's Joy and Turkey in the Straw, with alternate picking in AABB form.
lessons.explain: Fiddle tunes are the guitarist's best picking workout: continuous eighth notes, string crossings and a clear AABB form with eight bars per part. Pick down on the beat and up on the and, always, even when you cross strings. Soldier's Joy is in D and Turkey in the Straw in G.
lessons.show: Tab of the A parts of both tunes with the pick directions; a form chart A A B B.
practice: Technique: String Crossing Both Ways at 60 bpm.
Player: Soldier's Joy, the A part and then the B part in wait mode, then the whole tune at 72, then 88 bpm.
Player: Turkey in the Straw the same way, with the app playing backup chords (G, C, D). Arkansas Traveler is next if you want a third.

lessons.title: Jigs in 6/8
lessons.goal: Pick a jig in 6/8, The Irish Washerwoman, in groups of three.
lessons.explain: A jig is in 6/8: two beats per bar, each made of three eighth notes. Pick each group down-up-down; when that feels comfortable, try down-up-down, up-down-up, which keeps strict alternation. Feel the lilt by giving the first note of each group a little more weight.
lessons.show: Tab of the A part of The Irish Washerwoman with both picking options marked; a rhythm line of 6/8.
practice: Rhythm: tap 6/8 groups with accents on 1 and 4.
Player: The Irish Washerwoman, the A part at 60 bpm (dotted-quarter beat), then the B part.
Player: the whole tune at 76, then 92 bpm; then Haste to the Wedding for a second jig.

units.title: Know the neck, read the music
units.goal: Name any note on the neck quickly and read standard notation in first and second position.

lessons.title: Strings 6 and 5, instantly
lessons.goal: Name any note on strings 6 and 5 in under three seconds.
lessons.explain: You know the natural notes on strings 6 and 5 from barre chords; now make them instant. Use landmarks: string 6 fret 5 (A) and string 6 fret 12 (E), string 5 fret 5 (D) and string 5 fret 12 (A), and the dots at frets 3, 5, 7, 9 and 12 as signposts. Sharps and flats are one fret either side of a natural.
lessons.show: Fretboard figure, frets 0 to 12, of strings 6 and 5 with all notes, the naturals in bold and the inlay dots shown.
practice: Fretboard: strings 6 and 5, one-minute rounds; aim for 25 right.
Mic (play-note): Dev names a note and you play it on string 6, then on string 5. Without a microphone: fretboard-find.
Lesson: type-answer, which note is string 5 fret 8? (F).

lessons.title: Every note on every string
lessons.goal: Find any note on all six strings using octave shapes.
lessons.explain: Octave shapes carry what you know on strings 6 and 5 across the neck: from string 6, the octave is two strings over and two frets up (string 6 fret 3 (G) to string 4 fret 5 (G)), and from string 5 the same (string 5 fret 3 (C) to string 3 fret 5 (C)). Across the B string the shape stretches by one fret: from string 4, two strings over and three frets up (string 4 fret 2 (E) to string 2 fret 5 (E)), and the same from string 3 to string 1. And string 1 has exactly the same notes as string 6.
lessons.show: Fretboard figure with the octave shapes drawn between the string pairs 6-4, 5-3, 4-2 and 3-1; a board showing every C on the neck.
practice: Fretboard: find every C, then every F#, on all six strings, one minute each.
Mic (play-note): Dev names a note and a string and you play it. Without a microphone: fretboard-find.
Technique: Octave Shapes with Muting: the G major scale in octaves on strings 6 and 4, with finger 1 muting the string in between.
Live Fretboard: if you have a camera, point it at the neck and let it label the notes under your fingers.

lessons.title: Reading music: strings 1 to 3
lessons.goal: Read standard notation on strings 1 to 3 in first position, in C major.
lessons.explain: Standard notation shows rhythm exactly, and it is what most printed music uses. Guitar music is written in the treble clef an octave higher than it sounds. Start with the top three strings in first position: the open string 3 (G) is written on the second line from the bottom, the open string 2 (B) on the middle line and the open string 1 (E) in the top space.
lessons.show: A staff with the notes of strings 1 to 3 in first position (G A B C D E F G) above a matching fretboard figure; the first 4 bars of Reading: First Position in C.
practice: Lesson: staff-read, name 10 notes from the staff.
Lesson: staff-place, put the note for string 2 fret 1 (C) on the staff.
Player: Reading: First Position in C from notation only (tab hidden), in wait mode, then at 60 bpm.

lessons.title: Reading all six strings
lessons.goal: Read across all six strings in first position, in G major with F#.
lessons.explain: The low strings take you below the staff onto ledger lines: the open string 6 (E) is written below three ledger lines. G major has one sharp in its key signature, F#, so every F is played as F#: string 4 fret 4 (F#) and string 1 fret 2 (F#). Read ahead: let your eyes stay a beat in front of your fingers.
lessons.show: A staff with the first-position notes of strings 4 to 6 and their ledger lines; the key signature of G with its F#; the first 4 bars of Reading: First Position in G.
practice: Lesson: staff-read, 10 notes on strings 4 to 6.
Player: Reading: First Position in G from notation, in wait mode, then at 60 bpm.
Player: Minuet in G (melody) from notation, the first half, in wait mode.

lessons.title: Sharps, dots, ties and second position
lessons.goal: Read in D and A major with dotted rhythms and ties, and start reading in second position.
lessons.explain: D major adds C#, at string 5 fret 4 (C#) and string 2 fret 2 (C#), to the F#, and A major adds G#, at string 3 fret 1 (G#). A dot makes a note half as long again, and a tie joins two notes into one longer sound, even across a bar line. In second position finger 1 sits at fret 2, so you no longer need the open strings.
lessons.show: Staff examples of a dotted quarter and of a tie across a bar line; the key signatures of D and A; a fretboard figure of second position (finger 1 at fret 2).
practice: Rhythm: tap dotted-quarter-and-eighth patterns and tied notes from notation.
Player: Reading: Sharps and Dotted Rhythms from notation, in wait mode, then at 60 bpm.
Player: Reading: Second Position, the first 8 bars.
Player: the Dance of the Sugar Plum Fairy theme from notation, light and detached, checking every accidental.

lessons.title: Read a real piece: Minuet in G
lessons.goal: Play the Minuet in G melody from notation, start to finish, while the app plays the bass.
lessons.explain: This minuet, long credited to Bach and now attributed to Christian Petzold, has two halves, each repeated, and lies mostly in first position. Because guitar music is written an octave higher than it sounds, the guitar part reads exactly like the keyboard's right hand. Watch the repeat signs: the road map is part of reading.
lessons.show: Notation of the minuet's upper voice with the repeat signs highlighted; a fretboard figure of the one shift up string 1 in the second half.
practice: Lesson: staff-read, the notes of bars 1 to 4.
Player: notation only, in wait mode, the first half; then the second half.
Player: the whole piece with repeats at 80, then 100 bpm, with the app playing the bass.

units.title: Improvising with intent
units.goal: Make solos follow the chords with arpeggios, chord tones and target notes, build them from motifs, and add the Dorian and Mixolydian colours.

lessons.title: Arpeggios
lessons.goal: Play the triad arpeggios of C major in first position and use them as a source of melody.
lessons.explain: An arpeggio is a chord played one note at a time, and it is the most direct way to make a solo fit the chords, because every note is a chord tone. Play each chord of C major as an arpeggio from its root: C (C E G), Dm (D F A), Em (E G B), F (F A C), G (G B D), Am (A C E). Then build a short melody out of them.
lessons.show: Tab of Triad Arpeggios in First Position; fretboard figures of the C and F arpeggios with roots, thirds and fifths coloured.
practice: Player: Triad Arpeggios in First Position at 60, then 80 bpm, alternate picked.
Lesson: chord-tones drill, for example which notes are in Em? (E G B).
Jam: jam track fifties-i-vi-iv-v in C at 72 bpm: arpeggiate each chord as it comes.

lessons.title: Chord tones on the beat
lessons.goal: Improvise over C, Am, F and G, putting a chord tone on beat 1 of every bar.
lessons.explain: A solo sounds connected to the band when its strong beats land on chord tones, the root, third or fifth of the chord being played. In between, any note of the scale works as a passing note. So the game is: on every beat 1, play a note of the current chord.
lessons.show: The four chord-tone sets (C: C E G; Am: A C E; F: F A C; G: G B D) on a fretboard figure of the E-shape position of C major (frets 7 to 10).
practice: Jam: jam track fifties-i-vi-iv-v in C at 66 bpm: one note per bar, on beat 1, always a chord tone.
Jam: jam track fifties-i-vi-iv-v in C again, now with two notes per beat between the downbeats.
Record: one minute; listen to how the downbeats lock with the chords.

lessons.title: Aim for the third
lessons.goal: Aim for the third of each new chord exactly at the change.
lessons.explain: The third tells the ear whether a chord is major or minor, so landing on it at a change is the strongest move you have. Over C, Am, F and G the thirds are E, C, A and B. Plan each phrase to arrive on the next chord's third right on the change, and your solo starts to sound composed.
lessons.show: Fretboard figure (frets 7 to 10) with the four thirds highlighted; a line drawing a phrase travelling to each target.
practice: Lesson: fretboard-find, tap the third of each chord in this position.
Jam: jam track fifties-i-vi-iv-v in C at 66 bpm: play only the thirds, one per bar; then approach each one from a step above or below.
Jam: jam track fifties-i-vi-iv-v in C at 72 bpm: a free solo that lands on the thirds at the changes.

lessons.title: Motifs and space
lessons.goal: Build a solo from one short motif, repeated and varied, with space between phrases.
lessons.explain: Great solos are not strings of licks; they develop an idea. Take a short motif, three to five notes, play it, repeat it, then vary it: change the rhythm, move it to another chord tone, add a bend at the end. Leave space between phrases so the band and the listener can breathe.
lessons.show: An original 2-bar motif by Dev and four variations as tab: same rhythm with new notes, same notes with a new rhythm, moved up the neck, extended with a bend.
practice: Player: Dev's motif and its four variations at 72 bpm.
Jam: jam track minor-i-bvi-bvii in A at 92 bpm: one motif, at least four variations, and a bar of rest after each phrase.
Record: a two-minute solo; count how often you came back to your motif.

lessons.title: Two new colours: Dorian and Mixolydian
lessons.goal: Hear and use two new colours: Dorian (minor with a bright sixth) and Mixolydian (major with a flat seventh).
lessons.explain: A Dorian is A minor with F# instead of F: it sounds minor but brighter, and the D chord in its vamp, Am to D, carries that F#. A Mixolydian is A major with G instead of G#: it sounds major but bluesy and relaxed, and its vamp is A to G. Many fiddle tunes live here: Old Joe Clark and Red Haired Boy are A Mixolydian, and Drunken Sailor, which you already know, is E Dorian.
lessons.show: Fretboard figures of A Dorian (A B C D E F# G) and A Mixolydian (A B C# D E F# G) in fifth position with the colour notes F# and G marked; chord boxes of the vamps Am (x02210) to D (xx0232) and A (x02220) to G (320003).
practice: Player: Mode Study: A Dorian at 72 bpm, then Mode Study: A Mixolydian.
Jam: jam track mixolydian-i-bvii in A at 104 bpm: improvise, landing on G at least four times.
Player: Old Joe Clark at 80, then 96 bpm: every G is natural; then Red Haired Boy, the same mode in a longer tune, in wait mode.

lessons.title: A solo with a story
lessons.goal: Play a planned two-chorus blues solo with a beginning, a climb and an ending.
lessons.explain: A solo with a story has a shape: start low and simple with a motif; build by moving up the neck, playing more notes and adding bends; peak in the second chorus; then wind down and end clearly on the home note. Plan it on paper first, then let it breathe when you play.
lessons.show: A two-chorus map of the 12-bar with the planned shape drawn as a line rising and falling, and the boxes for each section: boxes 5 and 1 low, boxes 2 and 3 for the climb, box 4 for the peak.
practice: Create: plan your solo: which boxes, which motif, where the peak is.
Jam: jam track blues-quick-change in A at 92 bpm: your two choruses, three takes.
Record: the best take, checked against Dev's list: a motif, space, at least two techniques, target notes at the changes and a clear ending on A.

units.title: By ear, in time, in a band
units.goal: Find keys, chords and melodies by ear, move songs to any key, lock in with a band and shape your tone, then play a full band arrangement.

lessons.title: Finding the key by ear
lessons.goal: Find the key of a piece by ear: its home note, and whether it is major or minor.
lessons.explain: Almost every song has a home note, the one that feels like rest at the end. Hum along, find the note you keep wanting to land on, and find it on string 6 or 5: that is the root of the key. Then listen to the home chord: major or minor?
lessons.show: Audio examples (original phrases and public-domain tunes) with a reveal card showing the home note on the neck and the key.
practice: Ear: the home-note drill: hear a phrase and play the note that sounds like home; the microphone checks it. Without a microphone: choose it on a keyboard figure.
Ear: major or minor, ten short excerpts.
Lesson: listen-choice, which key is this tune in? (Swing Low, Sweet Chariot, played by the app in D, then in G).

lessons.title: Chords by ear
lessons.goal: Work out the chords of a simple song by ear, from its bass notes and the I, IV, V and vi of its key.
lessons.explain: Most songs use a handful of chords from their key, so once you know the key you have a short list to try: I, IV, V and vi first. Listen to the bass, which usually plays each chord's root; find the bass notes on string 6 or 5, then decide major or minor for each chord. Today the app plays Amazing Grace in A and you work out its chords without a chart.
lessons.show: A blank chord chart of Amazing Grace with the bar lines; the I, IV, V and vi chords of A (A, D, E, F#m) as a menu; a reveal card at the end.
practice: Ear: the bass-note drill: hear a bass line and play it on string 6 or 5. Without a microphone: tap it on a fretboard figure.
Ear: the chord-in-key drill, I, IV, V or vi?
Player: Amazing Grace played by the app in A with the chords hidden: write them bar by bar, then compare with the reveal.

lessons.title: A melody by ear
lessons.goal: Learn a melody by ear, phrase by phrase, without tab: Shenandoah.
lessons.explain: Learning by ear is a superpower, and it is learned in small steps: listen to one phrase until you can sing it, find its first note, then find the rest one note at a time. Most melodies move by step or by small leaps, so the next note is usually close by. When you have it, check it against the tab.
lessons.show: Audio of Shenandoah phrase by phrase with a loop button; a fretboard figure that shows only the first note; the tab, revealed at the end.
practice: Ear: melodic dictation, three-note and four-note phrases.
Player: Shenandoah, audio only, one phrase on loop at a time; find each phrase on the guitar.
Player: compare with the revealed tab and play the whole melody at 60 bpm.

lessons.title: Any song, any key
lessons.goal: Use transposition and the capo to put any song in a key that suits a singer and your hands.
lessons.explain: You change key by moving every chord the same distance, and with roman numerals that is easy, because I-IV-V means the same thing in every key. A capo does the moving for you: a song in Bb, Eb and F becomes the shapes G, C and D with the capo at fret 3. Nashville numbers write a chart as 1, 4, 5, so a band can play it in any key on the spot.
lessons.show: A chart written in numbers (1 | 4 | 1 | 5) with three keys under it (G, A, D); a table of capo positions for a song in Bb, Eb and F.
practice: Lesson: choice, with the capo at fret 3 you play the G, C and D shapes: which chords sound? (Bb, Eb, F).
Lesson: type-answer, move G, Em, C, D up a whole step (A, F#m, D, E).
Jam: jam track folk-i-iv-i-v in Bb at 100 bpm: capo at fret 3, play the G-shape version; then play it again with barre chords and no capo.
Player: O Come, All Ye Faithful with the capo at fret 3, so the G shapes sound in Bb; then try other capo frets and keep the one that suits your voice.

lessons.title: Locking in with the band
lessons.goal: Play rhythm guitar in a band: lock with the drums, leave space for others, and follow the song's sections.
lessons.explain: In a band your job is to make the song feel good, not to fill every gap. Lock your strum to the kick drum and snare, play less when someone sings or solos, and play bigger in the chorus than in the verse. Count-ins, endings and section changes are where bands fall apart, so count, look up, and follow the chart.
lessons.show: A song chart with sections (intro, verse, chorus, solo, outro) over the I-V-vi-IV progression, dynamics marked (verse soft, chorus loud), and a two-guitar arrangement: one strumming open chords, one playing triads high up.
practice: Technique: Metronome on 2 and 4 at 80 bpm, folk strum on G.
Jam: jam track pop-axis in G at 96 bpm: follow Dev's section chart, palm-muted eighths in the verse and full strums in the chorus.
Jam: jam track pop-axis in G again, now as the second guitar, with triads on strings 3 to 1.

lessons.title: Tone and dynamics
lessons.goal: Shape your tone with your hands: picking position, attack and dynamics from very soft to very loud.
lessons.explain: Most of your tone is in your hands. Pick near the bridge for a bright, tight sound and near the neck for a warm, round one; dig in hard for an edge, or brush lightly for a whisper. Dynamics, playing soft and loud on purpose, are the cheapest way to make anything sound more musical.
lessons.show: A figure of the guitar marking three picking zones (near the bridge, the middle, near the neck) with audio of the same chord played in each; a dynamics line from pp to ff.
practice: Technique: Dynamic Control: one arpeggio pp, p, mf, f, ff; the microphone level meter shows the result. Without a microphone: Record it and listen.
Ear: listen-choice, which picking zone is this? Dev's example played near the bridge, in the middle and near the neck.
Jam: jam track fifties-i-vi-iv-v in G at 72 bpm: four bars soft, four loud, then a slow crescendo.

lessons.title: The gig
lessons.goal: Lead a full band arrangement, with rhythm, a solo and an ending, and get ready for Professor Varga.
lessons.explain: Your final gig with Dev is a 12-bar blues in A, played the way a band would: an intro with the turnaround, two choruses of shuffle rhythm with your seventh-chord shapes, two choruses of solo, a chorus of comping behind the band, and an ending. Then Elena takes over. She will ask more of you, and you are ready.
lessons.show: A gig chart for the blues in A: intro (turnaround), 2 choruses of rhythm, 2 choruses of solo, 1 chorus of comping, an ending on A7 (575655).
practice: Tuner: tune; then Technique: warm up.
Jam: jam track blues-turnaround in A at 96 bpm: the whole gig chart, three takes.
Record: the best take, checked against Dev's list: time, tone, dynamics, target notes and a clear ending.
Lesson: the hand-over check for Elena: any major, minor or seventh chord in two places, all five pentatonic boxes, C major in five positions, and eight bars read at sight.

courses.title: Mastery with Prof. Elena Varga
courses.promise: You can improvise and compose in every mode, comp jazz standards with shells, drop-2, drop-3 and extended voicings, play chord melody with clean voice leading, spell the changes in your lines, command economy and sweep picking, legato, tapping and harmonics, play classical repertoire with proper technique, sight-read up the neck and in odd meters, transcribe by ear, arrange and compose for solo guitar, and practise and perform like a professional, without needing a teacher to tell you what comes next.

units.title: Practice and precision
units.goal: Measure where you stand, practise deliberately, and make your time and picking precise.

lessons.title: The audition
lessons.goal: Play an audition that shows Elena where you stand, and set goals with numbers in them.
lessons.explain: I listen before I teach. Play me five things: C major through its five positions, any major, minor or seventh chord in two places, a Travis pattern, eight bars read at sight and one chorus of improvisation across the pentatonic boxes. Then we write down numbers, not adjectives: tempos, clean notes out of ten, clean changes per minute.
lessons.show: An audition card with the five items and the measure for each (tempo, notes clean out of 10, changes per minute); a blank goal sheet.
practice: Metronome: C major through all five positions, then the E-shape and A-shape positions alone in eighth notes at the fastest tempo you can play cleanly three times running; note it.
Mic (play-chord): Elena names six chords, two major, two minor and two sevenths, and you play each one in two places on the neck. Without a microphone: chord-build, two shapes for each.
Chords: one-minute changes from F (133211) to Bb (x13331); note the clean changes per minute.
Record: 8 bars of Travis Picking on C, G7 and Am at the fastest tempo at which the thumb stays steady; note the tempo.
Player: Reading: Second Position, bars 9 to 16, which Dev's course left unplayed, at sight at 60 bpm with the tab hidden; note how many bars were clean.
Jam: jam track blues-12-bar in A at 92 bpm: one chorus of improvisation through at least three of the five boxes; Record it.
Practice Plan: write three goals, each with a number and a date.

lessons.title: Deliberate practice
lessons.goal: Practise deliberately: one precise target, slow enough to be right, immediate feedback and small steps up.
lessons.explain: Repetition is not practice; repetition of the right thing, attended to, is. Choose one target per block, find the tempo at which it is correct nine times out of ten, and raise it in small steps only when it stays correct. Spacing practice across days and mixing topics within a session generally beats long blocks of one thing, even though the blocks feel more productive at the time; and a recording made at the start and the end of a session tells you more than how it felt.
lessons.show: The tempo-ladder graph from the Technique screen: a passage climbing from 60 to 120 bpm in 4 bpm steps, one rung up after each clean pass and one rung back after two passes in a row that are not clean; a sample interleaved session plan.
