practice: Technique: choose one exercise (for example String Crossing Both Ways), find the tempo at which it is clean, and climb the ladder for ten minutes; log the top clean tempo.
Practice Plan: rebuild your routine as interleaved blocks of 8 to 12 minutes.
Record: the passage at the start and the end of the session; listen once for time, once for tone and once for phrasing, and write one sentence for each.

lessons.title: Time that does not need the click
lessons.goal: Make your time independent of the click: play with it on 2 and 4, on the offbeats, and with long gaps.
lessons.explain: A metronome on every beat flatters you. Put it on 2 and 4, then only on the and of each beat, then on beat 1 of every second bar; if you still land with it, your time is your own. Record and check: rushing in fills and dragging in hard passages are the usual sins.
lessons.show: Metronome settings: a click on 2 and 4; offbeats only; one click every 8 beats; a timing graph from the Rhythm trainer showing early and late hits.
practice: Technique: Metronome on 2 and 4, a scale in eighth notes at 80 bpm.
Rhythm: the timing drill with the click on the offbeats only; aim for the trainer's tightest rating.
Metronome: one click every two bars; play a strumming pattern for two minutes and land with the click each time it returns.

lessons.title: Clean picking
lessons.goal: Clean up alternate picking: small motions, string crossings in both directions, and both hands exactly together.
lessons.explain: At speed, every wasted millimetre costs you. Keep the pick close to the strings, move from the wrist or forearm consistently, and master both escapes: crossing to the next string after a downstroke feels different from crossing after an upstroke, and both must be clean. The fretting finger lands just before the pick strikes; late by a hair, and the note buzzes.
lessons.show: A slow-motion animation of the pick path for each of the two string crossings; tabs of Hands in Sync and String Crossing Both Ways.
practice: Technique: Hands in Sync at 40 bpm; Record it and listen for buzz or gaps.
Technique: String Crossing Both Ways, both patterns, up the ladder.
Technique: Alternate Picking: Chromatic in sixteenths, up the ladder.

lessons.title: Three notes per string
lessons.goal: Play the major scale three notes per string, the fingering built for speed, and connect it to the CAGED positions.
lessons.explain: Three notes per string gives every string the same picking pattern and makes long runs even. G major pattern 1 starts at string 6 fret 3 (G), stays within frets 3 to 8 and ends at string 1 fret 8 (C). CAGED tells you where the chords are; three notes per string tells your hands how to run. You need both.
lessons.show: Fretboard figure of G major 3NPS pattern 1 (string 6 fret 3 (G), string 6 fret 5 (A), string 6 fret 7 (B), up to string 1 fret 5 (A), string 1 fret 7 (B), string 1 fret 8 (C)) with the G roots and the E-shape G (355433) inside it.
practice: Scales: G major, 3NPS pattern 1, alternate picked at 60 bpm.
Scales: patterns 2 and 3; note where each one overlaps a CAGED position.
Technique: Scales in Every Key, Full Neck, the first three keys of its circle (C, G, D), as a long-term daily routine.

units.title: The modes in practice
units.goal: Hear each mode as a colour, improvise in all seven over vamps that define them, and compose in one.

lessons.title: Modes as colours
lessons.goal: Hear each mode as a colour over its own drone, rather than as a major scale started somewhere else.
lessons.explain: The modes of the major scale share their notes but not their home, and the home is everything. Over a drone on A, each mode has a note that defines it: Dorian's major sixth (F#), Phrygian's flat second (Bb), Lydian's sharp fourth (D#), Mixolydian's flat seventh (G), Aeolian's flat sixth (F) and Locrian's flat fifth (Eb). Think A Dorian is A minor with F#, not G major from A.
lessons.show: A table of the seven modes on A with their notes, the defining note of each highlighted: Ionian A B C# D E F# G#, Dorian A B C D E F# G, Phrygian A Bb C D E F G, Lydian A B C# D# E F# G#, Mixolydian A B C# D E F# G, Aeolian A B C D E F G, Locrian A Bb C D Eb F G; audio of each over an A drone.
practice: Ear: the mode-recognition drill over a drone, starting with Ionian, Dorian, Mixolydian and Aeolian.
Scales: each mode on A in fifth position, slowly, over the drone.
Lesson: match-pairs, each mode and its defining degree.

lessons.title: Dorian and Aeolian
lessons.goal: Improvise in A Dorian and A Aeolian over their vamps and make the difference audible.
lessons.explain: Both are minor; the sixth decides. Over Am to D the F# in the D chord makes it Dorian; over Am, F and G the F makes it Aeolian. Land the sixth on strong beats and the listener hears the mode. Do not play the scale like a staircase: phrase toward the colour note.
lessons.show: Fretboard figures of A Dorian and A Aeolian in fifth position with F# and F marked; the two vamps.
practice: Mic (play-note): Elena names the mode, Dorian or Aeolian, and you play its sixth in fifth position: string 2 fret 7 (F#) or string 2 fret 6 (F). Without a microphone: fretboard-find.
Player: Mode Study: A Dorian, then Mode Study: A Aeolian, at 72 bpm.
Jam: jam track dorian-i-iv in A at 100 bpm (Am7, D7): two choruses with F# on a strong beat in every phrase.
Jam: jam track minor-i-bvi-bvii in A at 96 bpm: the same with F.

lessons.title: Mixolydian and Lydian
lessons.goal: Play A Mixolydian and A Lydian over their vamps, phrasing toward G and D#.
lessons.explain: Mixolydian is major with a flat seventh: the A to G vamp, the sound of a lot of rock and fiddle music. Lydian is major with a raised fourth: the A to B vamp, where the B chord carries D#, the bright, floating note film composers love. Each is one note away from major, and that note is the whole story.
lessons.show: Fretboard figures of A Mixolydian and A Lydian in fifth position with G and D# marked; the vamps A (x02220) to G (320003) and A (x02220) to B (x24442).
practice: Mic (play-note): Elena names the mode and you play its colour note in fifth position: string 4 fret 5 (G) for Mixolydian, string 3 fret 8 (D#) for Lydian. Without a microphone: fretboard-find.
Player: Mode Study: A Mixolydian, then Mode Study: A Lydian, at 72 bpm.
Jam: jam track lydian-i-ii in A at 72 bpm: D# on strong beats.
Player: Red Haired Boy at 80, then 96 bpm, in A Mixolydian.

lessons.title: Phrygian and the flamenco cadence
lessons.goal: Play A Phrygian, the Phrygian-dominant colour of flamenco, and the Andalusian cadence with rasgueado.
lessons.explain: Phrygian's flat second, Bb over A, falls to the root with a dark, heavy pull (Locrian shares it, but its flat fifth makes it another world). In flamenco the home chord is usually major (E with G#), which turns the scale into Phrygian dominant, E F G# A B C D. The Andalusian cadence, Am G F E, walks down to that E; play it with the four-finger rasgueado.
lessons.show: Fretboard figures of A Phrygian (A Bb C D E F G) and E Phrygian dominant; chord boxes of Am (x02210), G (320003), F (xx3211) and E (022100); notation of the rasgueado fan.
practice: Player: Mode Study: A Phrygian at 72 bpm.
Technique: Rasgueado Basics on E, then Am, up the ladder.
Player: Andalusian Cadence with Rasgueado at 80 bpm, including the E Phrygian melody in bars 9 to 16.

lessons.title: Locrian, the unstable mode
lessons.goal: Hear why Locrian rarely serves as a home, and use its colour over a half-diminished vamp.
lessons.explain: Locrian has a flat second and a flat fifth, so its home chord is diminished: it never quite settles, which is why so little music stays there. Over Am7b5 (x0101x) to Bbmaj7 (x1323x) you can hear it as a colour, dark, suspended and uneasy. Use it the way a painter uses black: sparingly and on purpose.
lessons.show: Fretboard figure of A Locrian (A Bb C D Eb F G) with Bb and Eb marked; chord boxes of Am7b5 (x0101x) and Bbmaj7 (x1323x).
practice: Player: Mode Study: A Locrian at 66 bpm.
Ear: listen-choice, Phrygian or Locrian? Listen to the fifth.
Jam: jam track locrian-i-bii in A at 66 bpm.

lessons.title: Compose in a mode
lessons.goal: Write and play an original 16-bar piece in a mode of your choice, over a vamp that defines it.
lessons.explain: A mode lives or dies by its harmony: the chord that contains the defining note must be there, and the strong V-to-I pull of major and minor must not be. I-II for Lydian, i-IV for Dorian, I-bVII for Mixolydian, i-bII for Phrygian. Write a vamp, then a melody that lands on the colour note at least four times on strong beats, and end on the tonic.
lessons.show: Four vamp templates on A (Lydian I-II, Dorian i-IV, Mixolydian I-bVII, Phrygian i-bII) with chord boxes; a 16-bar melody grid.
practice: Create: choose a mode and write a 2-chord vamp and a 16-bar melody on the grid.
Jam: play your piece in A over the backing for your mode: jam track lydian-i-ii, jam track dorian-i-iv, jam track mixolydian-i-bvii or jam track phrygian-i-bii.
Record: a performance; Elena listens for the colour note on strong beats and a clear tonic.

units.title: Advanced picking
units.goal: Add economy and sweep picking, string skipping, hybrid picking and controlled speed to your alternate picking.

lessons.title: Economy picking
lessons.goal: Use economy picking on three-notes-per-string runs, sweeping each string change in the direction you are already moving.
lessons.explain: Economy picking alternates on each string, but when you cross to the next string in the direction the pick is already travelling, you continue the stroke instead of reversing it. Ascending with three notes per string: down-up-down, then down again on the next string in one motion. It saves movement, and it also changes the accent pattern, so practise it slowly with a click.
lessons.show: Tab of Economy Picking on G major three notes per string with the stroke marks and the sweeping string changes highlighted.
practice: Technique: Economy Picking at 60 bpm, ascending only, then descending.
Mic (play-phrase): one octave of the run, economy picked, at 60 bpm; the microphone checks every note sounds, in order. Without a microphone: Record it and listen.
Metronome: sixteenths with the first note of each beat accented, to keep the time true while the strokes change.
Technique: climb the ladder toward 132 bpm over the coming weeks.

lessons.title: Sweep picking on three strings
lessons.goal: Sweep a three-string triad in one stroke each way, with every note separate.
lessons.explain: A sweep is one continuous pick stroke across several strings, one note per string, like a slow strum that the fretting hand turns into single notes. The fretting hand does the hard part: each finger lifts the moment its note has sounded, so the notes never ring together. Start painfully slowly.
lessons.show: Tab of Sweep Picking: Three Strings: Am at string 3 fret 14 (A), string 2 fret 13 (C), string 1 fret 12 (E), then C at string 3 fret 12 (G), string 2 fret 13 (C), string 1 fret 12 (E), with the stroke marks.
practice: Technique: Sweep Picking: Three Strings at 50 bpm in triplets.
Mic (play-phrase): one sweep up and down; the microphone checks the three notes in order. Without a microphone: Record it and listen for notes ringing together.
Technique: up the ladder in 5 bpm steps.

lessons.title: Sweep picking on five strings
lessons.goal: Sweep a five-string A minor arpeggio and play the Sweep-Picked Arpeggios study.
lessons.explain: Five strings: string 5 fret 12 (A), string 4 fret 14 (E), string 3 fret 14 (A), string 2 fret 13 (C), string 1 fret 12 (E), then a slide or hammer to string 1 fret 17 (A) and back down. Strings 4 and 3 at fret 14 need one finger rolled from one to the other: roll, do not barre, or the notes bleed together.
lessons.show: Tab of the five-string shape with its fingering and the roll marked; tab of Sweep-Picked Arpeggios.
practice: Technique: Sweep Picking: Five Strings at 50 bpm.
Player: Sweep-Picked Arpeggios, in wait mode, then at 60 bpm.
Record: at your top clean tempo; listen for bleeding notes.

lessons.title: String skipping
lessons.goal: Skip strings cleanly with alternate picking, from octaves to pentatonic lines.
lessons.explain: Skipping a string with the pick is a jump, and the jump must not change your time. Start with octaves, string 6 fret 5 (A) to string 4 fret 7 (A), then play A minor pentatonic box 1 on the string pairs 6 and 4, 5 and 3, 4 and 2, and 3 and 1. Wide intervals sound fresh after years of stepwise scales.
lessons.show: Tab of String Skipping; a fretboard figure of box 1 split into skipped string pairs.
practice: Mic (play-phrase): the octave pairs, string 6 fret 5 (A) to string 4 fret 7 (A) and string 5 fret 5 (D) to string 3 fret 7 (D); the microphone checks both notes of each pair. Without a microphone: the Player in wait mode.
Technique: String Skipping at 60 bpm, up the ladder.
Jam: jam track funk-one-chord-minor in A at 96 bpm: improvise using skipped strings only.
Record: a stepwise phrase and a skipped one, and compare them.

lessons.title: Hybrid picking
lessons.goal: Combine the pick with the middle and ring fingers for country lines and wide arpeggios.
lessons.explain: Hybrid picking keeps the pick between thumb and index and frees the middle (m) and ring (a) fingers to pluck higher strings, at the same time or in between. Over C (x32010): the pick on string 5, m on string 2, the pick on string 4, a on string 1; then pinch the pick and m together. You get the reach of fingerstyle with the attack of a pick.
lessons.show: Tab of Hybrid Picking with the pick, m and a marked.
practice: Technique: Hybrid Picking at 60 bpm, then up the ladder.
Jam: jam track country-ii7 in G at 110 bpm: bass notes with the pick, chord stabs with m and a.
Player: Devil's Dream, the A part, first with the pick alone, then with hybrid picking.

lessons.title: Speed, safely
lessons.goal: Raise your top tempo safely with speed bursts, and keep a tremolo even at speed.
lessons.explain: Speed is built in short bursts above your comfortable tempo, each followed by rest, not by grinding at the edge for minutes. Tremolo picking, very fast alternation on one note, needs a loose wrist and a tiny motion. Then return to your comfortable tempo: it will feel slower than it used to.
lessons.show: Tab of the Speed Bursts figure (string 1 fret 8 (C), string 1 fret 7 (B), string 1 fret 5 (A), string 2 fret 8 (G)) and of Tremolo Picking; the burst-and-rest pattern as a rhythm line.
practice: Technique: Speed Bursts: once, twice, then four times in a row, with a beat of rest between bursts.
Technique: Tremolo Picking on the open string 1, sixteenths, then thirty-seconds at no more than half the tempo, changing notes on the beat.
Player: In the Hall of the Mountain King with its tempo ramp from 60 toward 160 bpm, strictly alternate picked; then the William Tell galop and the Caprice No. 24 theme as longer goals.

units.title: Legato, tapping and harmonics
units.goal: Play fluid legato, tap with the picking hand, sound every kind of harmonic, bend wide and in tune, and play slide in open G.

lessons.title: Three-notes-per-string legato
lessons.goal: Play G major three notes per string with one pick stroke per string and every note equally loud.
lessons.explain: Pick the first note on each string and hammer the other two going up; going down, pick the first and pull off the rest. Weak hammers and lazy pull-offs show up at once as uneven volume. The fretting hand has to do the pick's work, so practise slowly and listen.
lessons.show: Tab of Three-Notes-per-String Legato (G major from string 6 fret 3 (G)) with the picked notes, hammers and pull-offs marked.
practice: Technique: Three-Notes-per-String Legato at 60 bpm, ascending, then descending.
Mic (play-phrase): one octave of the run; the microphone checks every note sounds. Without a microphone: Record it and listen for missing notes.
Technique: up the ladder toward 132 bpm over the coming weeks.

lessons.title: Hammer-ons from nowhere
lessons.goal: Start notes and runs with a hammer-on alone, with no picked note before it.
lessons.explain: A hammer-on from nowhere lands on a string that is not already ringing, so it must be fast and precise enough to make the note by itself. It frees the picking hand to rest, mute or tap. Begin on string 3 fret 7 (D), string 2 fret 8 (G) and string 1 fret 5 (A), then start whole legato runs this way.
lessons.show: Tab of Hammer-On from Nowhere with the hammer sign and no pick stroke on the first note.
practice: Technique: Hammer-On from Nowhere at 60 bpm.
Mic (play-note): each hammered note alone; the microphone checks it sounds clearly. Without a microphone: Record it.
Technique: combine it with the 3NPS legato run, starting each string with a hammer.

lessons.title: Tapping
lessons.goal: Tap with the picking hand to play wide arpeggios on one string, in triplets.
lessons.explain: Tapping uses the picking hand as a third finger on the fretboard: tap string 1 fret 12 (E) with the middle finger, pull off to string 1 fret 5 (A), hammer string 1 fret 8 (C), and repeat. The pull-off from the tap is the motion that matters: flick slightly sideways off the string. Mute the other strings with both hands.
lessons.show: Tab of Lick: Tapping Arpeggios over Am, F, G and E with T over the tapped notes; the other shapes on string 1: F at frets 13, 5 and 8, G at frets 15, 7 and 10, E at frets 12, 4 and 7.
practice: Technique: Tapping Triplets at 50 bpm on the Am shape.
Player: Lick: Tapping Arpeggios at 60, then 80 bpm, in triplet eighths.
Record: listen for whether the tapped note is as loud as the others.

lessons.title: Harmonics: natural, artificial and pinch
lessons.goal: Play natural, artificial (harp) and pinch harmonics, cleanly and in tune.
lessons.explain: A natural harmonic sounds when you touch a string lightly right over fret 12, 7 or 5 and pick: an octave, an octave and a fifth, and two octaves above the open string. An artificial harmonic does the same twelve frets above any fretted note, with the picking hand both touching and plucking. A pinch harmonic is the squeal you get when the edge of the thumb brushes the string just after the pick.
lessons.show: Fretboard figure of the natural harmonic points over frets 12, 7 and 5; tabs of Harmonics Melody and of Artificial (Harp) Harmonics, string 5 fret 3 (C) touched over fret 15.
practice: Technique: Natural Harmonics on all six strings over frets 12, 7 and 5.
Player: Harmonics Melody at 60 bpm.
Technique: Artificial (Harp) Harmonics, then Pinch Harmonics on string 3 fret 7 (D) with a little overdrive.

lessons.title: Wide bends, in tune
lessons.goal: Bend a step and a half in tune and add vibrato at the top of a bend.
lessons.explain: A step-and-a-half bend, three frets' worth, needs all three fingers, a turning wrist and a confident push: hear the target, string 2 fret 8 (G), before you bend up to it from string 2 fret 5 (E). Hold it, add a narrow vibrato at the top, and release in time. Nobody is impressed by a wide bend that misses.
lessons.show: Tab of Step-and-a-Half Bend with its target note; a pitch line of bend, vibrato and release.
practice: Technique: Step-and-a-Half Bend: the target first, then the bend; the microphone checks the pitch. Without a microphone: alternate target and bend and compare by ear.
Technique: Bending Vibrato in Time at the top of a whole-step bend.
Jam: jam track blues-slow-12-8 in A at 56 bpm: one chorus in which every phrase ends on an in-tune bend.

lessons.title: Slide guitar in open G
lessons.goal: Retune to open G and play a slide blues with a bottleneck, in tune over the fret wires.
lessons.explain: Open G is D G D G B D from string 6 to string 1: strum the open strings and you hear a G chord, so the slide can play whole chords lying across all six strings at one fret, G at fret 12, C at fret 5 and D at fret 7. Touch the strings lightly, directly over the fret wire rather than between frets, and mute behind the slide with trailing fingers.
lessons.show: A tuning card (D G D G B D); tab of Open G Slide Blues with every fret checked in this tuning; a fretboard figure with frets 5, 7 and 12 marked as the C, D and G chords.
practice: Tuner: retune to open G: strings 6, 5 and 1 go down a whole step (E to D, A to G, E to D).
Technique: Slide (Bottleneck) Intonation, first in standard tuning on string 1 over frets 12, 10, 7 and 5.
Player: Open G Slide Blues in wait mode, then at 60 bpm.
Tuner: back to standard tuning when you finish.

units.title: Jazz harmony and comping
units.goal: Comp the major and minor ii-V-I with shells, guide tones, drop-2, drop-3 and extended voicings, in swing and bossa rhythms.

lessons.title: Shell voicings on a ii-V-I
lessons.goal: Comp a ii-V-I in C with three-note shells: root, third and seventh.
lessons.explain: The third and the seventh define a chord's quality; the fifth adds almost nothing unless it is altered (as in m7b5), so jazz guitarists drop it. The shells: Dm7 (x535xx), G7 (3x34xx) and Cmaj7 (x324xx). The root moves between strings 5 and 6, so the hand barely moves.
lessons.show: Chord boxes of the three shells with root, third and seventh labelled; notation of the comp in quarter notes and in the Charleston rhythm.
practice: Mic (play-chord): the three shells. Without a microphone: chord-build.
Player: Jazz Comping: Shell Voicings on ii-V-I, bars 1 to 8 (short quarter notes), at 100 bpm.
Player: bars 9 to 16 in the Charleston rhythm (beat 1 and the and of 2).
Jam: jam track jazz-ii-v-i in C at 110 bpm, shells only.

lessons.title: Guide tones
lessons.goal: Find the guide-tone lines of a ii-V-I and hear how its thirds and sevenths move by step.
lessons.explain: Through Dm7, G7 and Cmaj7, each seventh falls a half step or stays to become the next chord's third: C, the seventh of Dm7, falls to B, the third of G7, which stays as the seventh of Cmaj7; F, the third of Dm7, stays as the seventh of G7 and falls to E, the third of Cmaj7. These two lines, C B B and F F E, are the skeleton of the harmony and of good solos.
lessons.show: Staff and fretboard figure of the two guide-tone lines, C B B and F F E, on strings 3 and 4; audio of the lines alone, then over the bass.
practice: Lesson: fill-blanks, the third and the seventh of Dm7, G7 and Cmaj7.
Mic (play-phrase): each guide-tone line in half notes over the progression. Without a microphone: the Player in wait mode.
Jam: jam track jazz-ii-v-i in C at 100 bpm: play the guide-tone lines, then decorate them.

lessons.title: Drop-2 voicings
lessons.goal: Voice-lead a ii-V-I with drop-2 voicings on strings 4 to 1, and move it to F.
lessons.explain: A drop-2 voicing takes a close four-note chord and drops its second-highest note an octave, which gives a playable four-string grip. On strings 4 to 1: Dm7 (xx3535), G7 (xx3433), Cmaj7 (xx2413). Watch the voices: F stays, C goes to B, D stays, A goes to G; then F goes to E, B stays, D goes to C and G stays. Move every shape up 5 frets and you are in F.
lessons.show: Chord boxes of the three voicings, each voice coloured, with arrows showing its motion; the same progression in F (Gm7, C7, Fmaj7) between frets 6 and 10.
practice: Mic (play-chord): the three voicings in C. Without a microphone: chord-build.
Player: Jazz Comping: Drop-2 Voicings at 100 bpm in C, then in F.
Jam: jam track jazz-ii-v-i in F at 110 bpm with the drop-2 shapes.

lessons.title: Drop-3 voicings
lessons.goal: Play a ii-V-I with drop-3 voicings, the root on string 6 or 5 and a string skipped inside the grip.
lessons.explain: A drop-3 voicing drops the third-highest note of a close chord an octave, which leaves a skipped string inside the grip. With the root on string 5, Dm7 (x5x565); with the root on string 6, G7 (3x343x) and Cmaj7 (8x998x). They sound full and piano-like, and the root in the bass makes them ideal when there is no bass player.
lessons.show: Chord boxes of the three drop-3 grips with the skipped string marked x; the motion of each voice between them.
practice: Mic (play-chord): the three grips. Without a microphone: chord-build.
Jam: jam track jazz-ii-v-i in C at 100 bpm: drop-3 grips four to the bar, short and even.
Lesson: chord-build, build Gm7, C7 and Fmaj7 as drop-3 grips by moving the shapes.

lessons.title: Ninths and thirteenths
lessons.goal: Comp a ii-V-I with ninth and thirteenth voicings and hear which extension each chord takes.
lessons.explain: Extensions are the notes above the seventh, the 9, 11 and 13, and they are what makes jazz harmony shimmer. On guitar you rarely play them all: drop the fifth and often the root, keep the third and seventh, and add one colour. Dm9 (x5355x), G13 (3x345x) and Cmaj9 (x3243x) all keep their guide tones, and their top voice moves E, E, D.
lessons.show: Chord boxes of the three voicings with each tone labelled (root, third, seventh, ninth, thirteenth); audio of the plain sevenths, then the extended voicings.
practice: Mic (play-chord): Dm9, G13 and Cmaj9. Without a microphone: chord-build.
Ear: listen-choice, plain seventh or extended chord, and which extension?
Jam: jam track jazz-ii-v-i in C at 110 bpm: alternate a chorus of shells with a chorus of these voicings.

lessons.title: The minor ii-V-i
lessons.goal: Comp the minor ii-V-i in A minor and hear the harmonic-minor colour of its V.
lessons.explain: In minor the ii chord is half-diminished and the V borrows the raised seventh from harmonic minor: Bm7b5 (x2323x), E7 (xx2434), Am7 (xx2213). The G# in E7 is what makes the V pull home; over it, play A harmonic minor (A B C D E F G#).
lessons.show: Chord boxes of the three voicings; a fretboard figure of A harmonic minor in fifth position with G# marked.
practice: Mic (play-chord): the three voicings. Without a microphone: chord-build.
Player: Jazz Comping: Minor ii-V-i, bars 1 to 8, at 100 bpm swung, then the bossa version.
Player: bars 9 to 16, the melody over it, with G# on the E7.
Jam: jam track latin-bossa-minor-loop in A at 120 bpm (Am7, Dm7, Bm7b5, E7b9).

lessons.title: Comping and the bossa groove
lessons.goal: Comp like a jazz guitarist behind a soloist: varied rhythms, turnarounds and a bossa groove.
lessons.explain: Comping means accompanying, and complementing: short chords, varied rhythms, space for the soloist. Learn three rhythms well: four to the bar, the Charleston, and anticipations on the and of 4. Then the bossa: the thumb on the root on 1 and 3 and the fingers in a syncopated two-bar pattern over Am7 (5x555x) and D7 (x5453x).
lessons.show: Rhythm lines of the three comping rhythms; tab of Bossa-Style Groove; the I-vi-ii-V turnaround in C as shells.
practice: Player: Bossa-Style Groove at 100, then 120 bpm.
Jam: jam track jazz-i-vi-ii-v in C at 120 bpm: comp with shells, changing the rhythm every four bars.
Jam: jam track dorian-i-iv in A at 110 bpm (Am7, D7): the bossa groove from the study.

units.title: Voice leading and chord melody
units.goal: Connect chords smoothly, use triads and line cliches, play chord melody, and reharmonise a melody.

lessons.title: Voice leading
lessons.goal: Connect chords by moving each voice as little as possible and keeping common tones.
lessons.explain: Voice leading treats a progression as several melodies moving together. Keep common tones where they are, move the other voices by the smallest step, and prefer contrary motion between the outer voices. On guitar that means choosing inversions instead of always grabbing the root-position shape.
lessons.show: Staff and fretboard figures of C, Am, F and G as close triads on strings 3 to 1: C (x-x-x-5-5-3), Am/C (x-x-x-5-5-5), F/C (x-x-x-5-6-5) and G/B (x-x-x-4-3-3), each voice coloured.
practice: Mic (play-chord): the four voicings in order. Without a microphone: chord-build.
Lesson: order, arrange inversions of C, Am, F and G so the top voice moves only by step.
Jam: jam track fifties-i-vi-iv-v in C at 66 bpm with these voicings.

lessons.title: Triads on every string set
lessons.goal: Play major and minor triads in all inversions on strings 4 to 2 as well as 3 to 1, and voice-lead a progression on each set.
lessons.explain: Every triad has three inversions on each group of three neighbouring strings, so learn them as families by their bass note: root, third or fifth. Then voice-lead: one progression, one string set, no jump larger than two frets. The Canon progression is the classic workout.
lessons.show: Fretboard figures of C in its three inversions on strings 4 to 2: C (x-x-10-9-8-x), C/G (x-x-5-5-5-x) and C/E (x-x-2-0-1-x); the strings 3 to 1 shapes from Dev's course beside them.
practice: Mic (play-chord): the three inversions on each string set. Without a microphone: chord-build.
Lesson: fretboard-find, Am in all three inversions on strings 4 to 2.
Jam: jam track classical-canon in D at 66 bpm: voice-lead the Canon progression on strings 4 to 2.

lessons.title: Line cliches
lessons.goal: Play line cliches: a chord held while one voice moves by half steps.
lessons.explain: A line cliche holds a chord and moves one voice chromatically: Am, AmMaj7, Am7, Am6, with the moving voice falling A, G#, G, F#. In open position the line walks down string 3 from fret 2 to the open string, then lands on F# at the top of Am6: Am (x02210), AmMaj7 (x02110), Am7 (x02010), Am6 (x02212). The major version rises instead: C, Caug, C6, C7, with the fifth climbing G, G#, A, Bb.
lessons.show: Chord boxes of Am (x02210), AmMaj7 (x02110), Am7 (x02010) and Am6 (x02212) with the moving voice A, G#, G, F# highlighted.
practice: Mic (play-chord): the four chords, letting the moving voice sing. Without a microphone: chord-build.
Jam: jam track line-minor-down in A at 66 bpm.
Jam: jam track line-major-up in C at 66 bpm (C, C+, C6, C7): find voicings where the fifth rises G, G#, A, Bb.

lessons.title: Chord melody
lessons.goal: Play chord-melody arrangements with the melody always on top: the First Ballad study and Danny Boy.
lessons.explain: Chord melody plays the tune and its harmony at once: put the melody note on the highest string you are using and build the chord beneath it on the strong beats; between them, the melody runs alone. The melody must always be the highest and loudest note, so choose each voicing by its top note, not by habit.
lessons.show: Tab of Chord Melody: First Ballad with the melody notes highlighted; a fretboard figure of C, Am, F and G7 voicings with different top notes.
practice: Player: Chord Melody: First Ballad, in wait mode, then at 60 bpm.
Lesson: chord-build, given a melody note on string 1 and a chord symbol, build a voicing beneath it.
Mic (play-chord): four of the study's voicings, C, Am, F and G7, each with its melody note on top. Without a microphone: chord-build.
Player: Danny Boy (chord melody), the first 8 bars in wait mode, then the whole piece at 54 bpm with rubato.

lessons.title: Reharmonisation
lessons.goal: Reharmonise a melody with secondary dominants and a tritone substitution, keeping the melody on top.
lessons.explain: Reharmonising keeps the melody and changes the chords under it. Two dependable moves: put a secondary dominant before a diatonic chord (in F, D7 before Gm7, because D7 is the V of G), and replace a dominant with the dominant a tritone away (Gb7 for C7: C7 has E and Bb, Gb7 has the same two pitches spelled Fb and Bb). Test every new chord against the melody note: if it clashes, it is wrong, however clever it looks.
lessons.show: Two versions of an original 8-bar phrase in F: plain (Fmaj7, Dm7, Gm7, C7) and reharmonised (Fmaj7, D7, Gm7, Gb7), as staff and chord boxes.
practice: Ear: listen-choice, plain or reharmonised, and which chord changed?
Lesson: choice, which chord is the tritone substitute of G7? (Db7).
Jam: jam track jazz-tritone-sub in F at 100 bpm: comp the substitution with drop-2 grips.

lessons.title: A jazz-ballad arrangement
lessons.goal: Play the 32-bar AABA jazz-ballad chord melody with secondary dominants and a tritone substitution.
lessons.explain: This is a full arrangement: an original AABA ballad in F on Fmaj7, Dm7, Gm7 and C7, with a D7 leading to Gm7 and Gb7 in place of C7. The B section must contrast, so take the voicings higher or thinner there. Balance is the test: the melody sings and the harmony sits beneath it.
lessons.show: Tab and notation of Chord Melody: Jazz Ballad with Reharmonisation, with the A A B A sections marked and the reharmonised bars highlighted.
practice: Player: the first A section in wait mode, then the B section.
Player: the whole 32 bars at 56, then 66 bpm.
Record: a performance; Elena listens for the melody on top and for clean voice leading through the reharmonised bars.

units.title: Arpeggios and playing the changes
units.goal: Spell the harmony in your lines with seventh arpeggios, guide tones, approach notes, enclosures, substitutions and altered sounds.

lessons.title: Seventh-chord arpeggios
lessons.goal: Play the seven diatonic seventh arpeggios of C major in fifth position and outline Dm7, G7 and Cmaj7.
lessons.explain: Arpeggios are the shortest path from chords to lines. In fifth position run each diatonic seventh up and down: Cmaj7 C E G B, Dm7 D F A C, Em7 E G B D, Fmaj7 F A C E, G7 G B D F, Am7 A C E G, Bm7b5 B D F A. Then make an 8-bar melody over Dm7, G7 and Cmaj7 that outlines them.
lessons.show: Tab of Seventh-Chord Arpeggios in C; fretboard figures of the Dm7, G7 and Cmaj7 arpeggios in fifth position with each role coloured.
practice: Player: Seventh-Chord Arpeggios in C at 60, then 80 bpm.
Lesson: chord-tones drill, the notes of each diatonic seventh of C.
Mic (play-phrase): the Dm7, G7 and Cmaj7 arpeggios in fifth position, up and down. Without a microphone: the Player in wait mode.
Jam: jam track jazz-ii-v-i in C at 100 bpm: arpeggios only, changing exactly with the chords.

lessons.title: Horizontal and vertical
lessons.goal: Choose between one scale for a whole passage (horizontal) and a sound for each chord (vertical).
lessons.explain: Over Dm7, G7 and Cmaj7 you can think of one C major scale throughout: horizontal, easy and smooth. Or you can think of each chord's own arpeggio and tensions: vertical, precise, and the way the harmony becomes audible in the line. Good players switch, horizontal for long stretches in one key and vertical where the harmony moves or leaves the key.
lessons.show: Two original 4-bar lines over the ii-V-I, one horizontal (the C major scale) and one vertical (an arpeggio on each chord), as tab with the chord tones marked.
practice: Player: both lines at 80 bpm; listen to how the second one spells the changes.
Jam: jam track jazz-ii-v-i in C at 100 bpm: one chorus horizontal, one vertical.
Jam: jam track secondary-v-of-vi in C at 92 bpm (C, E7, Am, F): over E7 go vertical, because its G# is not in C major.

lessons.title: Approach notes and enclosures
lessons.goal: Approach chord tones from a half step below and enclose them from above and below.
lessons.explain: A chromatic approach note, a half step below a chord tone on the weak part of a beat, makes the target sound inevitable. An enclosure surrounds the target: a scale step above, a half step below, then the target. Aim these at the thirds of each chord and your lines start to sound like jazz.
lessons.show: Staff and tab of approaches and enclosures into E, the third of Cmaj7 (D# to E; F, D#, E), and into B, the third of G7 (A# to B; C, A#, B).
practice: Mic (play-phrase): each enclosure into E, then into B. Without a microphone: the Player in wait mode.
Lesson: fill-blanks, complete the enclosure of F, the third of Dm7: G, E, F.
Jam: jam track jazz-ii-v-i in C at 96 bpm: one enclosure at every chord change.

lessons.title: Arpeggios a third up
lessons.goal: Play the arpeggio built on a chord's third to reach its upper extensions.
lessons.explain: Over Cmaj7, an Em7 arpeggio (E G B D) gives you the third, fifth, seventh and ninth: a richer sound with no new shapes to learn. Over Dm7, Fmaj7 (F A C E) does the same; over G7, Bm7b5 (B D F A). The principle never changes: start on the third.
lessons.show: Fretboard figures of Em7 over Cmaj7, Fmaj7 over Dm7 and Bm7b5 over G7, with each note labelled by its degree in the underlying chord.
practice: Mic (play-phrase): each substitute arpeggio over its chord. Without a microphone: the Player in wait mode.
Lesson: choice, which arpeggio gives you the ninth over Am7? (Cmaj7).
Jam: jam track jazz-ii-v-i in C at 100 bpm: the substitute arpeggios only.

lessons.title: The altered dominant
lessons.goal: Play altered tensions over a dominant chord with the altered scale, and resolve them by step.
lessons.explain: A dominant seventh can carry altered tensions, the b9, #9, b5 and #5 (or b13), all of which push harder toward resolution. The altered scale holds them all: G altered is G Ab Bb Cb Db Eb F, which is Ab melodic minor starting on G. Resolve each tension by step into the C chord: Ab to G, Eb to E, Db to C.
lessons.show: Fretboard figure of G altered in one position around fret 3 with the tensions labelled; staff of three resolutions into Cmaj7.
practice: Ear: listen-choice, plain G7 or altered? Six rounds.
Scales: G altered in one position, played over a G7alt drone.
Jam: jam track jazz-ii-v-i in C at 92 bpm: the altered scale over G7 only, resolving by step into the Cmaj7 bar.

lessons.title: Going outside, and coming back
lessons.goal: Step outside the key on purpose, by side-slipping or with a tritone-substitute arpeggio, and resolve convincingly.
lessons.explain: Playing outside only convinces when you come back: tension needs release. Two safe ways out: side-slip a phrase a half step up and back, or play the tritone substitute's arpeggio over the V (Db7 over G7). Commit to it, keep the rhythm strong, and land on a chord tone of the next chord; timidity is what makes outside notes sound wrong.
lessons.show: Tab of an original line that side-slips from A minor pentatonic to Bb minor pentatonic and back over Am7; a Db7 arpeggio over G7 resolving to Cmaj7.
practice: Player: both example lines at 80 bpm.
Jam: jam track funk-one-chord-minor in A at 96 bpm: side-slip one phrase per chorus and come home.
Jam: jam track jazz-ii-v-i in C at 100 bpm: Db7 arpeggios over the G7 bar, resolving into the Cmaj7.

units.title: Harmonic and melodic minor in practice
units.goal: Play and hear the harmony of harmonic and melodic minor, Phrygian dominant, the Neapolitan and augmented sixth, and minor-key repertoire.

lessons.title: The harmony of harmonic minor
lessons.goal: Play the chords of A harmonic minor and hear what its raised seventh does to them.
lessons.explain: Raise the seventh of A minor to G# and three things change: V becomes E7, vii becomes G#dim7 and III becomes augmented. In sevenths: AmMaj7, Bm7b5, Cmaj7#5, Dm7, E7, Fmaj7, G#dim7. Much minor-key music mixes the two forms: natural minor in the melody, harmonic minor at the cadences.
lessons.show: A table of the seven seventh chords of A harmonic minor with a movable voicing for each; a fretboard figure of A harmonic minor in fifth position with G# highlighted.
practice: Lesson: fill-blanks, the qualities of the harmonic-minor sevenths.
Jam: jam track classical-minor-cadence in A at 66 bpm (Am, Dm, E7, Am): A harmonic minor, landing on G# over the E7.
Player: Rondo alla Turca (theme) at 80, then 108 bpm: its opening turn, B A G# A, is the raised seventh at work.
Player: Hungarian Dance No. 5 (theme), a second harmonic-minor showpiece, as a duet with the app on the chords: mark its sudden slow-downs and speed-ups and make them yours.

lessons.title: Phrygian dominant and the solea cycle
lessons.goal: Play E Phrygian dominant over the flamenco vamp and the 12-beat solea cycle.
lessons.explain: The fifth mode of A harmonic minor, E F G# A B C D, is Phrygian dominant, and over E major it sounds instantly Spanish. The solea compas counts 12 beats with accents on 3, 6, 8, 10 and 12, that is groups of 3, 3, 2, 2 and 2: clap it before you play it. Rasgueado goes on the accents, thumb strokes in between.
lessons.show: Fretboard figure of E Phrygian dominant in open position with G# and F marked; the 12-beat compas wheel with its accents; chord boxes of E (022100) and F (xx3211).
practice: Rhythm: clap the 12-beat cycle with its accents, counting aloud.
Player: Flamenco Rhythm: the 12-Beat Cycle, rasgueado on the accents, slowly, then faster.
Jam: jam track flamenco-phrygian-vamp in E at 96 bpm (E, F): a short falseta of your own in E Phrygian dominant.

lessons.title: The harmony of melodic minor
lessons.goal: Play the chords of A melodic minor and use the jazz-minor sound over AmMaj7 and D7.
lessons.explain: Melodic minor as jazz uses it, with the same notes going up and down, is A B C D E F# G#. Its sevenths: AmMaj7, Bm7, Cmaj7#5, D7, E7, F#m7b5, G#m7b5. Its tonic chord, AmMaj7, is dark and cinematic, and IV7 (D7) in a minor key adds a bright, bluesy lift.
lessons.show: A table of the seven chords with voicings; a fretboard figure of A melodic minor in fifth position with F# and G# highlighted.
practice: Mic (play-chord): AmMaj7 (x02110) and D7 (x57575). Without a microphone: chord-build.
Scales: A melodic minor in two positions.
Jam: jam track line-minor-down in A at 66 bpm: A melodic minor over the AmMaj7 bar, A Dorian over the Am7 and Am6 bars.

lessons.title: Minor-key showpieces
lessons.goal: Play two minor-key showpieces: the Habanera from Carmen and In the Hall of the Mountain King.
lessons.explain: Bizet's Habanera opens with a chromatic descent from D, D C# C B Bb A, over a D minor habanera bass, and its refrain turns to D major: check every accidental. Grieg's Mountain King, here in E minor, repeats its theme faster and louder each time, and its chromatic notes are part of the tune, not mistakes.
lessons.show: Notation and tab of the Habanera's opening descent with the accidentals highlighted; the Mountain King's tempo ramp as a graph from 60 to 160 bpm.
practice: Player: Habanera (Carmen), the student part, in wait mode, then at 60 and 72 bpm with the app's bass.
Player: In the Hall of the Mountain King with the tempo ramp; stop the ramp at your top clean tempo and note it.
Ear: listen-choice, is the Habanera's refrain in D minor or D major? (major).
Player: a third minor-key character piece, the Funeral March of a Marionette in D minor, 6/8, sneaky and short with sudden accents.

lessons.title: The Neapolitan and the augmented sixth
lessons.goal: Hear and play the Neapolitan sixth and the augmented sixth chord on their way to the dominant in A minor.
lessons.explain: Two chromatic chords make minor-key cadences dramatic. The Neapolitan, Bb major over D in A minor (bII in first inversion), moves to E7, its Bb falling toward the G# and A of the cadence. The German augmented sixth stacks F A C D#, and its F and D# close in on E from a half step on each side; on guitar it sounds exactly like F7, the same pitches with D# spelled Eb.
lessons.show: Chord boxes of Bb/D (xx0331) and E7 (020100); the German sixth on the staff, and the F7 (131211) grip that sounds the same.
practice: Mic (play-chord): Am, Bb/D, E7, Am. Without a microphone: chord-build.
Jam: jam track classical-neapolitan in A at 60 bpm.
Jam: jam track classical-augmented-sixth in A at 60 bpm: hear the F and the D# open out to E.

lessons.title: Bach in minor: the Prelude BWV 999
lessons.goal: Play Bach's Prelude BWV 999 in D minor: an even arpeggio over a bass, with a steady dominant pedal near the end.
lessons.explain: This prelude, written for lute and moved here from C minor to D minor, is one continuous arpeggio over a bass on each downbeat. Every bar is a chord: name each one before you play it, and you will memorise the piece within a week. The long dominant pedal near the end, the bass holding A while the harmony moves above it, must stay rock steady.
lessons.show: Notation and tab of the first 8 bars with each bar's chord written above it; the pedal-point section highlighted.
practice: Lesson: name the chord of each of the first 8 bars from its notes (chord-tones drill).
Player: two bars at a time in wait mode, then the first half at 50 bpm.
Player: the whole prelude at 60, then 72 bpm.

units.title: Classical technique
units.goal: Sit and pluck like a classical guitarist, play arpeggios, two voices, slurs, shifts, vibrato, tone colour and tremolo.

lessons.title: Classical position and the two strokes
lessons.goal: Sit in classical position and play free strokes and rest strokes with good tone.
lessons.explain: The classical position raises the guitar: left foot on a footstool (or a support under the guitar), the guitar on the left thigh, the headstock about eye level, so the fretting hand reaches the whole neck with a straight wrist. The free stroke (tirando) plucks the string and clears the next one; the rest stroke (apoyando) plucks and comes to rest on the next string toward string 6, for a fuller, louder tone. If you use nails, keep them smooth and shaped to follow the fingertip.
lessons.show: A posture card for the classical position (the drawing is in gaps); tab of Rest Stroke Scale (i-m): C major on strings 3 to 1 in first position.
practice: Technique: Posture: Sitting and Standing, the classical version.
Technique: Rest Stroke Scale (i-m) at 60 bpm, strictly alternating i and m.
Mic (play-note): one note with a free stroke, then with a rest stroke; compare the two on the level meter. Without a microphone: Record both.

lessons.title: Right-hand arpeggios
lessons.goal: Play right-hand arpeggio patterns evenly, from p-i-m to patterns with a, pinches and repeated fingers.
lessons.explain: Giuliani's 120 right-hand studies on just C and G7 remain the classic workout, each one isolating a pattern. Plant the fingers, keep the hand still and let each finger move from its knuckle. Evenness is the measure: no note louder, no note late.
lessons.show: Tab of three of the Giuliani studies (p-i-m-i, p-i-m-a-m-i and a pinch pattern) on C (x32010) and G7 (320001).
practice: Technique: Free-Stroke Arpeggios (p i m a), up the ladder.
Player: Arpeggio Studies from Op. 1, one study per day, at 60, then 72 bpm.
Player: Aguado's Estudio in A minor, a short arpeggio study with no barre chords, in wait mode, then at 66 bpm.
Record: one study; listen for any finger that is louder or late.

lessons.title: Two voices: Carulli and Sor
lessons.goal: Play two voices with thumb and fingers in Carulli's Andantino and Sor's first lesson.
lessons.explain: Two voices on one guitar: the thumb plays the bass, i and m the melody, and each voice keeps its own note lengths. In Carulli's Andantino, Op. 241 No. 5, bass and melody are clearly separated; Sor's Op. 60 No. 1 asks the two voices to move independently in first position. Sustain the bass notes for their full value, because lifting a finger early is the commonest fault.
lessons.show: Notation and tab of the first 8 bars of each piece, the bass with stems down and the melody with stems up.
practice: Player: Andantino, Op. 241 No. 5, in wait mode, then at 60 and 72 bpm.
Player: Lesson in C, Op. 60 No. 1, the first half in wait mode.
Player: both pieces complete at their target tempos; then the Minuet in G with both voices on one guitar, the bass line with the thumb.

lessons.title: Slurs, shifts and partial barres
lessons.goal: Play classical slurs, guided shifts and partial barres cleanly in repertoire.
lessons.explain: Slurs are the classical hammer-on and pull-off; the pull-off should pluck the string slightly toward the next string so the lower note rings as loudly as the first. A shift is safest with a guide finger that stays on its string and glides. Partial barres cover only the strings you need, which spares the hand.
lessons.show: Tab of Clean Position Shifts (finger 1 gliding on string 3 from string 3 fret 2 (A) to string 3 fret 5 (C) and on to string 3 fret 9 (E)); a slur exercise; a partial-barre passage from Lagrima.
practice: Technique: Clean Position Shifts at 60 bpm.
Technique: Hammer and Pull Chains, classical style, with the fingertips.
Player: Lagrima, the E major section, in wait mode.

lessons.title: Vibrato and tone colour
lessons.goal: Use classical vibrato and tone colour (sul ponticello, sul tasto and the warm middle) to shape a melody.
lessons.explain: Classical vibrato rocks the fingertip along the string, toward the nut and away, so the pitch moves slightly above and below the note. Tone colour comes from where you pluck: near the bridge (sul ponticello) is bright and glassy, over the soundhole is round, and near the neck (sul tasto) is soft and warm. Use both to make a melody speak, not as decoration.
lessons.show: A figure of the three plucking zones with audio of one phrase in each; tab of Classical Vibrato on string 1 fret 7 (B).
practice: Technique: Classical Vibrato, four waves per beat at 60 bpm.
Player: Adelita, the opening phrase three times, once in each tone colour.
Player: Adelita complete, with Tarrega's slides, at 60, then 72 bpm.

lessons.title: Tremolo
lessons.goal: Play an even p-a-m-i tremolo, four notes per beat, so the repeated notes sound like one long melody.
lessons.explain: In tremolo the thumb plays a bass note and a, m and i repeat one melody note three times: p-a-m-i, four even sixteenths per beat. Unevenness is the enemy, so practise slowly, moving the accent to each finger in turn. When it is even, Recuerdos de la Alhambra opens up to you, and not before.
lessons.show: Tab of Classical Tremolo (p a m i) on the open string 1 over open bass strings; a rhythm line of the four accent rotations.
practice: Technique: Classical Tremolo (p a m i) at 40 bpm, accenting p, then a, then m, then i.
Record: a minute of tremolo; are all four notes of each group the same length?
Player: Recuerdos de la Alhambra, the first 4 bars, at 40 bpm.

units.title: Classical repertoire
units.goal: Play studies, Baroque dances, Romantic pieces, Bach and a Spanish masterpiece, and plan a summit piece.

lessons.title: Studies of the masters
lessons.goal: Play two 19th-century studies at tempo: Carcassi's Op. 60 No. 7 and Sor's Op. 35 No. 22.
lessons.explain: Studies are pieces with a technical purpose and real music in them. Carcassi's A minor study builds right-hand stamina with repeated treble notes inside arpeggios, and most guitarists play those with i-m-a. Sor's B minor study asks for a singing melody inside arpeggiated chords; he marks it Allegretto, so do not let it drag.
lessons.show: The first 4 bars of each, with the fingering of the repeated notes and the melody voice highlighted.
practice: Player: Carcassi Op. 60 No. 7 in wait mode, then at 72, 88 and 100 bpm.
Player: Sor Op. 35 No. 22 in wait mode, then at 60 and 76 bpm.
Record: one of them; check that the melody is louder than the accompaniment.

lessons.title: Baroque dances
lessons.goal: Play Baroque dances with their proper stresses: a sarabande leaning on beat 2, a bourree from its upbeat, a canarios with hemiola.
lessons.explain: Each Baroque dance has its step pattern, and the music keeps it: sarabandes in 3/4 often lean on beat 2, bourrees start on an upbeat and move in two, and canarios alternate 6/8 and 3/4 groupings. Play the dance, not just the notes. Bach's Bourree in E minor is also true two-part counterpoint: two lines, each one finished.
lessons.show: Notation of the opening bars of the de Visee Sarabande, the Bach Bourree and the Sanz Canarios with the dance stresses marked.
practice: Player: Sarabande in D minor (de Visee) at 50, then 60 bpm, leaning on beat 2; then Handel's Sarabande the same way.
Player: Bourree in E minor, the first half in wait mode, then at 80 and 112 bpm.
Player: Canarios at 56, then 66 bpm (dotted-quarter beat), making the 6/8 and 3/4 groupings audible.

lessons.title: Romantic guitar and rubato
lessons.goal: Play Romantic guitar music with expressive timing: Tarrega's Lagrima and Mertz's Romanze.
lessons.explain: Romantic music asks for rubato: time borrowed and paid back within the phrase, never simply lost. Lagrima moves from E major to E minor and back, so let the minor section darken in tone as well as in harmony. Mertz's Romanze in E minor is a song without words, and its melody must sing above the arpeggios.
lessons.show: Notation of each opening phrase with a rubato curve drawn above it, showing where to stretch and where to move on.
practice: Player: Lagrima complete at 56, then 66 bpm, freeing the tempo only inside phrases.
Player: Romanze in E minor, section by section in wait mode, then at 54 bpm.
Record: the Romanze; does each phrase come back to the beat by its end? Chopin's Prelude No. 7 is a short companion piece in the same spirit.

lessons.title: Longer forms: Gran Vals and Coste
lessons.goal: Play a longer piece with several sections, Gran Vals or Coste's study Op. 38 No. 1, and shape its form.
lessons.explain: Longer pieces need a plan: know the sections, decide the dynamic of each, and mark where you breathe. Gran Vals has several themes; Coste's A minor study, about 67 bars long, is a Romantic study in position playing. Practise the hardest bars first, then the joins between sections, and only then the whole.
lessons.show: A form map of Gran Vals (its themes in order) with a dynamics plan and the joins between sections marked.
practice: Player: the hardest 4 bars of Gran Vals on loop at 60 bpm, then the joins between sections.
Player: Gran Vals complete at 90, then 120 bpm.
Player: Coste Op. 38 No. 1 section by section, then complete at 72 and 96 bpm.
Player: a third long form, variations: Sor's Variations on Les Folies d'Espagne, Op. 15a, the theme and the first variation, keeping the sarabande lean on beat 2 of the Folia harmony.

lessons.title: Bach: chorale and rondo
lessons.goal: Play Jesu, Joy of Man's Desiring and the Gavotte en Rondeau, balancing the main line against its accompaniment.
lessons.explain: In Jesu, Joy the flowing triplets are written in 3/4, so the line feels like 9/8, and the chorale melody inside it must be voiced louder so it is heard. The Gavotte en Rondeau comes from the third violin partita: a rondo whose refrain returns between episodes, here in E major with a light bass added. With Bach, clarity of voices comes first, beauty second and speed a distant third.
lessons.show: Notation of the opening of each, the chorale melody or the refrain highlighted; the rondo map: refrain, episode, refrain, episode, refrain.
practice: Player: Jesu, Joy, the first 8 bars in wait mode, then at 60 and 72 bpm.
Player: Gavotte en Rondeau, the refrain, at 50, then 66 bpm (half-note beat).
Record: one section; can you hear the chorale or the refrain clearly above the accompaniment?

lessons.title: A Spanish masterpiece: Asturias
lessons.goal: Play Asturias: a repeated-note pedal against a moving line, with its slow middle section.
lessons.explain: Asturias began as a piano piece by Albeniz in 1892 and became a guitar piece through transcription; here it is in E minor. Its opening alternates a moving line with the open B string as a pedal, fast and even, and the middle section slows down and sings. Build it from the pedal outward: the open B must be metronomic before the line above it can be free.
lessons.show: Tab of the opening 4 bars with the pedal notes on the open string 2 (B) highlighted; a form map with the slow middle section.
practice: Technique: the pedal alone on the open string 2 (B), alternating fingers, at 80 bpm; then add the moving line.
Player: the opening section on loop at 80, 100, then 120 bpm.
Player: the middle section at a slow, singing tempo; then the whole piece.

lessons.title: Choose a summit
lessons.goal: Choose one summit piece, the Cello Suite Prelude, the E major Prelude BWV 1006a, Recuerdos de la Alhambra or the Chaconne, and plan three months of study.
lessons.explain: These are pieces that take months and repay years. The Cello Suite Prelude is a single line that implies its harmony and builds to a long climax; the E major Prelude from BWV 1006a races through long passages that alternate a moving line with the open string 1; Recuerdos is the tremolo piece; the Chaconne is a set of variations on a repeating harmony, well over ten minutes of music. Choose one, divide it into sections and plan weekly targets: learn, then shape, then perform.
lessons.show: A three-month plan template: weeks 1 to 4, learn the notes section by section; weeks 5 to 8, tempo and voicing; weeks 9 to 12, shaping and performance run-throughs.
practice: Practice Plan: build the three-month plan for your chosen piece, with a target for every week.
Player: the first section of your piece in wait mode.
Record: the first section at the end of week 1, to compare with week 12. For tremolo players, the Concert Tremolo Etude is the preparation for Recuerdos.

units.title: Sight-reading and rhythm
units.goal: Read fluently in any position, sight-read daily, and play odd meters, hemiola and polyrhythm.

lessons.title: Reading in fifth position
lessons.goal: Read fluently in fifth position, in C major and F major.
lessons.explain: Positions are how a reader stays fluent: the hand stays still and the notes fall under its four fingers. In fifth position finger 1 is at fret 5, and the Bb you know at string 3 fret 3 (Bb) is now played at string 4 fret 8 (Bb). Read by interval as well as by name: a step up on the staff is usually the next finger or the next string.
lessons.show: Fretboard figure of fifth position with the natural notes and Bb; a staff with the same notes.
practice: Lesson: staff-read in fifth position, 10 notes.
Player: Reading: Fifth Position and Flats, notation only, at sight at 60 bpm, then once more.
Fretboard: the fifth-position note game.

lessons.title: Seventh position, and choosing positions
lessons.goal: Read in seventh position and choose the position for a passage yourself.
lessons.explain: Seventh position covers frets 7 to 10 and suits G major and E minor. Choosing a position is a decision: where does the passage lie with the fewest shifts, and where does it sound best? Write your choice into the music; a fingering decided once saves a hundred hesitations.
lessons.show: Fretboard figure of seventh position; one passage shown in two possible positions, with the shifts counted for each.
practice: Player: Reading: Seventh Position at sight at 60 bpm, the 4/4 and the 6/8 sections.
Lesson: choice, for this 4-bar phrase, which position needs no shift?
Player: Reading: Seventh Position, the passages with sixteenth notes, at 50 bpm.

lessons.title: A sight-reading routine
lessons.goal: Follow a daily sight-reading routine: preview first, keep the beat, never stop.
lessons.explain: Sight-reading is a different skill from reading slowly: you must keep going. Before playing, take thirty seconds: key, meter, highest and lowest notes, and any rhythm that looks hard. Then play at a tempo slow enough that you never stop, with your eyes a little ahead; ten minutes of new material every day beats an hour once a week.
lessons.show: The 30-second preview checklist; a sight-reading score card (bars played without stopping).
practice: Player: one 8-bar passage you have never played, every day, at sight at 60 bpm with the tab hidden: a new section of a reading study, or a songbook melody you do not know.
Player: Duet: Baroque-Style Duo in D minor at sight, the upper voice, with the app playing the bass.
Practice Plan: add a daily 10-minute sight-reading block.

lessons.title: Reading through the whole neck
lessons.goal: Read a piece that moves through positions I, V, VII, IX and XII with changing meters.
lessons.explain: Real music does not stay in one position. Find the shifts in advance, mark them, and practise each shift as a tiny exercise of its own: the last note before it and the first note after it. The Shifting study changes meter between 4/4, 3/4 and 6/8 and uses keys with up to four sharps or flats, so check each key signature before you begin.
lessons.show: Notation of the first 8 bars of the Shifting study with the shift points and target fingers marked.
practice: Player: Reading: Shifting Through the Neck, the shift points alone, on loop.
Player: the whole study at 50, then 66 bpm.
Lesson: the key-signature drill up to four sharps and four flats.

lessons.title: Fives and sevens
lessons.goal: Feel and play in 5/4 and 7/8 as groups of twos and threes.
lessons.explain: An odd meter is felt as unequal groups: 5/4 as 3+2 or 2+3, 7/8 as 2+2+3, 3+2+2 or 2+3+2. Count the groups, not the total: in 7/8 as 2+2+3, say one-two, one-two, one-two-three. Accent the first note of each group and the meter suddenly feels natural.
lessons.show: Rhythm lines of 5/4 (3+2) and 7/8 (2+2+3) with the group accents; metronome settings with an accent at the start of each group.
practice: Rhythm: tap 5/4 as 3+2, then as 2+3; then 7/8 as 2+2+3.
Metronome: 7/8 at 160 eighth notes per minute with accents on eighths 1, 3 and 5; strum Em on every eighth, accenting the groups.
Technique: Odd Meters: 5/4 and 7/8, up its ladder: Em in 5/4 grouped 3+2 and then 2+3, Am in 7/8 grouped 2+2+3 and then 3+2+2.
Create: write a 2-bar riff in 7/8 on A minor pentatonic and loop it.

lessons.title: Hemiola and three against two
lessons.goal: Play hemiola (3/4 against 6/8) and the three-against-two polyrhythm cleanly.
lessons.explain: Hemiola regroups six beats as two threes or three twos: 6/8 against 3/4, the heartbeat of Sanz's Canarios and of much Latin American music. Three against two plays both at once: one part plays three even notes while the other plays two, and they meet on the beat. Say nice cup of tea and the rhythm falls into place.
lessons.show: Rhythm lines of 6/8 and 3/4 over the same six eighth notes; the 3:2 grid with the combined rhythm; tab of the hemiola bars of Canarios.
practice: Rhythm: tap three with one hand and two with the other at 60 bpm, saying nice cup of tea.
Mic (play-phrase): the thumb in two and the fingers in three, on open strings. Without a microphone: Rhythm, the same as a two-hand tap.
Player: Canarios at 66 bpm, making the 3/4 bars audible against the 6/8; then the solea cycle's 3+3+2+2+2 again.

units.title: Composition and arranging
units.goal: Write progressions and melodies, arrange for solo guitar, put piano music on the guitar, write counterpoint, and compose in an open tuning.

lessons.title: Writing a progression
lessons.goal: Write your own progression using chord functions, a borrowed chord and a clear cadence.
lessons.explain: A progression is a journey from home and back: tonic, away (subdominant), tension (dominant), home. Within that, colour is free: borrow iv or bVII from the parallel minor, add a secondary dominant, delay the cadence with a deceptive vi. Write four bars that leave home and four that return, and play them to someone who knows no theory: if they feel the ending, it works.
lessons.show: A function map (tonic, subdominant, dominant) with the diatonic chords of C and the borrowed chords Fm, Ab and Bb; Elena's original example progression: C | Am | Fm | G7 | C.
practice: Create: write an 8-bar progression in C with at least one borrowed chord and one cadence.
Jam: jam track borrowed-iv-minor in C at 72 bpm, to hear the minor iv in context.
Record: your progression strummed, then with a melody improvised over it.

lessons.title: Writing a melody
lessons.goal: Write an 8-bar melody with a clear phrase structure: a question, an answer and a high point.
lessons.explain: A period is two phrases, a question and an answer: the first ends open (on a half cadence, or on a note other than the tonic), the second ends closed on the tonic. Give the melody one high point, roughly two thirds of the way through, and approach it by step. Repetition is your friend: state a motif, repeat it, then vary it.
lessons.show: An original 8-bar period by Elena in G with the motif, the half cadence in bar 4, the high point in bar 6 and the authentic cadence in bar 8 marked.
practice: Create: write an 8-bar period over your progression from the last lesson, or over I-IV-V-I.
Scan: write it out by hand and photograph it, or type it in as tab, so the Player can play it back to you.
Record: perform it over the backing and judge: does bar 4 ask and bar 8 answer?

lessons.title: Arranging a melody for solo guitar
lessons.goal: Arrange a traditional melody for solo guitar: choose the key, put the melody on top, add a bass, then fill in.
lessons.explain: Choose the key that puts the melody on the top strings and the bass on open strings where possible; for many tunes that means D, G, A, E or C. Then work in layers: the melody alone; the melody with a bass note on each strong beat; then inner notes only where the hand allows. Simpler is usually better: two good voices beat four crowded ones.
lessons.show: Three layers of an arrangement of The Ash Grove in G as tab: melody only, melody and bass, and the full setting.
practice: Player: Danny Boy (chord melody) as a model: play its first 8 bars and name the three layers, melody, bass and filling, as you hear them.
Create: arrange Shenandoah, or another traditional tune from the songbook, in D: layer 1, then layer 2, then layer 3.
Scan: write it out or type it in as tab so the Player can play it back.
Record: your arrangement, and compare it with your plan.

lessons.title: Piano music on the guitar: ragtime
lessons.goal: Play ragtime on guitar, a syncopated melody over an alternating bass, in The Entertainer.
lessons.explain: Joplin wrote for piano, and a guitar can carry both hands only if the arrangement chooses well: the thumb alternates the bass on the beats, the syncopated melody sits on top, and inner notes go when the hand cannot reach them. Joplin marked The Entertainer Not fast; take him at his word. Maple Leaf Rag, moved to G major, is the next summit.
lessons.show: Notation and tab of the first 4 bars of the A strain of The Entertainer, the bass with stems down and the melody with stems up, with the syncopations marked.
practice: Player: The Entertainer, the A strain, in wait mode, then at 56 and 72 bpm.
Player: the B strain the same way, then the whole arrangement.
Player: Maple Leaf Rag, the A strain in wait mode, as a long-term project.

lessons.title: Counterpoint: the invention
lessons.goal: Play, and then write, two-voice counterpoint: an invention with a subject imitated between bass and treble.
lessons.explain: Counterpoint is two melodies that are each complete and that fit together: contrary motion, independent rhythms and consonances on the strong beats. The Two-Voice Invention study states a short subject in one voice and imitates it in the other, modulates to G major and returns to E minor. Play it, then write eight bars of your own on the same plan.
lessons.show: Notation of the first 4 bars of the invention with the subject bracketed in each voice.
practice: Player: Bach's Bourree in E minor, the first half, as a model: the bass line alone, the treble alone, then both, hearing each line as a finished melody.
Player: Two-Voice Invention for Solo Guitar, section by section, in wait mode.
Player: the whole invention at 50, then 66 bpm.
Create: an 8-bar two-voice piece: a 2-bar subject in the treble, imitated in the bass.

lessons.title: The fugue exposition
lessons.goal: Play a fugue exposition: the subject, the answer at the fifth, and a third entry with a countersubject.
lessons.explain: A fugue exposition introduces its subject in each voice in turn: the subject in the tonic, the answer at the fifth, then a third entry, while the earlier voices carry on with a countersubject. On one guitar that means three voices sharing six strings, so keep each entry clear by its register and its tone colour.
lessons.show: Notation of the Fugue Exposition with each entry labelled (subject, answer, third entry) and the countersubject coloured; drop D tuning marked if the arrangement uses it.
practice: Player: Fugue Exposition for Solo Guitar, each entry alone, then two voices together.
Player: the whole exposition, slowly.
Away from the guitar: sing the subject, then hum it while you play the countersubject.

lessons.title: Composing in DADGAD
lessons.goal: Compose in DADGAD with open strings as drones, and play the DADGAD Air.
lessons.explain: DADGAD (D A D G A D from string 6 to string 1) is the Celtic guitarist's tuning: open strings ring as drones under melodies, and the open chord is neither major nor minor until a finger adds the third. Retune strings 6, 2 and 1 down a whole step. Then forget your shapes and listen.
lessons.show: A tuning card (D A D G A D); tab of the DADGAD Air with every fret checked in this tuning; a fretboard figure of the D major scale in DADGAD at frets 0 to 5.
practice: Tuner: retune to DADGAD (strings 6, 2 and 1 down a whole step).
Player: DADGAD Air at 60, then 80 bpm.
Create: an 8-bar air of your own in DADGAD with at least two open strings as drones; then Tuner, back to standard.

units.title: Transcription and performance
units.goal: Transcribe melodies, harmony and solos by ear, memorise securely, and prepare and give a recital.

lessons.title: Transcribing a melody
lessons.goal: Transcribe a melody by ear into notation: key, meter, rhythm and pitch.
lessons.explain: Transcription trains the ear more than anything else. Work in passes: first the form and the key, then the rhythm of one phrase (tap it), then the pitches, then check every note against the recording. Write it in notation, because the act of writing forces you to decide.
lessons.show: Audio of an original 8-bar melody by Elena with a loop control; an empty staff; the reveal at the end.
practice: Ear: the melodic dictation drill, four bars at a time.
Ear: transcribe Elena's 8-bar melody: key, meter, rhythm, then pitches.
Away from the guitar: write it out, compare it with the reveal and count your errors.

lessons.title: Transcribing harmony
lessons.goal: Transcribe a chord progression by ear: the bass line first, then the qualities, then the extensions.
lessons.explain: Harmony transcription works from the bottom up. Find the bass line and sing it: most of the time it gives you the roots. Then decide each chord's quality (major, minor, dominant, diminished), and only then listen for sevenths and extensions.
lessons.show: Audio of a progression from the catalog; an empty chart with rows for the bass, the quality and the extensions.
practice: Ear: bass-line dictation.
Ear: the chord-quality drill with sevenths.
Jam: Elena plays jam track jazz-i-vi7-ii-v in C, then jam track classical-deceptive in C, with the chart hidden: write each progression, then reveal it.

lessons.title: Transcribing a solo
lessons.goal: Transcribe a short improvised solo, learn to play it, and analyse what makes it work.
lessons.explain: Learning a solo by ear teaches phrasing, which no book can. Transcribe a short solo, Elena's example or a recording you own for your private study, learn it at tempo, then analyse it: where does it target chord tones, where does it leave space, what is its motif? Then write a solo of your own in the same style.
lessons.show: Audio of an original two-chorus blues solo by Elena with a loop control; an empty tab and staff.
practice: Ear: transcribe Elena's solo two bars at a time.
Player: play your transcription along with the audio, then without it.
Away from the guitar: annotate it: chord tones on strong beats, motifs, space, techniques.

lessons.title: Memorising securely
lessons.goal: Memorise a piece securely, with several kinds of memory backing each other up.
lessons.explain: Finger memory alone can fail under pressure, and it tends to fail at the worst moment. Back it up with aural memory (you can sing it), visual memory (you see the shapes and the score) and analytical memory (you know the harmony and the form). Test it: start from any section, play it in your head away from the guitar, and write out the form.
lessons.show: A memory map of the piece you are learning (Lagrima or the Prelude BWV 999 make good first subjects): its form, keys and cadences, and a starting point for each section.
practice: Away from the guitar: write the form and the chords of your current piece from memory.
Player: pick five bars at random and start the piece from each of them.
Away from the guitar: play the first section in your head, at tempo, with your eyes closed.

lessons.title: Preparing to perform
lessons.goal: Prepare for performance: practise performing, manage nerves and recover from mistakes.
lessons.explain: Nerves are normal and partly useful: they mean you care. What helps is preparation that includes performing: run-throughs for a friend or for the recorder, with no restarts allowed. On the day, slow your breathing, start a touch slower than you think, and if something goes wrong keep the beat and rejoin at the next phrase; the audience follows your confidence, not your notes.
lessons.show: A performance-preparation checklist: three run-throughs a week for the month before, one dress rehearsal, a warm-up plan, and recovery points marked in the score.
practice: Record: a complete run-through with no restarts, as if live.
Away from the guitar: mark three recovery points in your piece where you can rejoin.
With others: play your piece for one person this week.

lessons.title: The recital
lessons.goal: Give a 15-minute recital of contrasting pieces and write your own plan for the next year.
lessons.explain: A recital is a programme, not a list: open with something secure, put the most demanding piece in the middle, and end with something that leaves them smiling. Include one piece of your own, one classical piece, and one jazz or blues performance. Afterwards write your plan for the next year: you no longer need a teacher to tell you what is next, only the habit of asking.
lessons.show: A programme builder with slots for an opener, a centrepiece, an original, a jazz or blues piece and a closer, timed to about 15 minutes; for example Gran Vals to open, Asturias as the centrepiece and the jazz-ballad chord melody as the jazz piece.
practice: Practice Plan: build the programme and a four-week preparation schedule.
Record: the full recital, start to finish, introducing each piece in one sentence.
Practice Plan: write your goals for the next year: repertoire, technique, theory and ear.
